bundle.domain: Comprehensive diabetes medical evaluation — the diabetes STATUS / history record (ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 Section 4, cross-checked against WHO Classification of Diabetes Mellitus 2019 and WHO PEN 2020). Complication screening (eye, foot, kidney) deliberately excluded.

features.whyItMatters: Age <35 at onset is one of the features ADA lists as most useful for identifying type 1 diabetes, and drives the decision to start/continue insulin rather than oral agents. ADA states misdiagnosis occurs in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Diabetes history: characteristics at onset) and Section 2 (AABBCC approach)
features.standardVersion: Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl.1):S61–S88, doi 10.2337/dc26-S004; Section 2 at S27–S49, doi 10.2337/dc26-S002
features.quote: Characteristics at onset (e.g., age and symptoms and/or signs)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Frequently unknown or approximate where the diagnosis was made at another facility with no transferable record; capture alongside diagnosis_date_precision rather than forcing a number.

features.whyItMatters: Duration >10 years is an explicit ADA trigger for bone mineral density testing in postmenopausal women and men aged >=50 (Table 4.4), and duration drives how aggressively to pursue complication surveillance.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.4 (Individuals who should receive BMD testing)
features.quote: Diabetes duration >10 years
features.resourceLimitedNote: Derive from age_at_diagnosis_years where an exact date is unavailable; do not require a calendar date.

features.display: How precisely the diagnosis date is known

options.display: Approximate — patient reports 'about N years ago'

features.whyItMatters: Determines whether duration-based thresholds (e.g. the >10 year BMD trigger) may be acted on or must be treated as uncertain, preventing a soft recollection being hardened into a screening decision.
features.standard: Implementation adaptation — no ADA/WHO source defines this field
features.resourceLimitedNote: This is the common case, not the exception, where care has moved between facilities without records.

features.whyItMatters: Unintentional weight loss and ketoacidosis at presentation are two of the features ADA names as most useful for identifying type 1 diabetes; an asymptomatic laboratory-only diagnosis instead demands confirmatory retesting before committing the person to lifelong therapy.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 Section 2 (diagnostic tests, features useful in determining type 1) and Section 4 Table 4.1; symptom list cross-checked against WHO PEN 2020 diabetes module
features.quote: The features most useful in determination of type 1 diabetes include younger age at diagnosis (<35 years), lower BMI (<25 kg/m 2 ), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and plasma glucose >360 mg/dL (>20 mmol/L) at presentation

features.display: Test on which the diagnosis was made

options.display: Random plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) with classic symptoms
2-h plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L on 75 g OGTT

features.whyItMatters: ADA requires two abnormal results in the absence of unequivocal hyperglycaemia. If the only evidence is a single point-of-care reading or an unrecorded test, the correct next action is confirmatory testing, not treatment escalation — and a diagnosis first made in pregnancy must be reclassified postpartum.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Table 2.1 (Criteria for the diagnosis of diabetes in nonpregnant individuals); point-of-care option per WHO PEN 2020
features.quote: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests, which may be obtained at the same time (e.g., A1C and FPG), or the same test at two different time points.
features.requires: Laboratory glucose or NGSP-certified A1C for most options; capillary meter for the point-of-care option
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO PEN states FPG is the most practical test in low-resource settings on cost grounds and that point-of-care devices may be used to diagnose diabetes if laboratory services are not available — so poc_capillary_only must be a first-class option, not an error state.

features.display: Diagnosis confirmed by a second abnormal result
features.whyItMatters: An unconfirmed asymptomatic diagnosis is the single commonest reversible error in a transferred diabetes record; recording 'no' schedules a confirmatory test instead of a lifetime of medication.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2, Table 2.1 footnote
features.quote: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests
features.resourceLimitedNote: Repeat laboratory testing may not be affordable; a documented 'no' should route to the cheapest confirmatory option (repeat FPG) rather than an A1C.

features.display: Diabetes type as recorded by a prior clinician

options.display: Slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes of adults (previously LADA)
Other genetic syndrome associated with diabetes

features.whyItMatters: The recorded type decides whether insulin may ever be withdrawn, and whether autoimmune thyroid and coeliac screening are indicated (ADA recs 4.6, 4.7 apply to type 1 only). ADA warns classification at presentation is often wrong, so the recorded label must be stored as a claim, never as ground truth.
features.standard: WHO Classification of Diabetes Mellitus 2019, Table 1; ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 Section 2
features.quote: Unclassified diabetes — Used to describe diabetes that does not clearly fit into other categories. This category should be used temporarily when there is not a clear diagnostic category especially close to the time of diagnosis
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO chose this classification precisely because it uses 'easy and readily available clinical parameters' rather than C-peptide or autoantibodies; keep 'unclassified' selectable so clinicians are not forced into a false binary.

features.display: Where the recorded type came from

options.display: Documented in a clinical record by a clinician
Inferred by this service, not previously documented

features.whyItMatters: Keeps a prior clinician's label separate from any inference this tool makes, so a suggested reclassification (e.g. type 2 to type 1) is presented as a proposal to a clinician rather than silently overwriting the record. ADA notes misdiagnosis in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes.
features.standard: Implementation adaptation — supported by, but not defined in, ADA SoC 2026 Section 2

features.whyItMatters: Decides whether a doubtful type label can actually be resolved or must be managed clinically; where none are available, treatment must be driven by insulin requirement and ketosis history rather than by a laboratory reclassification that will never arrive.
features.standard: WHO Classification of Diabetes Mellitus 2019, section 2.4
features.quote: additional diagnostic tests that are either not standardized or not routinely available in most clinical settings, e.g. measurement of C-peptide, β-cell-specific autoantibodies
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO explicitly designed the 2019 classification so it does not depend on these; expect 'none' to be the default answer in most district facilities. Never gate a treatment recommendation on a result the site cannot obtain.

options.display: Insulin started within 1 year of diagnosis
Insulin started more than 1 year after diagnosis

features.whyItMatters: Distinguishes type 1 from ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes, where ADA states the initial insulin requirement is generally transient — i.e. it decides whether insulin can be safely withdrawn or must never be interrupted.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 Section 2; WHO Classification of Diabetes Mellitus 2019
features.quote: The initial requirement for insulin replacement therapy in individuals presenting with ketosis-prone diabetes is generally transient.
features.resourceLimitedNote: 'Insulin started then stopped' must be distinguished from insulin stopped because of stockout or cost — pair with medication_rationing.

features.whyItMatters: ADA lists prior history of hyperglycaemic crises as a risk factor for further hyperglycaemic crises; a positive count changes management to sick-day rules, never omitting basal insulin, ketone testing at home, and structured self-management education, which ADA states reduces DKA admissions.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 Section 6 (risk factors for hyperglycemic crises); Section 4 Table 4.1 (past hospitalizations)
features.quote: Prior history of hyperglycemic crises
features.resourceLimitedNote: Where admissions occurred at another facility, count is patient-reported; record as reported rather than discarding it.

features.whyItMatters: Recent or recurrent DKA moves management beyond dose adjustment — ADA states those with recurrent DKA often require extensive multisystemic behavioural interventions, and that most DKA occurs in people with established, not new, diabetes.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6
features.quote: those with recurrent DKA often require extensive multisystemic behavioral interventions

features.whyItMatters: Same ADA risk-factor logic as DKA, but HHS identifies a different phenotype (usually type 2, older, higher mortality) and changes the sick-day and hydration counselling given, and the threshold for admitting rather than treating as an outpatient.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6 (risk factors for hyperglycemic crises)
features.quote: Prior history of hyperglycemic crises

features.display: Recorded precipitant of the most recent hyperglycaemic crisis
features.whyItMatters: The precipitant, not the event, determines the intervention: rationing calls for a supply and financing fix, infection for sick-day rules, an SGLT2 inhibitor for drug withdrawal. Escalating the insulin dose is the wrong response to all three.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6 (risk factors for hyperglycemic crises table)
features.quote: Alcohol and/or substance use / High A1C level / Insulin rationing / SGLT2 (SGLT1/2) inhibitor use / Social determinants of health
features.resourceLimitedNote: Insulin rationing and stockout-driven interruption are likely to be the dominant precipitants in a Ugandan public-sector cohort; make them one-tap options rather than free text.

features.display: Level 3 (severe) hypoglycaemia episodes in the last 12 months
features.whyItMatters: ADA rec 6.19: one or more episodes of level 2 or 3 hypoglycaemia should prompt reevaluation of the treatment plan, including deintensifying or switching diabetes medications. This field is the direct trigger for stopping a sulfonylurea or reducing insulin.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Table 6.4 (Classification of hypoglycemia) and Recommendation 6.19
features.quote: Level 3 — A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia, irrespective of glucose level
features.resourceLimitedNote: Level 3 is defined by needing another person's help, NOT by a glucose value — so it is fully recordable without a meter. This is the one hypoglycaemia field that works everywhere.

features.display: Level 2 or 3 hypoglycaemia within the past 3–6 months
features.whyItMatters: ADA Table 6.5 lists this as a MAJOR clinical risk factor for hypoglycaemia; per rec 6.13 it must be weighed when choosing diabetes medicines and glycaemic goals — typically switching away from sulfonylureas and relaxing the A1C target.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Table 6.5 (major clinical and biological risk factors) and Recommendation 6.13
features.quote: Recent (within the past 3–6 months) level 2 or 3 hypoglycemia
features.requires: Glucose meter or CGM to confirm a level 2 (<3.0 mmol/L) event
features.resourceLimitedNote: Level 2 requires a measured glucose <3.0 mmol/L; without strips this is unrecordable. Allow 'symptomatic episodes, not measured' as a separate answer rather than forcing false negatives.

options.display: Always feels low glucose coming on
Not applicable — not at risk of hypoglycaemia

features.whyItMatters: ADA rec 6.11 requires at least annual screening; impaired awareness dramatically increases risk of level 3 hypoglycaemia and changes the plan to a less stringent glycaemic goal, structured education, glucagon provision and driving advice.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Recommendation 6.11 and single-question screen
features.quote: clinicians can ask a single question based on these tools such as “Can you always feel when your blood glucose is low?” and follow “No” responses with a more detailed evaluation
features.resourceLimitedNote: Pure history — the single-question screen needs no equipment and is the correct default where the Gold or Clarke instruments cannot be licensed.

features.display: Glucagon prescribed and available at home
features.whyItMatters: ADA rec 6.16 says glucagon should be prescribed for all individuals taking insulin or at high risk of hypoglycaemia; a 'no' generates a prescription and household training, or, where glucagon is unobtainable, an explicit alternative rescue plan.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6, Recommendation 6.16
features.quote: Glucagon should be prescribed for all individuals taking insulin or at high risk for hypoglycemia.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Glucagon is frequently unavailable or unaffordable outside referral hospitals; a 'no' here should not fire a nagging alert but should route to oral glucose/first-aid counselling, which ADA rec 6.17 also covers.

features.whyItMatters: Prevents re-trialling an agent that has already failed or been stopped for intolerance, and reveals whether apparent treatment failure was a dose problem or an access problem.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1
features.quote: Review of previous treatment plans and response

features.whyItMatters: Directly contraindicates re-prescribing; recorded at initial and every follow-up visit in the ADA table.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Medications and vaccinations)
features.quote: Medication intolerance or side effects

features.whyItMatters: ADA records this at every visit, and lists insulin rationing as a risk factor for hyperglycaemic crisis. A 'yes' means the correct response to poor control is to fix supply or cost — escalating the dose of a medicine the person cannot obtain will cause DKA, not improvement.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1; Section 6 hyperglycaemic crisis risk factors
features.quote: Medication-taking behavior, including rationing of medications and/or medical equipment
features.resourceLimitedNote: This is arguably the single highest-yield field in the whole record for a Ugandan public-sector cohort and should be asked non-judgementally at every visit, not annually.

features.display: Complementary, traditional or alternative medicine use
features.whyItMatters: Recorded by ADA at every visit; explains otherwise unexplained hypoglycaemia or hepatic derangement, and identifies people who have substituted herbal treatment for insulin — a direct DKA risk.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1
features.quote: Complementary and alternative medicine use
features.resourceLimitedNote: Concurrent use of traditional herbal preparations is common and under-disclosed; phrase the prompt neutrally.

options.display: Nurse or clinical officer at a health centre

features.whyItMatters: WHO PEN requires referral to a higher-level facility to start insulin; knowing the prescriber's level tells you whether an insulin recommendation can be actioned here or needs a referral, and whether a person is effectively self-medicating.
features.standard: Adapted for service delivery — supported by WHO PEN 2020 referral rule and ADA SoC 2026 Table 4.1 'Visits to specialists' / rec 4.2 interprofessional team, but the option list is not from a guideline
features.quote: REFER to higher-level health care facility for starting insulin
features.resourceLimitedNote: Cadre-specific prescribing rights vary by country; the option list must be configurable per deployment.

features.display: Where diabetes medicines are actually collected
features.whyItMatters: Determines whether the review interval can be aligned to the refill journey; if medicines are collected somewhere other than where the person is reviewed, a 3-month review is two trips, and non-collection will be misread as non-adherence.
features.standard: Implementation adaptation — no guideline source found for this field
features.resourceLimitedNote: Directly relevant where transport cost is the binding constraint; ADA's SDOH row names transportation access but does not model a collection point.

features.whyItMatters: Sets the recall date and identifies who is overdue. ADA sets at least 3–6 monthly then at least annually; WHO PEN's diabetes protocol reassesses every 3 months. This is the field that converts a guideline into an actual appointment.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4; cross-checked against WHO PEN 2020 diabetes protocol
features.quote: Follow-up visits should occur at least every 3–6 months individualized to the person and then at least annually.
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO PEN's 3-monthly reassessment is the more realistic anchor where each visit costs the patient a day's income and a fare; consider aligning the interval to the medicine supply duration.

features.display: Changes in medical or family history since last visit
features.whyItMatters: The ADA interval-history row, recorded at every follow-up and annual visit; new comorbidity or a new first-degree diagnosis changes drug choice and screening.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Interval history)
features.quote: Changes in medical or family history since last visit

features.whyItMatters: ADA Table 4.3 recommends hepatitis B vaccination for adults with diabetes aged under 60 (GRADE evidence type 1) — the highest-graded vaccine in the diabetes schedule. A 'no' or 'incomplete' generates a dose today.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.3 (vaccinations) and Recommendation 4.5
features.quote: Adults with diabetes aged <60 years; for adults aged ≥60 years, hepatitis B vaccine may be administered at the discretion of the treating clinician based on the person’s likelihood of acquiring hepatitis B infection
features.resourceLimitedNote: Adult hepatitis B vaccination is often not funded in national EPI programmes even where infant vaccination is; record status but do not assume availability.

features.whyItMatters: ADA states influenza vaccination in people with diabetes significantly reduces influenza and diabetes-related hospital admissions; a 'not received' triggers an offer, and Table 4.3 specifically directs that live attenuated influenza vaccine not be used.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.3
features.quote: All people with diabetes advised to receive a trivalent influenza vaccine and not to receive live attenuated influenza vaccine
features.resourceLimitedNote: Seasonal influenza vaccine is not routinely available in many low-income public health systems and 'season' is not well defined in equatorial countries; keep 'not available at this site' as an explicit answer so the field does not generate undeliverable advice.

features.whyItMatters: Which pneumococcal product was previously given determines what, if anything, is due next — ADA states PPSV23 is not indicated after PCV20, and that PPSV23 should follow PCV15 by at least 1 year. Recording only 'vaccinated' makes the next dose undecidable.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.3
features.quote: One dose is recommended for those who previously received PCV13; if PCV15 was used, follow with PPSV23 ≥1 year later; PPSV23 is not indicated after PCV20
features.resourceLimitedNote: The ADA schedule is CDC/ACIP-specific. Adult pneumococcal vaccine is largely unavailable in low-income public sectors; the field is still worth recording for people vaccinated abroad or privately.

options.display: Up to date with currently recommended doses

features.whyItMatters: ADA states people with diabetes are more likely to become severely ill with COVID-19 and recommends vaccination with an appropriate number of doses; the recorded status decides whether a dose is offered at this visit.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.3 and vaccination text
features.quote: People with underlying medical conditions, including diabetes, are more likely to become severely ill with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).
features.resourceLimitedNote: 'Up to date' is defined against a national schedule that changes; store the date and product rather than deriving currency from a hard-coded rule.

features.whyItMatters: Each has a distinct ADA-specified trigger — Tdap booster every 10 years, zoster at >=50 years, RSV at >=75 or >=60 at high risk — so recording them collapses three separate 'is anything due?' decisions into one field.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.3
features.quote: Zoster — ≥50 years of age — Two-dose Shingrix, even if previously vaccinated
features.requires: Tdap, recombinant zoster and RSV vaccines
features.resourceLimitedNote: Zoster and RSV vaccines are effectively unobtainable in most low-income public sectors; keep them recordable but never let their absence block a care plan.

features.whyItMatters: Part of the ADA initial evaluation and one of the AABBCC classification cues; a strong multigenerational history in a lean young person without autoantibodies raises monogenic diabetes, which may be treated with sulfonylurea rather than insulin.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Family history)
features.quote: Family history of diabetes in a first-degree relative
features.resourceLimitedNote: Pure history, no equipment — one of the few classification cues fully available at a district facility.

features.whyItMatters: Raises the prior probability of type 1 / slowly evolving immune-mediated diabetes and of the associated conditions ADA tells you to screen for — autoimmune thyroid disease (rec 4.6) and coeliac disease (rec 4.7).
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Family history) and Recommendations 4.6, 4.7
features.quote: Family history of autoimmune disorders

features.whyItMatters: Existing autoimmune disease reclassifies a person labelled type 2 towards type 1, and directly triggers ADA rec 4.6 (thyroid screening soon after type 1 diagnosis) and rec 4.7 (coeliac screening where symptoms or suspicion exist).
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 and Recommendations 4.6, 4.7
features.quote: Personal history of autoimmune disease

features.whyItMatters: ADA records this as part of the initial and annual evaluation. It decides which glycaemic measure is trustworthy: where a haemoglobinopathy is present, the A1C result cannot be used to set or judge the glycaemic target and fasting/random plasma glucose must be used instead.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1
features.quote: Presence of hemoglobinopathies or anemias
features.requires: Haemoglobin electrophoresis or sickling test to confirm; history alone otherwise
features.resourceLimitedNote: High-yield in sub-Saharan Africa where sickle cell trait and disease are common and A1C is already the scarcer test. Note: ADA Table 4.1 only directs that this be recorded — the inference that A1C becomes unreliable is standard clinical practice that I did not verify in a retrieved document this pass.

features.display: Measure used to assess glycaemic status
features.whyItMatters: WHO PEN states that if HbA1c is not available, fasting plasma glucose should be used as the treatment target. Recording which measure is in use prevents the tool from judging control against a target that does not apply, and from ordering a test the site cannot run.
features.standard: WHO PEN 2020 diabetes module (treatment goal); ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 laboratory evaluation
features.quote: If HbA1c is not available, fasting plasma glucose (FPG)
features.requires: NGSP-certified A1C assay, or laboratory/point-of-care glucose
features.resourceLimitedNote: A1C is often unavailable or paid out of pocket. WHO PEN treats FPG as the practical primary measure — the record must support a full care plan built on FPG alone.

features.whyItMatters: ADA repeats A1C at a visit only if a result is not available from the past 3 months, so the stored value and date decide whether to order the test today; A1C >8% is also a listed diabetes-specific trigger for bone mineral density testing (Table 4.4).
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Laboratory evaluation) and Table 4.4
features.quote: A1C, if the results are not available within the past 3 months or if earlier assessment is necessary
features.requires: NGSP-certified laboratory or point-of-care A1C analyser
features.resourceLimitedNote: Store mmol/mol as well as %; and treat a missing A1C as normal operation, not as an incomplete record.

features.whyItMatters: ADA directs vitamin B12 measurement in anyone taking metformin for more than 5 years; without this field, metformin-induced B12 deficiency is misattributed to diabetic neuropathy and the treatable cause is missed.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Laboratory evaluation)
features.quote: Vitamin B12 if taking metformin for >5 years
features.requires: Serum vitamin B12 assay to act on the trigger
features.resourceLimitedNote: B12 assay is often unavailable; where it is, an empirical B12 trial may be the pragmatic action — flag the trigger rather than blocking on the test.

features.whyItMatters: ADA lists history of metabolic surgery as a MAJOR risk factor for hypoglycaemia (Table 6.5), which mandates deintensification; transplantation implies immunosuppression that can itself cause or worsen hyperglycaemia.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Surgical and procedure history) and Section 6, Table 6.5
features.quote: Surgeries (e.g., metabolic surgery and transplantation)

features.whyItMatters: ADA records these at initial and annual visits; each changes prescribing directly — hypertension and dyslipidaemia set the statin and antihypertensive indication, obesity opens weight-management pharmacotherapy, and MASLD triggers the FIB-4 fibrosis pathway (rec 4.22a).
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Personal history of complications and common comorbidities)
features.quote: Common comorbidities (e.g., obesity, OSA, and MASLD)
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO PEN cautions that statins are recommended for people with type 2 diabetes over 40 'but only if this does not negatively impact access to glucose-lowering and blood pressure-lowering medication' — a comorbidity flag must not silently displace insulin from a constrained budget.

features.whyItMatters: ADA places OSA screening at initial, every follow-up and annual visits; a positive screen changes management by prompting referral for diagnosis and treatment, which bears on blood pressure and glycaemic control.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Behavioral factors)
features.quote: Screen for OSA
features.requires: Confirmatory sleep study for a positive screen
features.resourceLimitedNote: Polysomnography and CPAP are unavailable in most district settings; ADA Section 4 does not name a specific screening questionnaire, so the screen itself must be a licence-free question set.

features.whyItMatters: ADA records this at initial and annual visits; alcohol and substance use appear as risk factors for both hypoglycaemia (Table 6.5) and hyperglycaemic crisis, so a positive answer changes the drug choice away from sulfonylureas and adds explicit alcohol–hypoglycaemia counselling.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1; Section 6 Tables 6.5 and hyperglycaemic crisis risk factors
features.quote: Tobacco, alcohol, and substance use

features.display: How glucose is monitored at home

options.display: Meter with a reliable strip supply
Has a meter but cannot obtain strips

features.whyItMatters: Insulin titration and any recommendation that depends on detecting hypoglycaemia are unsafe without monitoring. Distinguishing 'has a meter but no strips' from 'no meter' changes the intervention from issuing a device to funding consumables.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Technology use)
features.quote: Glucose monitoring (meter/CGM): results and data use
features.requires: Glucose meter and test strips, or CGM
features.resourceLimitedNote: Strips are a recurring out-of-pocket cost and the commonest silent reason insulin regimens fail; ADA's own table treats rationing of 'medical equipment' as a first-class finding.

features.whyItMatters: Determines whether a dose recommendation is even expressible (pens do not deliver half-units in every device; vials and syringes are graded differently) and whether pump-specific review of settings applies.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Technology use)
features.quote: Review insulin pump settings and use and connected pen and glucose data
features.resourceLimitedNote: Pumps are effectively unavailable in the target setting; vial-and-syringe should be the default, and syringe-graduation mismatches (40 vs 100 units/mL) are a real dosing hazard worth capturing separately.

features.whyItMatters: ADA assesses this specifically for type 1 diabetes or type 2 on multiple daily injections; without it, flexible prandial dosing is unsafe and a fixed-dose regimen should be prescribed instead.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Behavioral factors)
features.quote: Assess familiarity with carbohydrate counting (e.g., type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes treated with MDI)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Carbohydrate counting assumes a quantified, packaged food supply; in staple-based diets the assessment should be about portion consistency, not gram counting.

features.whyItMatters: ADA lists food insecurity as a MAJOR social risk factor for hypoglycaemia (Table 6.5). A positive screen is a direct instruction to avoid sulfonylureas and fixed prandial insulin and to relax the glycaemic target — it changes the prescription, not just the referral.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 5 (Hunger Vital Sign) and Section 4 Table 4.1 SDOH row; Section 6 Table 6.5
features.quote: Households are considered at risk if they answer either or both of the following statements as “often true” or “sometimes true”
features.resourceLimitedNote: Two questions, no equipment — the highest value-per-second field in the record for this setting.

features.display: Reliable transport to reach the clinic
features.whyItMatters: ADA names transportation access within the social determinants row. Where transport is the binding constraint, the correct response is to lengthen the medicine supply and consolidate visits rather than schedule a 3-monthly review the person cannot attend.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 (Social life assessment)
features.quote: Identify social determinants of health (e.g., food security, housing stability, transportation access, financial security, and community safety)

features.whyItMatters: ADA rec 4.17 requires assessment at the initial visit and for decline at every subsequent visit, with referral to a disability specialist where function or diabetes self-management is affected; vision and dexterity limits also decide whether a person can safely draw up insulin.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 and Recommendation 4.17
features.quote: Disability assessment and use of assistive devices (e.g., physical, cognitive, vision and auditory, history of fractures, and podiatry)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Rehabilitation medicine, occupational therapy and speech-language pathology referrals named in rec 4.17 are largely unavailable outside national referral hospitals.

features.whyItMatters: ADA rec 4.14 states that in the presence of cognitive impairment the treatment plan should be simplified as much as possible and tailored to minimise hypoglycaemia risk — this field is the trigger for regimen simplification and a less stringent target.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Recommendation 4.14 and Table 4.1
features.quote: In the presence of cognitive impairment, diabetes treatment plans should be simplified as much as possible and tailored to minimize the risk of hypoglycemia.
features.requires: A cognitive screening instrument for formal assessment
features.resourceLimitedNote: Most cognitive screens are copyright-restricted or require certification and are not validated in local languages; keep 'suspected, not formally assessed' as a usable answer that still fires the simplification rule.

features.whyItMatters: ADA rec 4.13a names a history of fragility fracture as an independent indication to consider osteoporosis drug therapy in older adults with diabetes, and Section 4 states such a fracture in adults aged >=65 is diagnostic of osteoporosis regardless of BMD — so a 'yes' can start treatment without any scan.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Recommendation 4.13a and Table 4.4
features.quote: Consider osteoporosis drug therapy in older adults with diabetes who are at increased risk of fracture, including those with low bone mineral density (T-score ≤−2.5), history of fragility fracture, or elevated Fracture Risk Assessment Tool score
features.resourceLimitedNote: This is the one bone-health field that works without DXA, which is unavailable at most sites — ADA's own text makes a fragility fracture in the over-65s diagnostic on its own.

features.whyItMatters: ADA rec 4.15 requires referral for a dental exam at least once per year, and rec 4.16 requires coordinating glucose-lowering treatment around dental procedures; the interval decides whether a referral is issued today.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 4, Table 4.1 and Recommendations 4.15, 4.16
features.quote: People with diabetes should be referred for a dental exam at least once per year.

instruments.name: Gold score (single-question impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia)
instruments.purpose: Identify impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia in insulin-treated diabetes. Named by ADA SoC 2026 Section 6 as a validated tool for this purpose.
instruments.scoring: Single question 'Do you know when your hypos are commencing?' answered on a 7-point Likert scale where 1 = 'always aware' and 7 = 'never aware'.
instruments.cutoffs: Score >=4 indicates impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia.
instruments.licence: No open licence located. The item originates in Gold AE et al., Diabetes Care 1994;17:697–703 and is reproduced in the NICE NG17 evidence review; copyright for embedding in software was NOT confirmed. Do not embed the verbatim item without checking with the publisher. ADA's own licence-free alternative — 'Can you always feel when your blood glucose is low?' — is safe to embed as it is quoted directly in the Standards of Care.

instruments.name: Clarke hypoglycaemia awareness survey
instruments.purpose: Multi-domain assessment of impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia, including exposure to moderate and severe episodes and the glycaemic threshold for symptoms. Named by ADA SoC 2026 Section 6.
instruments.scoring: Each answer is rated A (aware) or R (reduced); the R ratings are summed. Two questions (Q5 and Q6) are combined to give one rating. Q4 is scored A if the person has had no severe episodes in the past year and R if one or more.
instruments.cutoffs: Four or more R ratings suggests impaired hypoglycaemia awareness; <=2 = normal awareness; 3 = borderline. If severe episodes in the past year are >=12, impaired awareness is concluded irrespective of other answers.
instruments.licence: No permission or copyright notice was printed on the reproduction I retrieved (a Diabetes on the Net clinical handout). Original instrument is Clarke WL et al., Diabetes Care 1995. Licence status for embedding is UNCONFIRMED — treat as restricted until written permission is obtained.

instruments.name: Diabetes Distress Scale (DDS-17) with DDS-2 screener
instruments.purpose: Measure diabetes-specific emotional distress across four domains: emotional burden, physician distress, regimen distress and interpersonal distress. ADA Table 4.1 requires screening for diabetes distress at initial and annual visits.
instruments.scoring: Each item rated 1 ('Not a Problem') to 6 ('A Very Serious Problem') for the past month. Sum items and divide by the number of items to give a mean item score. Total = all 17 items / 17. Subscales: Emotional Burden items 2,4,7,10,14 (/5); Physician Distress items 1,5,11,15 (/4); Regimen Distress items 3,6,8,12,16 (/5); Interpersonal Distress items 9,13,17 (/3). A 2-item screener (DDS-2) is administered first; a score of 3 or greater triggers the full DDS.
instruments.cutoffs: Mean item score 2.0–2.9 = moderate distress; >3.0 = high distress. Associations with behavioural management and biological variables such as A1C occur with scores >2.0. Any single item scored >3 is worth exploring.
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED. The instrument carries the printed notice '© William H. Polonsky & Lawrence Fisher'. The copy I retrieved grants no reuse permission. Do NOT embed the 17 items without written permission from the copyright holders. Original citation: Polonsky WH, Fisher L, Earles J, Dudl RJ, Lees J, Mullan JT, Jackson R. Assessing psychosocial distress in diabetes: Development of the Diabetes Distress Scale. Diabetes Care 2005;28:626–631. Cut-points: Fisher L, Hessler DM, Polonsky WH, Mullan J, Diabetes Care 2012;35:259–264.

instruments.name: Hunger Vital Sign (2-item food insecurity screener)
instruments.purpose: Screen for household food insecurity. ADA SoC 2026 Section 5 states any member of the health care team can use it, and food insecurity is a MAJOR social risk factor for hypoglycaemia in ADA Table 6.5.
instruments.scoring: Two statements about the past 12 months: 'Within the past 12 months, we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more.' and 'Within the past 12 months, the food we bought just didn't last, and we didn't have money to get more.' Each answered 'often true', 'sometimes true' or 'never true'.
instruments.cutoffs: Households are considered at risk if they answer either or both statements as 'often true' or 'sometimes true' (compared with 'never true').
instruments.licence: NOT VERIFIED. The item wording above is quoted directly from the ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 5; I did not retrieve the instrument's own licence terms from its originators (Children's HealthWatch). Confirm reuse terms before embedding, and confirm the wording translates meaningfully into local languages and food-purchasing patterns.

instruments.name: FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool)
instruments.purpose: Estimate 10-year probability of hip fracture and major osteoporotic fracture. ADA rec 4.13a uses an elevated FRAX score as one of the triggers to consider osteoporosis drug therapy in older adults with diabetes.
instruments.scoring: Inputs as labelled on the FRAX calculation tool: age, sex, weight, height, previous fracture, parent fractured hip, current smoking, glucocorticoids, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis, alcohol 3 or more units/day, and bone mineral density (BMD, optional). Returns 10-year probabilities.
instruments.cutoffs: Per ADA rec 4.13a: >=3% for hip fracture or >=20% for major osteoporotic fracture is 'elevated'.
instruments.licence: RESTRICTED / UNRESOLVED. FRAX® and FRAXplus® are registered trademarks; the tool is administered by Osteoporosis Research Ltd (UK) and originated at the University of Sheffield. Neither the University of Sheffield page nor the FRAXplus calculation tool page I retrieved states any terms permitting integration into third-party software. Do NOT reimplement the FRAX algorithm or embed the calculator without a written licence. Note also that FRAX is known to require diabetes-specific adjustment, which I did not verify.

instruments.name: FIB-4 (Fibrosis-4 index)
instruments.purpose: Risk-stratify adults with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes for significant liver fibrosis related to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. Required by ADA rec 4.22a as a calculated index.
instruments.scoring: A calculated index derived from age and routine laboratory values. NOTE: I did NOT retrieve the formula itself in this pass — only ADA's cut-offs and how they are used. Do not implement the calculation from memory.
instruments.cutoffs: Per ADA 2026: FIB-4 >=1.3 requires additional risk stratification by liver stiffness measurement with transient elastography, or the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test if elastography is unavailable (rec 4.23). Persistently elevated aminotransferases for >6 months with a low FIB-4 should prompt evaluation for other causes of liver disease (rec 4.22b).
instruments.licence: Not a questionnaire and not known to be copyright-restricted — it is a published index computed from routine labs. No licence document was retrieved, so this is not confirmed.

unverifiable: ACCESS ROUTE: diabetesjournals.org and PubMed both returned HTTP 403 to every request. ALL ADA text reported here was read from the free PubMed Central deposits: Section 4 = PMC12690184 (Diabetes Care 2025 Dec 8;49(Suppl 1):S61-S88, doi 10.2337/dc26-S004), Section 2 = PMC12690183 (S27-S49), Section 5 = PMC12690188 (S89-S131), Section 6 = PMC12690178 (S132-S149). Volume/page/DOI figures are taken from the PMC header lines, not from the publisher's own citation page.

Table 4.1 was extracted as HTML text from the PMC 2026 deposit. Older editions (2023, 2024) render Table 4.1 as a JPEG image, so if anyone cross-checks against those they will not find matching text. Table footnote markers (*, double-dagger, section-sign, double-vertical-line) appear in the extracted rows but I did not retrieve the footnote definitions, so the exact conditions attached to lipid profile, liver function tests, TSH, serum creatinine/eGFR, coeliac screening and serum potassium rows are NOT verified.
The ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes-2026 is assumed to be the current edition (published 2025-12-08). I did not verify that no interim update or erratum has been issued.

'How the diagnosis was made' is NOT a discrete row in ADA Table 4.1. The 2026 table says only 'Characteristics at onset (e.g., age and symptoms and/or signs)'. My diagnostic_test_used option list is assembled from ADA Section 2 Table 2.1 plus the WHO PEN point-of-care allowance; the field itself is my construction. (Earlier ADA editions reportedly used wording closer to 'characteristics at diagnosis (e.g., DKA, asymptomatic laboratory finding)' but I could NOT retrieve that wording from any edition — the tables were images.)

'Who prescribes' and 'where medicines are collected' are NOT in any guideline I retrieved. The option lists in diabetes_prescriber and medicine_collection_point are entirely my construction. The only supporting evidence is WHO PEN's instruction to 'REFER to higher-level health care facility for starting insulin' and ADA's SDOH row naming transportation access and financial security.

Medicine STOCKOUT, insulin cold-chain availability and days-of-supply-remaining were considered and deliberately NOT proposed as features: I searched the full text of the WHO PEN 2020 PDF for 'stock' and 'refill' and got zero hits, and found nothing in ADA. They are almost certainly the right fields for a Ugandan deployment, but I have no source and will not fabricate one.
type_label_provenance and diagnosis_date_precision are implementation adaptations with no guideline source. They are marked fetched:false.

The inference that HbA1c is unreliable in the presence of a haemoglobinopathy is standard clinical knowledge but I did NOT retrieve a document stating it in this pass. ADA Table 4.1 only directs that 'Presence of hemoglobinopathies or anemias' be recorded; it does not say what to do with it. Verify before wiring this into any rule.
Sickle cell trait/disease prevalence in Uganda, and any Ugandan-specific guidance, were not researched. Uganda Clinical Guidelines and the Uganda MoH NCD manual were NOT retrieved.

IDF was NOT retrieved. The task asked to cross-check IDF and WHO; only WHO sources were obtained (Classification of Diabetes Mellitus 2019, ISBN 978-92-4-151570-2; WHO PEN 2020, ISBN 978-92-4-000922-6). Any place where IDF adds to or differs from ADA is therefore unchecked. WHO HEARTS-D (the type 2 diagnosis and management module WHO PEN cross-references) was also not retrieved.

The WHO PEN PDF was read via a third-party mirror (knowledge-action-portal.com) because iris.who.int returned 403 to WebFetch. Text extraction had font-encoding corruption: several numeric thresholds in the diabetes protocol rendered as mojibake and are NOT reported here. The quoted strings I did report were clean.

ADA Table 4.3 vaccine recommendations are explicitly built on CDC/ACIP US schedules and reference the 2025 ACIP immunisation schedules. They should NOT be presented as globally applicable. National schedules (Uganda EPI) were not retrieved, and the availability judgements in my resourceLimitedNote fields for influenza, pneumococcal, zoster and RSV vaccines are my assessment, not sourced.

Licence status is UNCONFIRMED for the Gold score, Clarke score and Hunger Vital Sign; NOT DETERMINED for Pedersen-Bjergaard and HypoA-Q (instruments not retrieved); and UNRESOLVED for FRAX (no integration terms found on either the University of Sheffield page or the FRAXplus tool page). Only the DDS-17 carries an explicit copyright notice, and that notice grants nothing. Treat all of them as non-embeddable until legal review.
The DDS-2 two-item screener items were NOT reproduced in the document I read - only the routing rule ('Score is 3 or greater: Administer full DDS'). The two item texts are unknown to me.
The FIB-4 formula was not retrieved. Only ADA's cut-offs were.

ADA Section 4 does NOT name a specific OSA screening questionnaire (I searched the full text for STOP-Bang and found nothing), so osa_screen_result deliberately records a screen outcome rather than a named instrument's score.

Availability claims in resourceLimitedNote fields - glucagon, insulin pumps, CGM, DXA, polysomnography/CPAP, dental services, rehabilitation services, adult hepatitis B vaccine, B12 assay - are my clinical judgement about typical low-resource settings. None were sourced. WHO PEN does support the narrower claims about FPG being the practical test, point-of-care devices being acceptable, and insulin initiation requiring referral.

Whether syringe graduation mismatch (40 vs 100 units/mL) is a live hazard in the target setting is asserted from general knowledge, not sourced. It is mentioned only in a resourceLimitedNote, not proposed as a feature.
ADA recommendation 4.11 was extracted with an ambiguous grade ('C/B') by the page fetch; the true grade split across its two sentences was not resolved. No feature depends on it.

Also verbatim: 'misdiagnosis can occur in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes.' I suspected the AABBCC framework was invented and it is NOT — Section 2 states verbatim: 'Although not prospectively validated, the AABBCC approach is a useful tool to help distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes: Age...; Autoimmunity; Body habitus...; Background...; Control...; and Comorbidities.' audit.reason: I specifically tried to refute the 'section 2.4' citation, suspecting it pointed at the classification list rather than at tests. It holds. Section 2.4 begins at the heading 'WHO classification of diabetes 2019' and the autoantibody/C-peptide passage sits inside it before subsection 2.4.1: 'Autoantibodies against a variety of beta-cell components including glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65), islet antigen-2 (IA-2), zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8) and insulin...' and 'Endogenous insulin production can be assessed by measuring blood C-peptide... but is not routinely done clinically.' audit.reason: Section 6 is titled 'Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises' in the 2026 edition, so placing hyperglycaemic crises in Section 6 is correct (it was Section 16 in older editions — the agent did not make that error). audit.reason: Both supporting claims retrieved verbatim from Section 6: 'those with recurrent DKA often require extensive multisystemic behavioral interventions' and 'the majority of DKA cases occur in those with established diabetes compared with those with newly diagnosed diabetes'. audit.reason: The field and its Section 6 / Table 6.8 anchor are fine — 'Prior history of hyperglycemic crises' is confirmed in Table 6.8 and covers HHS. But the whyItMatters asserts HHS carries 'higher mortality', and that comparison is NOT in the cited article. Section 6 says only that 'both DKA and HHS impart a substantial risk of subsequent morbidity and mortality' and does not differentiate the two. The 'usually type 2, older' phenotype claim is likewise not quoted in the retrieved text. The claim is defensible in the wider literature but it is not in the source cited, which is the failure mode this audit exists to catch.
audit.correction: Rewrite whyItMatters to what the source actually supports and which is decision-bearing on its own: Section 6 states HHS 'is associated with greater volume depletion and is typically triggered by an acute illness' and that 'individuals with suspected HHS should be immediately evaluated and treated in the inpatient setting'. That is a stronger justification anyway — it names an admission decision. Drop the mortality comparison or cite a source that actually carries it.

audit.reason: Category error in the sourcing. Table 6.8 is 'Risk factors for hyperglycemic crises' — a standing-risk table — not a table of precipitants of a given episode, which is what this field records. Its confirmed contents are: type 1/absolute insulin deficiency, younger age, prior hyperglycaemic crises, prior hypoglycaemic crises, other diabetes complications, other chronic conditions, behavioural health conditions, alcohol/substance use, high A1C, insulin rationing, SGLT2 inhibitor use, social determinants of health. Rationing and SGLT2 inhibitors are therefore genuinely sourced. INFECTION is not in Table 6.8 — the article only says HHS is 'typically triggered by an acute illness'. So the infection option, the anchor of the sick-day-rules branch, is not supported by the cited table.
audit.correction: Keep the field — it names a genuinely different intervention per precipitant, which is good design. But re-label the source honestly: rationing and SGLT2-inhibitor options cite Table 6.8; infection/intercurrent illness should either cite the ADA hyperglycaemic crises consensus report or be flagged as an implementation adaptation, the way diagnosis_date_precision correctly was.
