audit.correction: This is the weakest field in the set on rule 5, and I flag it rather than fail it. It is an unstructured free-text catch-all that drives no rule and duplicates ground already covered by structured fields (family_history_diabetes_first_degree, known_comorbidities, personal_autoimmune_disease). A free-text box at every follow-up is exactly the sort of item clinicians learn to leave blank, which then erodes trust in the rest of the form. Consider making it a short prompted list rather than open text, or dropping it and relying on re-asking the structured fields.

audit.reason: The core field is sound — Table 4.3 confirmed to say 'Adults with diabetes aged <60 years; for adults aged >=60 years, hepatitis B vaccine may be administered at the discretion...' with 'GRADE type 1'. Both the <60 age cut and the GRADE type 1 grading are exact. But the added ranking claim, that this is 'the highest-graded vaccine in the diabetes schedule', is NOT in the source and is contradicted by it: I retrieved the full table and zoster (>=50 years, two-dose Shingrix) and RSV (>=75, or >=60 at high risk) are ALSO GRADE type 1. Hepatitis B is tied, not uniquely highest. Rec 4.5 is confirmed but is generic ('Provide routinely recommended vaccinations... as indicated by age (see Table 4.3). A'), not hepatitis B-specific.
audit.correction: Delete the 'highest-graded vaccine in the diabetes schedule' clause. Also correct the attribution framing across the whole vaccine block: Table 4.3's own caption is 'Highly recommended immunizations for people with diabetes (from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)'. These are ACIP/CDC recommendations reproduced by ADA, not ADA-originated — say 'ACIP/CDC, as tabulated in ADA Section 4 Table 4.3'.

audit.reason: Both claims verified. Table 4.3 confirmed: 'All people with diabetes advised to receive a trivalent influenza vaccine and not to receive live attenuated influenza vaccine' — so the LAIV prohibition is exact. Section 4 text confirmed verbatim: 'Influenza vaccination in people with diabetes has been found to significantly reduce influenza and diabetes-related hospital admissions.'
audit.correction: The table specifies a TRIVALENT vaccine, a detail the feature omits; include it if the field is to drive a product-level offer. Attribution should read ACIP/CDC via ADA Table 4.3.

audit.reason: The specific sequencing claims are exact, which is the part most likely to have been confabulated and was not. Table 4.3 confirmed: 'One dose is recommended for those who previously received PCV13; if PCV15 was used, follow with PPSV23 >=1 year later; PPSV23 is not indicated after PCV20.' Both the 'not indicated after PCV20' and the '>=1 year after PCV15' claims are verbatim. The design argument — that recording only 'vaccinated' makes the next dose undecidable — is correct.
audit.correction: resourceLimitedNote is missing and is needed. This is a US product schedule; PCV15/PCV20 are not part of Uganda's UNEPI adult programme and are largely unobtainable. A required select whose options are PCV13/PCV15/PCV20/PPSV23 will be unanswerable at Mulago and will teach clinicians to skip the block. Add an explicit 'not available in this setting' / 'unknown product' option and do not fire a 'dose due' prompt against products that cannot be sourced.

audit.reason: Section 4 text confirmed verbatim: 'People with underlying medical conditions, including diabetes, are more likely to become severely ill with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).' Table 4.3 confirmed to cover COVID-19 for 'All people 6 months of age and older' with 'Current initial vaccination and boosters', GRADE type 3.
audit.correction: Attribution should read ACIP/CDC via ADA Table 4.3. Note the source grades this GRADE type 3, the weakest tier in the table — worth reflecting so it is not prompted with the same insistence as hepatitis B.

audit.reason: All three triggers verified exactly against Table 4.3: Tdax/Tdap 'All adults; pregnant individuals should have an extra dose' with 'Booster every 10 years'; zoster '>=50 years of age' with 'Two-dose Shingrix, even if previously vaccinated'; RSV 'Adults aged >=75 years and those aged >=60 years and at high risk may receive a single dose'. The 10-year, >=50 and >=75/>=60 figures are all correct.
audit.correction: Same resourceLimitedNote gap as pneumococcal, and more acute here: Shingrix and RSV vaccine are essentially unavailable and unfunded in Uganda. Tdap/Td boosters are realistic; zoster and RSV are not. Gate the zoster and RSV prompts behind a site-level formulary flag rather than showing a permanently unactionable 'due' state.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim: 'Family history of diabetes in a first-degree relative'. The AABBCC link is real — 'Background (e.g., family history of type 1 diabetes)'. I also verified the monogenic claim rather than taking it on trust: Section 2 recommends testing for MODY in those with 'a family history of diabetes in successive generations (suggestive of an autosomal-dominant pattern of inheritance)' and describes monogenic diabetes as 'negative diabetes-associated autoantibodies, no obesity, and lacking other metabolic features, especially strong family history'. The sulfonylurea claim also holds: HNF1A-MODY and HNF4A-MODY individuals are 'sensitive to sulfonylureas', and for KATP neonatal diabetes '30-50%... will exhibit improved blood glucose levels when treated with high-dose oral sulfonylureas instead of insulin'.
audit.correction: None. Table 2.7 'Most common causes of monogenic diabetes' would be a tighter citation for the sulfonylurea leg.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim: 'Family history of autoimmune disorders' under Family history. Recs 4.6 and 4.7 retrieved verbatim and are correctly characterised — 4.6 covers autoimmune thyroid screening 'soon after diagnosis' in type 1, 4.7 covers coeliac screening in adults with type 1 'in the presence of gastrointestinal symptoms, signs, laboratory manifestations, or clinical suspicion'.
audit.correction: Minor precision: rec 4.7 is conditional on symptoms or suspicion, not universal in type 1. The feature states this correctly; keep that qualifier when implementing so the tool does not prompt blanket coeliac serology.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim: 'Personal history of autoimmune disease' under Personal history. The reclassification argument is supported by the confirmed AABBCC 'Autoimmunity' and 'Comorbidities' cues in Section 2, and recs 4.6/4.7 are correctly attributed.
audit.correction: None.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim: 'Presence of hemoglobinopathies or anemias'. The field is genuinely ADA-anchored and the decision it drives — which glycaemic measure is trustworthy — is real and high-stakes.
audit.correction: The interpretive claim that A1C cannot be used and FPG/random glucose must substitute is correct but is not sourced from Section 4. The proper citation is Section 2, Table 2.3 'Considerations related to the use and interpretation of laboratory measurements of glucose and A1C', which I confirmed exists. Add it. This matters more than usual for a Ugandan deployment given sickle cell trait prevalence.

audit.reason: Verified verbatim in the downloaded WHO PEN PDF, in the diabetes protocol's TREATMENT GOAL column: 'If HbA1c is not available, fasting plasma glucose (FPG) < 7 mmol/L or < 126 mg/dl'. The claim is exact. This is arguably the single most important field in the set for the target deployment — it prevents the tool judging control against a target that does not apply, and prevents it ordering a test the site cannot run.
audit.correction: None.

audit.reason: Both claims exact. Table 4.1 laboratory row retrieved verbatim: 'A1C, if the results are not available within the past 3 months or if earlier assessment is necessary', confirming the 3-month re-order logic. Table 4.4 confirmed to list 'A1C >8%' as a diabetes-specific BMD-testing trigger.
audit.correction: None.

audit.reason: I expected this to be an overstatement from memory and it is not. Table 4.1 laboratory evaluation carries the row verbatim: 'Vitamin B12 if taking metformin for >5 years'. The >5-year threshold is exactly as ADA states it, not a paraphrase of the older weaker 'consider periodic measurement' wording. whyItMatters names a real decision — distinguishing treatable B12 deficiency from diabetic neuropathy.
audit.correction: resourceLimitedNote: serum B12 assay is not reliably available at Ugandan district level. Where it cannot be run, the actionable fallback is an empirical B12 trial in a metformin-exposed patient with new neuropathy, which is cheap and safe — worth encoding rather than leaving the pathway dead-ended.

audit.reason: Table 6.5 confirmed to list 'History of metabolic surgery' under MAJOR clinical/biological risk factors for hypoglycaemia — the MAJOR designation claimed is exact. Table 4.1 surgical/procedure history anchors the field.
audit.correction: Low prevalence in the Ugandan beachhead; consider making this a collapsed/optional item rather than a prominent one so it does not consume attention that food_insecurity and medication_rationing deserve more.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 personal-history/comorbidity rows confirmed. Recs 4.22a, 4.22b and 4.23 all retrieved verbatim, including the FIB-4 >=1.3 stratification threshold and the transient-elastography-or-ELF fallback, so the MASLD/FIB-4 leg is real.
audit.correction: One inversion to fix. Rec 4.22a reads 'Screen adults with type 2 diabetes or with prediabetes, particularly those with obesity or other cardiometabolic risk factors or established cardiovascular disease, for their risk of having or developing cirrhosis... using a calculated FIB-4... even if they have normal liver enzymes.' So FIB-4 is indicated across adults with type 2 diabetes generally — it is NOT gated on a recorded MASLD comorbidity, as whyItMatters implies. Reword, otherwise the tool will under-trigger FIB-4 in exactly the population ADA wants screened.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row 'Screen for OSA' confirmed, and I checked the visit columns specifically rather than accepting the claim: it is ticked at initial, every follow-up and annual, so 'ADA places OSA screening at initial, every follow-up and annual visits' is accurate.
audit.correction: whyItMatters is the thinnest of the confirmed set — the action is 'refer for diagnosis and treatment', and polysomnography and CPAP are largely inaccessible in the target setting, so the referral often terminates nowhere. Keep the field (ADA mandates it at every visit) but add a resourceLimitedNote and define what a positive screen does locally, e.g. weight management and positional advice, so it is not a dead-end question.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 behavioural rows confirmed. Both risk-factor legs verified: Table 6.5 lists 'Alcohol or substance use disorder' among social/cultural/economic risk factors for hypoglycaemia, and Table 6.8 lists 'Alcohol and/or substance use' as a risk factor for hyperglycaemic crises. The feature does not claim MAJOR status, which is correct — in Table 6.5 it sits under OTHER, not MAJOR.
audit.correction: None. The restraint in not calling it a MAJOR factor was accurate and I checked it specifically.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim: 'Glucose monitoring (meter/CGM): results and data use'. The field is properly ADA-anchored and whyItMatters names a genuine decision — insulin titration and any hypoglycaemia-dependent advice are unsafe without monitoring.
audit.correction: The 'has a meter but no strips' vs 'no meter' distinction is an implementation refinement not found in ADA, but it is the correct refinement for this deployment (strip cost, not device access, is usually the binding constraint) and it changes the intervention. Keep it; just do not imply ADA drew that distinction.

audit.reason: The only Table 4.1 technology row bearing on insulin delivery is, verbatim, 'Review insulin pump settings and use and connected pen and glucose data'. That row presupposes a pump or a connected pen and says nothing about vials, syringes or delivery method as a recorded attribute. The stated rationale — 'pens do not deliver half-units in every device; vials and syringes are graded differently' — appears nowhere in ADA Section 4; it is implementation reasoning presented under an ADA citation with fetched:true. The pump-settings-review half of whyItMatters IS supported; the delivery-method half is not.
audit.correction: Split it. Keep a pump/connected-pen review item cited to the confirmed Table 4.1 row, and re-label the delivery-method select as an implementation adaptation with fetched:false — the same honest treatment given to diagnosis_date_precision and medicine_collection_point. The field itself is clinically necessary (in Uganda vial-and-syringe predominates and dose expressibility genuinely differs), so this is a sourcing fix, not a deletion.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim including the qualifier the feature claimed: 'Assess familiarity with carbohydrate counting (e.g., type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes treated with MDI)'. The 'type 1 or type 2 on multiple daily injections' scoping is exact, and the decision named (fixed-dose regimen instead of flexible prandial dosing) is real and safety-relevant.
audit.correction: None.

audit.reason: Strongest social field in the set. Table 6.5 confirmed to list 'Food insecurity' under MAJOR social/cultural/economic risk factors for hypoglycaemia — the MAJOR claim is exact. Section 5 confirmed to carry the Hunger Vital Sign with the two items quoted accurately. whyItMatters correctly identifies that this changes the prescription (avoid sulfonylureas and fixed prandial insulin, relax the target), not merely the referral — which is the right standard for this form.
audit.correction: See the Hunger Vital Sign instrument verdict — the licence is better than the agent reported and this can be embedded.

audit.reason: I checked whether 'transportation' was actually named or merely inferred, since that was a plausible embellishment. It is named. The Table 4.1 SDOH row reads verbatim: 'Identify social determinants of health (e.g., food security, housing stability, transportation access, financial security, and community safety)'. The feature's careful phrasing — 'ADA names transportation access within the social determinants row' — is precisely accurate rather than overclaimed.
audit.correction: None. The named action (lengthen medicine supply, consolidate visits rather than schedule an unattendable 3-monthly review) is a real decision and well suited to the deployment.

audit.reason: Both legs verified. Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim: 'Disability assessment and use of assistive devices (e.g., physical, cognitive, vision and auditory, history of fractures, and podiatry)' — the assistive-device element is explicitly present, not inferred. Rec 4.17 retrieved verbatim confirming assessment 'at the initial visit and for decline in function at each subsequent visit' and the referral requirement.
audit.correction: The vision/dexterity-to-draw-up-insulin inference is not ADA's words but follows directly from the row's 'vision' and 'physical' examples and is a real safety decision. Acceptable as stated.

audit.reason: Rec 4.14 retrieved verbatim: 'In the presence of cognitive impairment, diabetes treatment plans should be simplified as much as possible and tailored to minimize the risk of hypoglycemia. B' The claimed trigger — regimen simplification and a less stringent target — is exactly what the recommendation says. 'Cognitive impairment or dementia' is independently confirmed as a MAJOR risk factor in Table 6.5.
audit.correction: None.

audit.reason: Both claims exact, including the striking one I expected to fail. Rec 4.13a retrieved verbatim: 'Consider osteoporosis drug therapy in older adults with diabetes who are at increased risk of fracture, including those with low bone mineral density (T-score <=-2.5), history of fragility fracture, or elevated Fracture Risk Assessment Tool score (>=3% for hip fracture or >=20% for major osteoporotic fracture). B' And Section 4 states verbatim: 'A low-trauma fracture... of the hip, pelvis, vertebra, or forearm in adults aged >=65 years is diagnostic of osteoporosis, regardless of BMD.' So the claim that a yes can start treatment without any scan is correct.
audit.correction: None — and this is the highest-value field in the bone block precisely because it is the one that works without imaging. Given DXA and FRAX are both unavailable locally (see FRAX verdict), this field should be the primary osteoporosis trigger in the Ugandan configuration, not a supplement to BMD.

audit.reason: Both recommendations retrieved verbatim. Rec 4.15: 'People with diabetes should be referred for a dental exam at least once per year. E' Rec 4.16: 'Coordinate efforts between the medical and dental teams to appropriately adjust glucose-lowering medication and treatment plans prior to and in the postdental procedure period as needed. B' Attribution exact.
audit.correction: Note rec 4.15 is graded E (expert consensus), the weakest ADA grade — do not surface it with the same urgency as A-graded items. Add a resourceLimitedNote on dental access.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim: 'Identify surrogate decision maker and advanced care plan'. The related row 'Identify existing social supports' is also present. whyItMatters names a real and specific decision — who may be contacted and consented for a patient found with impaired consciousness, and who should be trained to give rescue treatment — which ties it directly to the glucagon field.
audit.correction: None.

audit.reason: Both legs verified. Table 4.2 ('Essential components for assessment, planning, and referral') confirmed to include 'Family planning for individuals of childbearing potential' under referrals for initial care management. Section 6 confirmed verbatim: 'Up to 2% of pregnancies with pregestational diabetes (most often type 1 diabetes) are complicated by DKA.' The 2% figure is exact.
audit.correction: The teratogen list (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, statins) is correct clinical practice but was not verified in the two cited sections — it sits in ADA Section 15 (Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy). Add that citation or mark that leg as unverified.

audit.reason: Table 4.1 row retrieved verbatim: 'Height, weight, and BMI'. Section 2 confirmed verbatim that 'lower BMI (<25 kg/m2)' is among the features most useful in determining type 1, and the AABBCC 'Body habitus (e.g., BMI <25 kg/m2)' cue is present. Both legs of whyItMatters — classification and weight-management pathway — are supported.
audit.correction: None.

audit.reason: Agent's licence caution CONFIRMED as correct and appropriately conservative. Source verified: NBK343319 is real and is NICE Guideline No. 17, 'Type 1 Diabetes in Adults: Diagnosis and Management' (NICE, August 2015). It contains the item verbatim: 'This scoring system is based on the response to a single question: "Do you know when your hypos are commencing?"... Results are expressed by a 7-point Likert scale, where 1 = "always aware" and 7 = "never aware". IAH is suggested by a value of more than or equal to 4.' Wording, scale and >=4 cutoff all exact. The underlying item is Gold AE et al., Diabetes Care 1994 — ADA-copyright, and reproduction inside a NICE guideline confers no downstream licence. Do not embed verbatim.
audit.correction: One citation correction: NBK343319 is the FULL NICE NG17 guideline, not an 'evidence review' as described. Separately, the agent's proposed licence-free substitute is CONFIRMED safe and I verified it independently — ADA Section 6 gives the example screening question verbatim as 'Can you always feel when your blood glucose is low?', with 'No' responses to be followed by more detailed evaluation. Embed that instead.

audit.reason: Licence caution CONFIRMED correct. I downloaded and text-extracted the Diabetes on the Net handout and searched it for any rights notice: there is NO copyright line, no permission statement and no attribution to Clarke anywhere in the document. The agent's description of that absence is exactly accurate. Scoring verified verbatim and matches the agent's account precisely: 'Four or more R ratings suggests impaired hypoglycaemia awareness; <=2=normal awareness; 3=borderline'; Q4 'A if never; R if one or more. If >= 12, conclude impaired awareness irrespective of other answers'; Q5/Q6 combined into a single rating ('R = answer to Q5 < answer to Q6'). Underlying instrument is Clarke WL et al., Diabetes Care 1995 — ADA copyright. An unattributed third-party handout is the weakest possible provenance for a reuse decision.
audit.correction: Treat as restricted, as the agent advised. Note ADA Section 6 classes Clarke among the LONGER questionnaires (with HypoA-Q), not the single-question tools — the agent had this right.

audit.reason: Honest non-retrieval, correctly reported, with no fabricated item wording, scoring or cutoff — the failure mode this audit is designed to catch is absent. I independently confirmed the one claim actually made: ADA Section 6 does name the Pedersen-Bjergaard tool as a single-question instrument for impaired hypoglycaemia awareness, alongside Gold (single-question) and Clarke/HypoA-Q (longer questionnaires), and notes the tools show good agreement.
audit.correction: Keep in unverifiable until the primary source is retrieved. Do not implement from memory. Given the confirmed licence-free ADA question exists, there is no need to pursue this one.

audit.reason: Honest non-retrieval, correctly reported. No item count, scoring or cutoff invented. I confirmed the sole claim made — ADA Section 6 names HypoA-Q as a longer questionnaire evaluating multiple domains of impaired hypoglycaemia awareness. The agent's flag that it did not read the separate impaired-awareness-subscale validation paper is a good example of the generosity with unverifiable that this brief requires.
audit.correction: Keep in unverifiable. Do not implement.

audit.reason: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED status CONFIRMED — this is the most consequential licence call in the set and the agent got it exactly right. I downloaded and text-extracted the PDF and found the notice verbatim: 'DDS 5.8.15 (c) William H. Polonsky & Lawrence Fisher'. The wrapper additionally carries 'Copyright (c) 2016 Canadian Diabetes Association'. No reuse permission is granted anywhere in the document. Every scoring detail also checks out exactly: mean item score 2.0-2.9 moderate, >3.0 high, associations with behavioural management and A1C at >2.0; subscales Emotional Burden (2,4,7,10,14), Physician Distress (1,5,11,15), Regimen Distress (3,6,8,12,16), Interpersonal Distress (9,13,17); and the DDS-2 rule 'Score is 3 or greater Administer full DDS'. Both citations are accurate.
audit.correction: Do NOT embed the 17 items. Written permission from Polonsky and Fisher is required. Note the retrieved copy is a Canadian Diabetes Association reproduction, so CDA's wrapper copyright is a second layer to clear if that specific layout were reused.

audit.reason: This is the one licence verdict I am OVERTURNING, in the permissive direction. The agent marked it 'NOT VERIFIED' and advised confirming before embedding. I went to the originators at Children's HealthWatch and confirmed the opposite of a restriction: 'There is no fee or license required to use the Hunger Vital Sign(TM).' The only condition is proper citation of Hager ER, Quigg AM, Black MM, et al. (2010). The two items are also confirmed identical between the ADA Section 5 reproduction and the originators' own page, so the wording the agent captured is correct.
audit.correction: Upgrade to free-to-embed, with the Hager et al. (2010) citation displayed and the (TM) preserved. This unblocks the instrument behind food_insecurity — the highest-value social field in the set, and one that per confirmed Table 6.5 changes the prescription. The agent's caution was procedurally right but left a safe, free tool needlessly blocked. Its second caveat should be KEPT and is the real issue: the wording is US-derived and assumes a cash food-purchasing pattern, so it needs local-language validation before use at Mulago, where subsistence production makes 'the food we bought' a poor fit.

audit.reason: RESTRICTED status CONFIRMED. The URL is live and is the FRAXplus calculation tool; copyright line verified as '(c)2008-2026 - Osteoporosis Research Ltd, UK', with FRAX(R) and FRAXplus(R) confirmed as registered trademarks and the tool originating at the University of Sheffield. The page provides content 'on an "as is" and "as available" basis' and states NO terms permitting third-party software integration. The twelve input fields listed by the agent all match. ADA rec 4.13a independently confirms the >=3% hip / >=20% major osteoporotic thresholds verbatim. The do-not-reimplement instruction is correct and should be enforced.
audit.correction: Add a second, independent blocker the agent did not identify, which matters more than the licence for this deployment: FRAX is country-calibrated and there is NO Uganda FRAX model. Even with a licence, the >=3%/>=20% probabilities are not computable for the target population, so rec 4.13a's FRAX limb is inert at Mulago. Configure prior_fragility_fracture as the operative osteoporosis trigger instead — it is the limb of rec 4.13a that needs neither a licence, a scan, nor a country model.

audit.reason: The 'not copyright-restricted' assessment is sound — FIB-4 is a published index computed from routine labs, not a questionnaire, and no licence document exists to retrieve. The agent's discipline in refusing to write the formula from memory was correct. All ADA cut-offs verified verbatim: rec 4.23 requires that FIB-4 >=1.3 get 'additional risk stratification by liver stiffness measurement with transient elastography, or, if unavailable, the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test', and rec 4.22b covers persistently elevated aminotransferases >6 months with low FIB-4.
audit.correction: Partial upgrade: the agent said the inputs were not retrieved, but rec 4.22a names them explicitly — FIB-4 is 'derived from age, ALT, AST, and platelets'. The four inputs are therefore sourced; only the algebraic form still needs a primary citation (Sterling et al. 2006) before implementation. resourceLimitedNote to add: transient elastography (FibroScan) and the ELF test are both unavailable in most Ugandan settings, so rec 4.23's entire stratification limb dead-ends locally even though FIB-4 itself is computable from a CBC and LFTs.

bundle.domain: Current glucose-lowering treatment and access to it (type 2 diabetes) — therapy by class, insulin regimen pattern and technique, self-monitoring, and medication access

options.display: None — diet and physical activity only
Dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist

features.whyItMatters: Fixes which rung of the ladder the patient is on, so the engine proposes the NEXT step rather than a step already taken. WHO PEN/HEARTS-D sequence is metformin then sulfonylurea then human insulin; ADA 2026 Table 9.2 adds the comorbidity-driven classes. It also drives the hypoglycaemia-risk flag (sulfonylurea or insulin present) and the contraindication checks (metformin and eGFR).
features.standard: WHO PEN 2020, section 2.2 Diabetes (TREAT); WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2; ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9, Table 9.2
features.quote: Metformin is recommended as the first-line medicine in the treatment of diabetes. Sulfonylurea (e.g. gliclazide) is recommended as the second-line treatment, and human insulin as the third-line treatment.
features.resourceLimitedNote: The last six options are largely theoretical at Ugandan public primary level. WHO PEN's core primary-care medicine list contains only metformin, glibenclamide and insulin; the WHO EML 24th List (2025) adds gliclazide, empagliflozin and semaglutide but carries NO DPP-4 inhibitor and NO thiazolidinedione. Keep the options for private/tertiary patients, but do not let the UI imply availability.

options.display: Stopped — contraindication (kidney, liver, cardiac, respiratory, alcohol, prior lactic acidosis)
Stopped — not available / out of stock

features.whyItMatters: Separates 'metformin is off the table' from 'metformin failed' from 'metformin never actually reached the patient'. If contraindicated or not tolerated, first-line becomes a second-generation sulfonylurea and metformin must never be re-proposed. If it was stopped for stock-out or cost, the correct action is to restore supply, NOT to add a second agent — adding one would escalate therapy on the basis of an untreated patient.
features.standard: WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2 (Pharmacological management; Metformin contraindications)
features.quote: A second-generation sulfonylurea (preferably gliclazide) can be used as initial (first-line) treatment when metformin is contraindicated or not tolerated.
features.requires: None — history. Confirming the CKD contraindication needs eGFR (<30 mL/min/1.73 m2), which requires a serum creatinine assay.
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO PEN lists serum creatinine only under 'add when resources permit', so at many facilities the eGFR<30 contraindication cannot be confirmed and must be recorded as clinically suspected.

features.whyItMatters: Agent name only, no dose. Glibenclamide is the wrong agent in specific people and the decision is a within-class switch, not an escalation: it is not recommended at age 60+, in severe liver disease, where hypoglycaemia is a concern (falls risk, impaired awareness, lives alone), or in drivers/machine operators. Recording 'sulfonylurea' alone hides that decision.
features.standard: WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2 (Glibenclamide); WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, 24th List (2025), section 18.5.2
features.quote: Hypoglycaemia is a possible side-effect of sulfonylurea, more frequent with glibenclamide than with gliclazide. / Glibenclamide is not recommended in: people aged 60 years or older ... / EML 18.5.2: gliclazide* ... *glibenclamide not suitable above 60 years.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Sharp mismatch to flag: WHO PEN's core primary-care medicine list names GLIBENCLAMIDE, while HEARTS-D and the EML both prefer gliclazide. The agent actually on the shelf may be the one the guidelines de-prioritise, so 'switch to gliclazide' can be an unavailable recommendation. Pair the prompt with the stock-out field.

options.display: Indicated — no one able to inject / cannot store

features.whyItMatters: WHO explicitly treats insulin as sometimes unsuitable for non-clinical reasons, and each reason has a different action: cost or stock-out means escalate supply or use an oral third agent; 'no one to inject' means either a once-daily regimen with a trained family member or facility-administered dosing; declined means counselling, not a prescription. Without this field an insulin-indicated patient simply looks non-adherent.
features.standard: WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2 (Intensification when metformin and sulfonylurea fail; footnote 2)
features.quote: Insulin treatment could be unsuitable when it is more costly than oral agents, or when circumstances make its use difficult (e.g. persons who live alone and are dependent on others to inject them with insulin).

features.whyItMatters: Human vs analogue is a cost and hypoglycaemia decision, not a preference. WHO advises against routine analogue use on cost grounds; ADA recommends human insulin as a lower-cost option where there are cost-related barriers, while noting higher hypoglycaemia risk with NPH/premixed human insulin than analogues. Knowing which one is in use decides whether a switch is a cost rescue or a hypoglycaemia rescue.
features.standard: WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2 footnote 1; ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Recommendation 9.30 and Table 9.2)
features.quote: HEARTS-D: "Insulin analogues are not recommended for routine use as they are substantially more costly than human insulin and there is considerable uncertainty over their benefits, especially in people with type 2 diabetes." / ADA 9.30: "In adults with diabetes and cost-related barriers, consider use of lower-cost medications for glycemic management (i.e., metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, and human insulin)..."
features.requires: None — history; ideally verify against the vial/pen label
features.resourceLimitedNote: The WHO EML 24th List (2025) carries human short- and intermediate-acting insulin AND long- and rapid-acting analogues, so both tiers are 'essential' on paper. In practice the 2021 WHO insulin access report describes a market shift toward higher-priced analogues that is beginning in low-income countries and may raise the price of human insulin.

features.whyItMatters: Pattern, not dose, is what decides the next move. WHO's primary-care insulin protocol starts as bedtime NPH added to continuing metformin and sulfonylurea. ADA states that when injecting before meals is not feasible, the plan converts to two doses of premixed insulin — so a patient who cannot inject at midday should be moved to premixed twice daily rather than basal-bolus. Pattern also determines where to look when control fails (fasting vs postprandial) and flags overbasalization.
features.standard: WHO HEARTS-D 2020, Annex 1 (Protocol for treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus with insulin); ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Insulin therapy in type 2 diabetes; Fig. 9.5)
features.quote: ADA: "...for an individual treated with basal insulin in whom additional prandial coverage is desired but administering insulin prior to one or more meals is not feasible, the medication plan can be converted to two doses of a premixed insulin." / HEARTS-D Annex 1: "START with 10 units intermediate-acting insulin (NPH) at bedtime. Continue metformin and sulfonylurea."
features.resourceLimitedNote: Pump/AID is not on the WHO EML or the WHO PEN essential-technologies list; keep it in the option set for completeness but never propose it as a step.

features.whyItMatters: A count, not a dose. It sets the consumable quantity that must actually be dispensed (needles or syringes per month) and is the feasibility test for a regimen: if syringes are rationed or reused, a four-injection plan is not deliverable and the regimen must be simplified rather than the patient labelled non-adherent.
features.standard: WHO, Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal, 2021, section 3.8.1 (Devices for dose administration of insulin)
features.quote: A study reported inadequate provision of syringes for the injection of insulins in about half of the surveyed public health systems in low- and middle-income countries. When available, prices of syringes were often high (i.e. up to US$ 0.97 per syringe)...

features.whyItMatters: Device determines which consumable must be supplied and whether a switch of insulin product is even possible: pen devices need brand-specific needles that may be unavailable or dearer than syringe needles, so prescribing a pen insulin to a patient who can only obtain syringes creates a guaranteed interruption.
features.standard: WHO, Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal, 2021, section 3.8.1
features.quote: ...pen devices often require specific needles, which may not be available or are more costly than needles required for conventional dose administration from a vial.
features.requires: None — history; ideally sight the device

features.whyItMatters: WHO names dependence on others to inject as a reason insulin may be unsuitable. If nobody in the household can inject and doses depend on a facility visit, a multi-injection regimen cannot be started at all — the decision is a once-daily regimen, a trained carer, or an oral third agent. It also identifies who needs the injection-technique training.
features.standard: WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2 footnote 2; ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Insulin Administration Technique)
features.quote: ...persons who live alone and are dependent on others to inject them with insulin.

features.whyItMatters: ADA makes examination of administration technique a component of the comprehensive evaluation. Apparent treatment failure caused by faulty technique must trigger retraining, not escalation of therapy — escalating on top of a technique error adds hypoglycaemia risk without fixing the cause.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Insulin Administration Technique; cross-reference Table 4.1)
features.quote: Ensuring that individuals and/or caregivers understand correct insulin administration technique is important to optimize glycemic management and insulin use safety.
features.requires: None — bedside observation; the patient must bring their device

features.whyItMatters: ADA notes the risk of inadvertent intramuscular delivery — with erratic absorption and unexplained hypoglycaemia — is higher with injections into limbs rather than truncal sites, and in leaner people. A patient injecting only into thigh or arm with unexplained lows should be moved to abdomen/buttock and a shorter needle before any change of insulin.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Insulin Administration Technique)
features.quote: IM risk is higher in younger, leaner individuals, with injections into limbs rather than truncal sites (abdomen, buttocks), and with longer needles.

options.display: Injects the same spot each time

features.whyItMatters: Rotation is the modifiable cause of lipohypertrophy. Recording 'no rotation' in a patient with erratic control means the intervention is re-education and a site plan — a cheap fix that must be tried before changing insulin type or adding an agent.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Insulin Administration Technique), citing FITTER Forward expert recommendations
features.quote: Injection or infusion site rotation is necessary to avoid lipohypertrophy, an accumulation of subcutaneous fat in response to the adipogenic actions of insulin at a site of multiple injections.

features.whyItMatters: Lipohypertrophy is the commonest examinable cause of unexplained hypoglycaemia and glycaemic variability in an insulin user. Finding it changes the plan to 'move injections to unaffected tissue and re-educate' and warns that absorption from healthy tissue will be faster — a safety issue that must be flagged before any intensification.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Insulin Administration Technique)
features.quote: Lipohypertrophy appears as soft, smooth raised areas several centimeters in breadth and can contribute to erratic insulin absorption, increased glycemic variability, and unexplained hypoglycemic episodes.
features.requires: Nothing — bedside inspection and palpation of injection sites
features.resourceLimitedNote: Free and equipment-free, which makes it one of the highest-value fields in a low-resource setting. Needs privacy for abdominal/buttock exposure, and a same-gender chaperone where culturally required — build that into the workflow or the field will be left blank.

features.whyItMatters: WHO reports that the cost of syringes has driven needle reuse in almost all surveyed low- and middle-income countries, compromising safe injection and exposing patients to infection. Recording it triggers two distinct actions — an infection/injection-site safety intervention, and a supply intervention to actually dispense enough needles — neither of which is prompted by a glucose value.
features.standard: WHO, Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal, 2021, section 3.8.1
features.quote: The unaffordable cost of syringes had led to reuse of needles in almost all countries surveyed, which had compromised safe injection of insulins and exposed patients to the risk of infections.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Ask this non-judgementally; reuse is usually a rationing decision, not carelessness. A tool that codes it as 'non-adherence' will get false negatives.

options.display: Cool place, no refrigeration (e.g. clay pot, shaded store)

features.whyItMatters: Cold-chain capacity at home decides whether insulin can be prescribed for home use at all. WHO records that people without home refrigeration may have to travel to a clinic daily for injections, and that ambient temperatures in many settings exceed the permitted in-use range. This changes the dispensing interval, the vial-vs-pen choice, the in-use expiry counselling, and sometimes the decision to use insulin at all.
features.standard: WHO, Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal, 2021, sections 3.1 and 3.5
features.quote: Manufacturers' specifications require unopened insulin vials to be stored at 2–8°C, while storage at room temperature (25–30°C) is usually permitted for the 4-week usage period during use. However, room temperatures in many settings often exceed these requirements. / ...people without access to refrigeration at home may need to travel daily to the nearest health clinic for injections and monitoring.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Do NOT let the tool imply that ambient storage is sanctioned. WHO cites a study suggesting stability up to 37°C over four weeks but explicitly states more research is needed; treat this field as a constraint to plan around, not as permission.

features.whyItMatters: WHO PEN makes SMBG an offer conditional on insulin use and clinical need, so this field decides whether a monitoring plan is even indicated. Practically it decides whether an insulin dose change can be made safely: a patient with no home readings cannot have insulin titrated remotely and must be reviewed in person, and a rising HbA1c with zero readings is a monitoring failure, not necessarily a drug failure.
features.standard: WHO PEN 2020, section 2.6 Self-care (Diabetes); ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 7 (Recommendations 7.10–7.13)
features.quote: People with type 1 and type 2 diabetes on insulin should be offered self-monitoring of blood glucose based on individual clinical need.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Strip supply, not clinical need, is usually the binding constraint. Record the frequency the patient ACHIEVES, not the frequency prescribed, and always read it alongside test_strip_supply — otherwise low frequency will be misread as non-adherence.

options.display: Before driving or other critical tasks

features.whyItMatters: Timing decides which part of the regimen can be adjusted. Fasting-only readings can justify a basal change but cannot detect postprandial failure; without overnight or bedtime readings, nocturnal hypoglycaemia is invisible and WHO's protocol explicitly forbids increasing insulin when nocturnal hypoglycaemia is occurring. This field is what makes a titration decision defensible.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 7 (Recommendation 7.11); WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2 (Monitoring of glycaemic control); WHO HEARTS-D Annex 1
features.quote: ADA 7.11: "...checking when fasting, prior to meals and snacks, after meals, at bedtime, in the middle of the night, prior to, during, and after exercise, when hypoglycemia is suspected... and prior to and while performing critical tasks such as driving." / HEARTS-D: "More informative is a combination of FPG and postprandial plasma glucose (2 hours after breakfast)."
features.resourceLimitedNote: Where strips are scarce, a structured few-point profile is far more useful than the same number of random readings; the field should support planning that, not just counting.

options.display: Owns a meter that is broken or has no batteries
No meter — tested at the facility only
No access to glucose testing at all

features.whyItMatters: ADA requires that people using CGM still have access to blood glucose monitoring at all times, and WHO PEN lists a glucometer and strips as core primary-care technologies. If the patient has no meter, home insulin titration is unsafe and the plan must switch to facility-based review intervals — a scheduling decision, not just a note.
features.standard: WHO PEN 2020, Annex 4.3 Essential technologies and tools; ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 7 (Recommendations 7.10, 7.12)
features.quote: WHO PEN Annex 4.3 TECHNOLOGIES: "...Glucometer / Blood glucose test strips..." / ADA 7.10: "People with diabetes should be provided with blood glucose monitoring (BGM) devices as indicated by their circumstances, preferences, and treatment."
features.requires: None to record; the meter itself is the resource in question
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO reports that in low-, middle- and upper-middle-income countries fewer than 50% of primary health care facilities have the supplies needed for glucose measurement, and that meter accuracy varies — a considerable proportion of marketed devices do not meet ISO accuracy standards. Do not treat a home reading as equivalent to a laboratory value.

features.whyItMatters: Strips are the recurring cost that quietly ends self-monitoring, and they are frequently excluded from schemes that do cover insulin. If strips are unavailable, prescribing an intensive regimen that depends on home readings is unsafe; the correct decision is a simpler, lower-hypoglycaemia-risk regimen with facility monitoring.
features.standard: WHO, Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal, 2021, section 3.8.2
features.quote: Studies have also noted that health insurance schemes in countries with limited resources, such as Ghana and the Plurinational State of Bolivia, sometimes provide insulin, but rarely provide the test strips for glucose monitoring.
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO describes a 'freemium' practice where meters are given free or cheap but lock the user into high-priced proprietary strips, with 90–97% of supplier revenue coming from strips. Record the meter BRAND alongside this if procurement decisions are ever driven from the record — strip compatibility is the real constraint.

features.whyItMatters: Where CGM is present, ADA recommends near-daily use and uninterrupted supply, and the metrics it produces (time in range, time below range) replace isolated glucose values as the basis for changing therapy. Where it is absent, none of those targets can be applied — so this field gates which glycaemic-assessment logic the tool is allowed to run.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 7 (Recommendations 7.15–7.18, Table 7.3)
features.quote: 7.16 In people with diabetes on insulin therapy, CGM devices should be used as close to daily as possible for maximal benefit. A People with diabetes should have uninterrupted access to their supplies to minimize gaps in CGM.
features.requires: CGM sensor, reader or smartphone, and a continuing sensor supply
features.resourceLimitedNote: Realistically absent at Ugandan public primary and most secondary level: CGM appears in neither the WHO PEN essential-technologies list nor the WHO EML 24th List. Every device ADA tabulates is a proprietary brand. Keep the field so private/tertiary patients can be recorded, but the engine must never propose CGM as a step in the resource-limited tier.

features.whyItMatters: Decides whether a refill must be issued at this visit rather than at the next scheduled one. A patient who leaves the clinic with under a week of insulin and a two-month review date will have a guaranteed interruption; catching it converts a future emergency presentation into a dispensing action today.
features.standard: WHO, Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal, 2021, section 3.5 (Supply and distribution chain management)
features.quote: A well-managed supply and distribution chain is critical to timely access to medicines and health products, as it ensures supply efficiency and continuity, and maintains product quality and affordability.
features.requires: None — history; ask the patient to bring packs
features.resourceLimitedNote: The WHO source supports supply continuity as a principle; it does not define numeric thresholds. The bands above are pragmatic and should be presented as prompts, not as a guideline-derived rule.

features.whyItMatters: This is the field that stops the ladder from being climbed for the wrong reason. Every WHO escalation and referral step is explicitly conditioned on the goal not being met DESPITE adherence. If glycaemia is uncontrolled because the patient had no medicine for three weeks, the correct action is to restore supply and re-review — adding a sulfonylurea or starting insulin on top of an interrupted regimen escalates hypoglycaemia risk while leaving the real cause untouched.
features.standard: WHO HEARTS-D 2020, Fig. 2 (Type 2 diabetes management protocol derived from WHO-PEN) and section 4 (Criteria for referral)
features.quote: IF goal not achieved despite adherence to medication and [lifestyle change] / Non-emergency referral should occur if...: glycaemia treatment goal is not achieved despite compliance to treatment with oral medication (and insulin)

options.display: Medicine out of stock at the facility
Could not travel to collect it
Ran out before the next appointment
Told to stop by a health worker
Using herbal or alternative therapy instead

features.whyItMatters: Each reason routes to a different intervention and they are not interchangeable: a stock-out escalates to the facility/pharmacy, unaffordability triggers a switch to a lower-cost class, inability to travel triggers a longer dispensing interval or community collection, and side effects trigger a change of agent. Collapsing all of these into 'non-adherent' produces the wrong action in most cases.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Recommendations 9.29–9.30) and Section 1 (Cost Considerations); WHO insulin access report 2021, section 3.5
features.quote: 9.29 Routinely assess all people with diabetes for financial obstacles that could impede their diabetes management. Clinicians, members of the diabetes care team, and social services professionals should work collaboratively, as appropriate and feasible, to support these individuals by implementing strategies to reduce costs, thereby improving their access to evidence-based care.
features.resourceLimitedNote: 'Using herbal or alternative therapy' is included because it is a real and common reason for interruption in this setting; it is a prompt for a conversation, not a judgement, and no such option is enumerated in the WHO or ADA sources.

features.whyItMatters: Separates system failure from patient behaviour, which is the difference between escalating to the pharmacy/district supply chain and counselling the patient. It also drives the immediate clinical workaround: if gliclazide is out but glibenclamide is on the shelf, the prescriber needs the age and hypoglycaemia-risk check before substituting within the class. Recorded across a clinic it is also the only signal that a facility has a supply problem.
features.standard: WHO PEN 2020, Annex 4.1 Health facility assessment (Medicines) and Annex 4.2 Core list of medicines; WHO insulin access report 2021 (Monitor and report shortages)
features.quote: WHO PEN Annex 4.1, Medicines: "Are essential NCD drugs available? (metformin, amlodipine, etc.)" / WHO 2021: "Monitor shortages of insulins through the Global Notification System for Shortages and Stockouts"
features.requires: None — history; corroborate with the facility pharmacy where possible
features.resourceLimitedNote: WHO PEN's core medicine list contains metformin, glibenclamide and insulin only — so a stock-out prompt built around gliclazide, SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs will not match what a Ugandan primary facility is expected to hold.

options.display: Skipped doses to make supply last
Delayed or did not fill the prescription

features.whyItMatters: ADA names this 'cost-related medication nonadherence' and makes a specific recommendation for what to do about it: move to lower-cost classes — metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones and human insulin — weighed against their hypoglycaemia and weight risks. It also identifies insulin rationing, which is a direct DKA and death risk. Two-thirds of people with chronic illness who skip medicines for cost never tell their clinician, so this must be an explicit field rather than an open note.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Recommendation 9.30) and Section 1 (Cost Considerations)
features.quote: Medication underuse due to cost has been termed "cost-related medication nonadherence"... Based on a national survey conducted in 2021, 18.6% of U.S. adults with type 1 diabetes and 15.8% of adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes reported rationing (i.e., skipping, taking less, and/or delaying) their insulin to save money.
features.resourceLimitedNote: ADA's cost discussion and its price tables (AWP/NADAC, US insulin copay caps) are US-specific and must not be surfaced to a Ugandan user. The BEHAVIOUR being captured is universal; the remedies ADA lists are not.

features.whyItMatters: Determines whether a proposed class is actually reachable for this patient before it is prescribed. A fully out-of-pocket patient cannot sustain an analogue insulin or an SGLT2 inhibitor, and a donated supply can end without warning — both change which rung of the ladder is safe to choose. It also identifies the schemes that cover insulin but not strips, which predicts monitoring failure.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Recommendation 9.29) and Section 1 (Tailoring Treatment for Social Context, Recommendation 1.7)
features.quote: 1.7 During clinical encounters, assess for social determinants of health, including food insecurity, A housing insecurity, financial barriers, health insurance and health care access, environmental and neighborhood factors, and social capital/social community support, B to inform treatment decisions, with referral to appropriate local community resources.
features.resourceLimitedNote: The option list is a local-context guess shaped for Uganda; ADA and WHO do not enumerate payment categories. Treat these values as configurable per country rather than as a standard-derived code set.

features.display: Travel time to where medicines are collected
features.whyItMatters: Sets the dispensing interval and, for insulin, decides whether a regimen is deliverable at all. WHO notes that people without home refrigeration may need to travel daily to the nearest clinic for injections and monitoring, and that travel may also be required when insulin is only prescribed at secondary or tertiary level. A four-hour journey makes a monthly refill and any facility-administered regimen unrealistic — the answer is a longer dispensing interval or a nearer collection point, not more counselling.
features.standard: WHO, Keeping the 100-year-old promise: making insulin access universal, 2021, section 3.5; WHO PEN 2020, Annex 4.1 Health facility assessment (Referral system)
features.quote: In many resource-limited countries, people without access to refrigeration at home may need to travel daily to the nearest health clinic for injections and monitoring. Travel may also be required if insulin prescriptions are only available from secondary or tertiary health care facilities. / WHO PEN Annex 4.1: "Nearest referral centre (approximately in kms)"
features.resourceLimitedNote: Travel TIME is more decision-relevant than distance in km where roads and transport costs dominate, though WHO PEN's facility form records km. No source defines a threshold at which management should change, so this field must inform a clinician judgement, not fire an automatic rule.

features.display: Can the patient feel their low glucose
features.whyItMatters: Impaired awareness dramatically raises the risk of severe (level 3) hypoglycaemia, and ADA recommends screening at least yearly in anyone at risk. A 'no' answer changes the plan concretely: relax the glycaemic target, avoid glibenclamide, deintensify rather than intensify, and it is one of HEARTS-D's named reasons not to use glibenclamide at all.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6 (Hypoglycemia risk assessment); WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2 (Glibenclamide)
features.quote: To efficiently screen for impaired hypoglycemia awareness in clinical practice, clinicians can ask a single question based on these tools such as "Can you always feel when your blood glucose is low?" and follow "No" responses with a more detailed evaluation.
features.resourceLimitedNote: One of the cheapest high-yield fields available: no equipment, one question, and it directly changes agent choice and target. Note the polarity carefully when coding — 'No' is the abnormal answer.

features.display: Severe hypoglycaemia requiring another person's help (last 12 months)
features.whyItMatters: Level 3 hypoglycaemia is defined by needing assistance, irrespective of the glucose reading, so it is capturable by history alone with no meter. Frequent severe hypoglycaemia is an explicit WHO reason to relax the HbA1c target (e.g. to <8%), and it should trigger stopping glibenclamide and reviewing insulin rather than intensifying.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 6 (Table 6.4 Classification of hypoglycemia); WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 2 (Targets for glycaemic control)
features.quote: Level 3: A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia, irrespective of glucose level. / HEARTS-D: "The HbA1c target can be relaxed (e.g. to <8% or <64 mmol/mol) in people with frequent severe hypoglycaemia, advanced complications or low life-expectancy."
features.requires: Nothing — history only, no glucose value needed
features.resourceLimitedNote: Deliberately defined by the need for assistance rather than by a measured glucose, so it remains recordable where no meter was present during the episode.

options.display: Not on insulin or at high hypoglycaemia risk

features.whyItMatters: ADA recommends glucagon for everyone taking insulin or at high hypoglycaemia risk, with carers taught where it is and how to give it. Where glucagon is genuinely unobtainable, that is not a nil finding — it changes the safety plan to oral carbohydrate rescue instructions for the household and a lower threshold for choosing a regimen with less hypoglycaemia risk.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 9 (Recommendation 9.28); WHO HEARTS-D 2020, section 3 (Hypoglycaemia)
features.quote: 9.28 Glucagon should be prescribed for all individuals taking insulin or at high risk for hypoglycemia. A Family, caregivers, school personnel, and others providing support to these individuals should know its location and be educated on how to administer it. Glucagon preparations that do not require reconstitution are preferred. B
features.requires: Glucagon supply (on the WHO EML 24th List, section 18.6, as 1 mg powder plus diluent)
features.resourceLimitedNote: HEARTS-D states plainly: "Intramuscular injection of glucagon can also resolve hypoglycaemia, but it is rarely available in primary care." The EML form requires reconstitution, which is exactly the presentation ADA de-prioritises. Expect 'not available in this setting' to be the modal answer and make the oral-carbohydrate rescue pathway the default teaching.

instruments.name: ARMS — Adherence to Refills and Medications Scale (12-item)
instruments.purpose: Self-reported medication adherence covering BOTH taking medicines as prescribed and refilling them on schedule. Developed and validated in low-literacy patients with chronic disease, which makes it the most defensible off-the-shelf option for this deployment; the refill subscale is the part that maps onto supply interruption rather than forgetfulness.
instruments.scoring: Each item scored 1–4 on a four-point scale ('none of the time', 'some of the time', 'most of the time', 'all of the time'). Item 12 is reverse-coded, then all items are summed. LOWER scores indicate better adherence.
instruments.cutoffs: PhenX reports that scores can be dichotomised as <=12 versus >12 for the full 12-item scale. Note that 12 is the floor of the scale, so this cut-off means 'any reported non-adherence at all'.
instruments.licence: NOT free for our use. Emory University holds copyright. The stated terms are academic and non-profit purposes only; commercial or for-profit use requires permission and a licence from the Emory OTT Licensing Team before use. Translation or modification is not permitted, any derivative work is owned by Emory, and the Emory copyright notice must be retained. CONSEQUENCE: MedSync must not embed ARMS items — nor a Luganda or Swahili translation — without an executed Emory licence. Until then, use unscored bespoke access questions (the features above) instead.

instruments.name: MMAS-8 — Morisky Medication Adherence Scale (8-item)
instruments.purpose: Widely cited self-reported medication adherence screen. Listed here specifically so it is ruled OUT rather than reached for by default, since it is the instrument most teams propose first.
instruments.scoring: Not reproduced here — the item wording and scoring algorithm are the copyrighted content and were deliberately not retrieved.
instruments.cutoffs: Not retrieved.
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED — cannot be embedded. Copyright is held by MMAS Research LLC (Donald E. Morisky). Use is protected by US copyright law and permission is required; a paid licence agreement must be obtained in advance. Enforcement is active and retrospective: papers have been retracted for unlicensed use and authors have been billed retroactive fees described as thousands to tens of thousands of dollars. The editorial warning reviewed here recommends that researchers instead use alternatives licensed under Creative Commons or open-source agreements. Do not implement MMAS-8 in MedSync in any form, including paraphrase.

instruments.name: Gold score (single-question impaired hypoglycaemia awareness)
instruments.purpose: Assessment of impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia in people on insulin or sulfonylureas — the risk state that should stop intensification and prompt a relaxed target and avoidance of glibenclamide.
instruments.scoring: NOT VERIFIED. I read only ADA's description of it, which names Gold as a validated single-question tool alongside Pedersen-Bjergaard, and Clarke and HypoA-Q as longer multi-domain questionnaires. I did not retrieve the Gold instrument itself, so its item wording, its Likert range and its cut-off are not confirmed here and must not be implemented from memory.
instruments.cutoffs: Not retrieved — do not encode a cut-off from this report.
instruments.licence: NOT VERIFIED. Do not embed Gold, Clarke, Pedersen-Bjergaard or HypoA-Q until each one's copyright status has been checked against the original publication.

instruments.name: ADA single screening question for impaired hypoglycaemia awareness
instruments.purpose: Practical bedside screen that ADA offers in place of a formal instrument: ask 'Can you always feel when your blood glucose is low?' and follow a 'No' with a more detailed evaluation. This is the wording implemented in the hypoglycaemia_awareness feature above.
instruments.scoring: Not a scored instrument. Binary/graded response; a 'No' response is the trigger for further evaluation.
instruments.cutoffs: Not applicable — 'No' is the actionable answer.
instruments.licence: Text quoted from the ADA Standards of Care 2026, which PMC carries under the notice that readers may use the work for educational, non-commercial purposes if properly cited and unaltered. This is a plain clinical question rather than a proprietary instrument, but confirm ADA reuse permissions before shipping the wording verbatim in a commercial product.

unverifiable: NO DOSE FIELDS ARE PROPOSED ANYWHERE IN THIS SET, by instruction. Note the consequence: insulin_regimen_pattern and insulin_injections_per_day cannot detect over- or under-dosing, and the WHO titration protocol (HEARTS-D Annex 1, adjust by 1-2 units at 3-day intervals) cannot be executed from these fields alone. Titration must stay with the clinician.

FITTER Forward specifics could NOT be retrieved. Mayo Clinic Proceedings (Klonoff DC, Berard L, Franco DR, et al. Mayo Clin Proc 2025;100:682-699, doi 10.1016/j.mayocp.2025.01.004) returned HTTP 403 and it is not open access on PMC. Search-engine summaries described injections at least 1 cm apart, quadrant rotation every 3-4 days, a 4 mm needle for everyone regardless of BMI, and lipohypertrophy screening 6-monthly for the first 2 years then annually. I did NOT read these in a retrieved document and they must not be encoded as guidance. What IS verified is ADA's own summary of that source: rotation is necessary, 4 mm pen needles reduce inadvertent IM delivery, and sites should be examined for lipohypertrophy.
Gold, Clarke, Pedersen-Bjergaard and HypoA-Q instruments: item wording, scoring, cut-offs and copyright status all unverified. Only ADA's one-sentence description of them was read.

Hunger Vital Sign and every other named food-insecurity screener: not retrieved. ADA Recommendation 1.7 requires assessing food insecurity, and it is directly relevant here because food insecurity plus a sulfonylurea or insulin is a hypoglycaemia risk, but I verified no specific instrument, its items or its licence.

MARS-5, Hill-Bone, DSMQ, the Insulin Treatment Appraisal Scale and other adherence or insulin-attitude instruments: not searched or retrieved. There may be a better-licensed alternative to ARMS that I have not surfaced.

No validated PATIENT-level instrument for medication access, affordability or stock-out exposure was found. The WHO/HAI medicine prices and availability methodology is a facility survey, not a patient questionnaire, and I did not retrieve it. Every access field above is therefore a bespoke item, not a validated scale — do not report them as a score.

UGANDA-SPECIFIC SOURCING IS ENTIRELY ABSENT. I did not retrieve the Uganda Clinical Guidelines, the Uganda Essential Medicines and Health Supplies List, National Medical Stores supply data, or any Mulago formulary. Which glucose-lowering classes are actually stocked at each Ugandan facility level is unverified, and the resourceLimitedNote fields extrapolate from WHO PEN and the WHO EML instead. This should be closed before deployment.

Specifically unverified: whether gliclazide (preferred by HEARTS-D and carried on the EML 24th List) or glibenclamide (the sulfonylurea on WHO PEN's core primary-care medicine list) is the agent actually available in Ugandan public facilities. The within-class switch logic in sulfonylurea_agent depends on this.

No source gives a numeric SMBG frequency target by regimen. ADA 7.11 lists the SITUATIONS in which to check but states no times-per-day figure, and WHO PEN conditions SMBG on 'individual clinical need' without quantifying it. The frequency bands in smbg_frequency are recording conveniences, not thresholds, and no rule should fire on them.

No source defines a threshold of travel time, distance, or days-of-supply-remaining at which management should change. Those three fields inform clinician judgement only; the option bands are pragmatic and unsourced.

WHO PEN and HEARTS-D are SILENT on CGM, injection site rotation, lipohypertrophy, needle length and needle reuse technique. Those fields rest on ADA 2026 plus the 2021 WHO insulin access report alone, so the resource-limited tier has no guidance of its own for them.

Insulin thermostability at ambient temperature is NOT settled. The WHO report cites Kaufmann et al. suggesting vials may remain stable at oscillating ambient temperatures up to 37C over four weeks, but states additional research is needed to determine efficacy and safety. Do not let insulin_home_storage imply that storage without refrigeration is sanctioned.
