Status is LICENCE_RISK rather than CONFIRMED because the operative state for a downstream implementer is unresolved: none of Gold, Clarke, Pedersen-Bjergaard or HypoA-Q has had its copyright status checked against its original publication, so none may be embedded.
audit.correction: Do not implement any of the four. Use the ADA single question instead (subject to the ADA licence caveat below), which is the only awareness item in this pack whose wording I actually verified.

audit.reason: The item wording is confirmed verbatim in ADA Section 6: clinicians 'can ask a single question based on these tools such as "Can you always feel when your blood glucose is low?" and follow "No" responses with a more detailed evaluation.' The characterisation as a plain clinical question rather than a scored proprietary instrument is fair, and 'No' being the actionable answer is correct. However the licence report is materially incomplete and understates the risk, which is why this is LICENCE_RISK rather than CONFIRMED.
audit.correction: The PMC notice on this article contains a clause that was omitted: '(c) 2025 by the American Diabetes Association. Readers may use this work for educational, noncommercial purposes if properly cited and unaltered. The version of record may be linked at https://diabetesjournals.org/care, but ADA permission is required to post this work on any third-party site or platform. This publication and its contents may not be reproduced, distributed, or used for text or data mining, machine learning, or similar technologies without prior written permission.' The prohibition on reproduction, distribution and machine-learning use without prior written permission bears directly on a commercial decision-support product that encodes ADA recommendations, and it applies to ADA Sections 1, 6, 7 and 9 — every ADA source in this pack, not just this question. Obtain written ADA permission before shipping any ADA-derived wording or logic. Separately, and unflagged anywhere in the submission: all three WHO sources (PEN 2020, HEARTS-D 2020, insulin access 2021) are CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO, i.e. NonCommercial plus ShareAlike. Clinical facts are not copyrightable, but verbatim reproduction of WHO's tables, protocol figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Annex 1) and bulleted contraindication lists in a commercial product would engage both the NC and SA terms. This needs a licensing decision before launch.

bundle.domain: Hypoglycaemia history and impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia (IAH)

features.display: Level 1 hypoglycaemia frequency (glucose <3.9 mmol/L / <70 mg/dL and ≥3.0 mmol/L / ≥54 mg/dL)
features.whyItMatters: Repeated level 1 exposure is the modifiable cause of blunted counterregulation and impaired awareness. ADA lists multiple recent level 1 episodes as a hypoglycaemia risk factor; a high count is the trigger to de-intensify insulin or secretagogue and raise glycaemic targets rather than intensify therapy.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 6 — hypoglycaemia classification and Table 6.5 risk factors
features.quote: Level 1: Glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L)
features.requires: Glucose meter with test strips, or CGM, to confirm the level; otherwise symptom-based self-report
features.resourceLimitedNote: Most Ugandan patients on insulin or glibenclamide self-monitor rarely or never — strip cost is the binding constraint. The 'unknown — not monitoring' option is mandatory so missing data is never silently recorded as zero episodes.

features.whyItMatters: ADA states that one or more level 2 or level 3 events should trigger reevaluation of the treatment plan, which may include de-intensifying or replacing glucose-lowering medication. This field is the direct trigger for that decision, and level 2 exposure is what drives progression to impaired awareness.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 6 — hypoglycaemia classification
features.quote: Level 2: Glucose <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)
features.requires: Meter or CGM able to read below 3.0 mmol/L
features.resourceLimitedNote: Distinguishing level 1 from level 2 requires an actual reading. Where no meter exists, do not force a choice — capture 'unknown' and rely on the symptom-threshold and third-party fields instead.

features.display: Number of level 3 (severe) hypoglycaemia episodes requiring help from another person — last 12 months
features.whyItMatters: The count of severe episodes in the past year is the strongest single predictor of another severe episode and of a hypoglycaemia-related driving collision, and is an ADA major risk factor. One or more mandates treatment de-intensification, a rescue plan and a driving conversation; two or more in 12 months roughly quadrupled driving-mishap risk in the prospective data cited by ADA.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 6 — level 3 definition; ADA Diabetes and Driving statement — risk quantification
features.standardVersion: ADA SoC 2024; ADA Diabetes and Driving 2014 (Diabetes Care 37(Suppl 1):S97–S103)
features.quote: Level 3: A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment
features.requires: History only — no equipment. Level 3 is defined by needing third-party assistance, not by a glucose value.
features.resourceLimitedNote: This is the highest-value field in the whole domain for a low-resource setting: it needs no meter, no lab and no CGM. Ask it of the patient and, where present, a household member, since the patient may have been unconscious for the event.

features.display: Time since most recent level 3 (severe) episode
features.whyItMatters: Recency, not just count, determines the plan. ADA asks physicians to state whether a severe episode requiring third-party intervention occurred within the previous 2 years and when it happened — that window drives licensing restriction. Recency also defines the 2–3 week strict-hypoglycaemia-avoidance period used to try to restore awareness.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — physician evaluation information set
features.quote: whether the driver has had an episode of severe hypoglycemia requiring intervention from another person within the previous 2 years (and when this happened)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Recall of exact dates is poor where there are no written records. Allow coarse buckets (this month / 1–3 months / 3–12 months / 1–2 years / >2 years / never) rather than forcing a date.

features.display: Lost consciousness due to hypoglycaemia in the last 12 months
features.whyItMatters: ADA specifies this exact question, with this exact 12-month lookback, as a screening item that should trigger formal fitness-to-drive evaluation. A positive answer changes three decisions at once: relax glycaemic targets, ensure a third-party rescue plan exists, and advise against driving pending review.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — short screening questionnaire for at-risk drivers
features.quote: whether the driver has, within the past 12 months, lost consciousness due to hypoglycemia
features.resourceLimitedNote: None — bedside history question. Ask a family member as well; patients cannot report their own loss of consciousness.

features.display: What was needed to treat the most recent severe episode

options.display: Oral sugar/carbohydrate given by another person

features.whyItMatters: Separates a severe episode retrieved with oral sugar by a relative from one that needed IV dextrose and admission. This grades the true severity, determines whether the household rescue plan worked or failed, and is the field that justifies prescribing glucagon or teaching an oral rescue protocol.
features.standard: Not a standardised item set — derived from the ADA level 3 definition (assistance required for recovery) and ADA recommendation 6.16 on glucagon provision
features.standardVersion: ADA SoC 2026 (recommendation 6.16, read via third-party summary)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Glucagon is frequently unavailable in Ugandan facilities, so 'oral carbohydrate given by another person' and 'IV dextrose' will dominate. Do not treat absence of glucagon use as evidence of lesser severity.

features.display: Confirmed low glucose readings at night — last month

options.display: Unknown — never checks glucose at night / no CGM

features.whyItMatters: Nocturnal hypoglycaemia is largely unwitnessed and is a principal driver of hypoglycaemia-associated autonomic failure. Detecting it changes the basal insulin dose and timing, prompts a bedtime snack (which ADA describes for preventing overnight hypoglycaemia), and is often the only correctable cause of impaired awareness.
features.standard: Field wording adapted from the nocturnal-hypoglycaemia item used in the Gold/Clarke/Pedersen comparison study; bedtime-snack rationale from ADA SoC Section 6
features.standardVersion: Gandhi et al., Diabetes Ther 2020 (CC BY-NC 4.0); ADA SoC 2024
features.quote: how often in the last month have you had readings < 3.5 mmol/L at night?
features.requires: Overnight glucose testing or CGM to answer positively
features.resourceLimitedNote: Without CGM or overnight finger-prick testing this field will almost always read 'unknown' in Uganda. A 'never' answer here is NOT reassurance — it usually means nobody looked. Pair it with the surrogate-symptom field and weight that more heavily.

options.display: Bed partner or family reports night sweating
Vivid dreams, nightmares or restless sleep
Unusual tiredness or feeling unwell on waking
Family found the patient confused or unrousable at night

features.whyItMatters: Where no overnight glucose data exists, these are the only route to detecting nocturnal hypoglycaemia. A positive surrogate cluster is sufficient to reduce or re-time the evening/basal insulin dose without waiting for a confirmatory reading, which is the realistic decision path in a facility without CGM.
features.standard: Not a standardised instrument — clinical surrogate set assembled for low-resource use
features.requires: History only; a household observer improves yield
features.resourceLimitedNote: Designed specifically for settings with no CGM. Include 'sleeps alone — no observer' so the engine can down-weight a negative answer rather than reading it as absence of nocturnal hypoglycaemia.

features.display: Glucose level at which the patient first notices any hypoglycaemia symptom
features.whyItMatters: This is the physiological definition of awareness. A threshold at or below 3.0 mmol/L means symptoms now arrive at or after the onset of cognitive impairment, so there is no usable warning. That finding drives raising glycaemic targets, a period of strict hypoglycaemia avoidance to try to restore the threshold, and a fitness-to-drive discussion.
features.standard: Construct underlying the Clarke questionnaire glycaemic-threshold items (anchored at 3.5 mmol/L in the minimally modified version) and the HypoA-Q symptom-level items
features.quote: adjusted glucose thresholds in questions 5–6 to 3.5 mmol/L
features.requires: Glucose meter or CGM readings paired with symptomatic episodes on at least a few occasions
features.resourceLimitedNote: Requires the patient to have measured glucose while symptomatic. Where strips are scarce, record a patient estimate and mark it explicitly as estimated so downstream logic can discount it; do not leave it blank, because the estimate still carries signal.

features.display: Symptom categories still experienced during hypoglycaemia

options.display: Autonomic — sweating, trembling, palpitations, hunger, anxiety
Neuroglycopenic — confusion, drowsiness, slurred speech, incoordination, odd behaviour, visual disturbance

features.whyItMatters: Loss of autonomic warning with isolated or predominant neuroglycopenic symptoms is the clinical signature of impaired awareness: the person becomes confused before they know they are low. That pattern alone makes driving unsafe and mandates target relaxation, and it is elicitable by history with no equipment whatsoever.
features.standard: Autonomic / neuroglycopenic / malaise symptom-level construct as used in the HypoA-Q symptom-level subscale; neuroglycopenic-predominance is the basis of the Gold ≥4 cut-off
features.quote: 6a BGLs at which autonomic symptoms occur … 6b BGLs at which neuroglycopenic symptoms occur … 6c BGLs at which malaise symptoms occur
features.resourceLimitedNote: None — this is the best equipment-free discriminator of impaired awareness available. Individual symptom wordings must be translated and cognitively tested locally; no validated Luganda version was found.

features.display: Gold score (1 = always aware of hypos starting … 7 = never aware)
features.whyItMatters: A score of ≥4 defines impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia, an ADA major risk factor for severe hypoglycaemia. Crossing that threshold changes the plan concretely: raise glycaemic targets, refer for structured hypoglycaemia-awareness education (ADA grade A), review driving, and re-screen at least annually.
features.standard: Gold score; ADA recommendation to screen at-risk individuals for impaired hypoglycaemia awareness at least annually
features.standardVersion: Gold AE, Macleod KM, Frier BM. Diabetes Care 1994;17(7):697–703; ADA SoC 2026 recommendation 6.11
features.quote: A score of ≥4 suggests impaired hypoglycaemia awareness; ≤2=normal awareness; 3=borderline.
features.resourceLimitedNote: The only IAH instrument realistically deployable in a busy Ugandan outpatient clinic: one item, no equipment, under a minute. Two problems: (a) no validated local-language translation was found, and (b) no open licence was found — see the instruments list before embedding the item text.

features.display: Pedersen-Bjergaard awareness category (how often aware a hypoglycaemic episode is starting)
features.whyItMatters: Gives a graded awareness category rather than a binary, and the 2022 update showed the middle 'intermediate' group carries a clinically distinct severe-hypoglycaemia risk from the normal group — so an 'Usually' answer is not a normal answer and should still lower the glycaemic target. Also the only one of the three instruments that captures complete unawareness as its own category.
features.standard: Pedersen-Bjergaard method (original and 2022 update)
features.standardVersion: Pedersen-Bjergaard U, Pramming S, Thorsteinsson B. Diabetes Metab Res Rev 2003;19(3):232–240; updated 2022
features.quote: Original method: Normal awareness ("Always"), Impaired awareness ("Usually"/"Occasionally"), Unawareness ("Never")
features.resourceLimitedNote: Equipment-free and quick. Critical implementation warning: two scoring conventions are in use and they are not interchangeable — original scoring gave 61% IAH prevalence in one cohort versus 7% with the revised convention on the same patients. The app must pin one convention and display which one it used on every stored result.

features.display: Awareness of hypos has declined compared with the past
features.whyItMatters: Distinguishes acquired, potentially reversible hypoglycaemia-associated autonomic failure from a long-standing state. A recent decline is the finding that justifies immediate strict hypoglycaemia avoidance and a review of regimen changes over the preceding 3 months, because awareness can be recovered.
features.standard: Construct from the HypoA-Q impaired-awareness subscale (item on being less aware of hypos than previously) — MedSync must use independently authored wording, not the instrument's
features.resourceLimitedNote: None. Note the licence constraint: HypoA-Q is supplied under non-commercial agreement, so this field must be worded independently and must not be presented as a HypoA-Q item or scored on its scale.

features.display: Other people notice the patient is hypoglycaemic before the patient does

options.display: Nobody regularly with the patient to say

features.whyItMatters: Third-party corroboration is objective evidence of impaired awareness and, unlike every glucose-based measure, needs no meter. In a facility with no monitoring this is the single most informative IAH question available, and a positive answer changes the decision to relax targets and to train a household member in rescue treatment.
features.standard: Construct from the HypoA-Q impaired-awareness subscale (item on others recognising hypoglycaemia first) — wording must be independently authored
features.requires: History only; ideally corroborated by an accompanying relative
features.resourceLimitedNote: Well suited to Ugandan practice where patients commonly attend with a relative. The 'no observer' option matters — patients living alone will otherwise answer 'never' and be falsely classified as aware.

features.display: Current glucose-lowering agents capable of causing hypoglycaemia
features.whyItMatters: Only insulin and insulin secretagogues cause hypoglycaemia, so this field determines whether the episodes are drug-induced and which specific drug to change. ADA lists intensive insulin therapy and basal insulin therapy among hypoglycaemia risk factors and directs that hypoglycaemia risk be weighed when selecting medication and glycaemic goals.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care Section 6, Table 6.5 (hypoglycaemia risk factors) and recommendation 6.13
features.standardVersion: ADA SoC 2024 (Table 6.5); recommendation 6.13 numbering from ADA SoC 2026
features.quote: Consider an individual's risk for hypoglycemia (see Table 6.5) when selecting diabetes medications and glycemic goals.
features.requires: Medication history; ideally sight of the actual packets
features.resourceLimitedNote: Glibenclamide is the sulfonylurea most widely stocked in Ugandan public facilities and is long-acting; naming it as its own option rather than lumping it under 'sulfonylurea' is what lets the engine flag the specific switch. Many patients cannot name their drug — allow entry from tablet appearance or the dispensing envelope.

options.display: Known kidney disease, stage not measured

features.whyItMatters: ADA lists end-stage kidney disease as a major hypoglycaemia risk factor and chronic kidney disease as an additional one. Reduced clearance of insulin and sulfonylureas produces prolonged, relapsing hypoglycaemia, so this field changes both the dose and the choice of agent — it is the usual reason to stop glibenclamide outright.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care Section 6, Table 6.5 — hypoglycaemia risk factors
features.quote: End-stage kidney disease
features.resourceLimitedNote: Creatinine is often unavailable at health-centre level and results may be days late. The 'known kidney disease, stage not measured' and 'not measured' options let the risk flag still fire on clinical grounds rather than the field being left empty.

features.whyItMatters: ADA lists cognitive impairment or dementia as a major hypoglycaemia risk factor. It means the patient may be unable to recognise or self-treat an episode regardless of awareness score, which mandates a caregiver-delivered rescue plan, higher glycaemic targets and regimen simplification rather than education aimed at the patient.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care Section 6, Table 6.5 — hypoglycaemia risk factors
features.quote: Cognitive impairment or dementia
features.resourceLimitedNote: Formal cognitive testing is rarely available and most screening tools are poorly validated in Ugandan languages and low-literacy populations. Accept a collateral history of functional decline as sufficient to set this flag.

features.display: Food insecurity, missed meals or fasting

options.display: Food insecurity — not always able to obtain food
Religious or cultural fasting (e.g. Ramadan, Lent)
Irregular meal times due to work or travel

features.whyItMatters: ADA lists food insecurity, low income, homelessness and fasting for religious or cultural reasons as major social risk factors for hypoglycaemia. This is the commonest correctable precipitant in low-income settings, and identifying it switches the intervention from a dose change to meal-timing and regimen redesign, plus pre-emptive dose reduction for planned fasting.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care Section 6, Table 6.5 — major social, economic and cultural risk factors
features.quote: Food insecurity … Fasting for religious/cultural reasons
features.resourceLimitedNote: This is arguably the highest-yield risk field in the Ugandan context and is routinely omitted from imported EMR templates. Ask it neutrally and non-judgementally; patients under-report. A positive answer should suppress any automated prompt to intensify therapy.

features.whyItMatters: ADA lists alcohol or substance use disorder as a hypoglycaemia risk factor and advises that glucose be monitored more frequently for several hours after even moderate alcohol intake. Alcohol causes delayed, often nocturnal, hypoglycaemia and blunts the response to it, so a positive answer changes bedtime carbohydrate advice, basal dose and the driving conversation.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care Section 6, Table 6.5; ADA Diabetes and Driving statement
features.standardVersion: ADA SoC 2024; ADA Diabetes and Driving 2014
features.quote: more frequently for several hours after moderate alcohol intake
features.resourceLimitedNote: Locally brewed spirits (waragi) carry very variable alcohol content, so quantity estimates in standard units are unreliable — the pattern categories are more robust than a units-per-week number here.

features.display: Identified precipitant for the hypoglycaemic episode(s)

options.display: Dose error or wrong insulin given

features.whyItMatters: ADA asks the assessing physician to state whether there was an explanation for the hypoglycaemia, because an explained one-off is managed with education while an unexplained or recurrent episode means the regimen or counterregulation has failed and therapy must be de-intensified. This distinction is also what licensing authorities weigh, and 'no explanation identified' is itself a clinically meaningful answer.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — physician evaluation information set
features.quote: whether there was an explanation for the hypoglycemia
features.requires: History only; renal precipitant needs creatinine
features.resourceLimitedNote: Concurrent malaria, HIV-related illness and undisclosed herbal remedy use are common local precipitants that imported option lists omit — the traditional/herbal medicine option is deliberately included.

options.display: Meter but limited or no strips

features.whyItMatters: ADA requires evidence of sufficient self-monitoring as part of assessing a driver with diabetes. Beyond driving, this field determines how much weight the rest of the record can bear: with no monitoring, episode counts are unreliable and the safe plan is higher targets plus symptom-based rules rather than tight glycaemic control.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — physician evaluation information set
features.quote: whether the driver provides evidence of sufficient self-monitoring of blood glucose
features.requires: Nothing to record; the capability itself requires a meter and consumable strips
features.resourceLimitedNote: Strip cost, not meter cost, is the real barrier — 'meter but limited or no strips' is the modal Ugandan answer and must be distinguishable from 'no meter'. This field should gate any decision-support rule that assumes glucose data exists.

options.display: Household member trained to treat an episode
Fast-acting sugar kept available at home
Carries fast-acting sugar when out of the house

features.whyItMatters: ADA directs that glucagon be prescribed for all individuals taking insulin or at high risk of hypoglycaemia, and that family and caregivers know its location and how to administer it. A patient with level 3 episodes and no rescue plan is the highest-yield intervention in the entire assessment: this field determines what is prescribed and, critically, who is taught.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care Section 6, recommendation 6.16 — glucagon prescribing and caregiver education
features.standardVersion: ADA SoC 2026 (read via third-party guideline summary, not the ADA text)
features.quote: Glucagon should be prescribed for all individuals taking insulin or at high risk for hypoglycemia.
features.requires: Glucagon requires supply chain, cost and cold-chain-independent storage
features.resourceLimitedNote: Glucagon is frequently unavailable and unaffordable in Ugandan practice, and ready-to-use preparations more so. The field deliberately allows 'trained household member + oral rescue supplies' as a first-class recorded plan rather than only recording the absence of glucagon — otherwise every Ugandan patient reads as having no plan.

features.whyItMatters: Gates whether the whole driving-safety branch and the licensing conversation apply at all. ADA treats commercial driving under a separate and stricter framework with periodic medical certification, so the vehicle category changes both the advice given and whether a formal fitness report is required.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — private versus commercial driving frameworks
features.quote: the rules for operating a commercial motor vehicle … are quite different and in many ways more cumbersome for people with diabetes, especially those who use insulin
features.resourceLimitedNote: Boda-boda riding is a very common Ugandan occupation carrying the same hypoglycaemia risk as car driving, but it sits outside any licensing-medical framework, so the risk is invisible unless the option list names it explicitly. It is included for that reason; the option itself is not from the ADA source.

features.display: Hypoglycaemia while driving in the last 12 months

options.display: Mild symptomatic episodes more than once
Severe episode needing assistance while driving

features.whyItMatters: ADA reports that a history of hypoglycaemia while driving is the strongest predictor of a future hypoglycaemia-related driving mishap — stronger than awareness scores. A positive answer mandates a pre-driving glucose rule and, where recurrent or severe, advice to stop driving pending review; it is also the trigger for licensing referral in many jurisdictions.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — predictors of driving mishaps
features.quote: The strongest predictors involved a history of hypoglycemia while driving
features.resourceLimitedNote: Patients may under-report for fear of losing a livelihood, which is more acute where driving is the sole income. Frame the question around safety planning rather than reporting, and record who supplied the answer.

features.display: Hypoglycaemia-related driving mishap or collision in the last 2 years
features.whyItMatters: ADA reports that two collisions in the previous 2 years raised the risk of a further driving mishap by 40%, and that a history of mishaps should be used as a basis for further assessment. This field, with its 2-year window, is what determines whether the patient is counselled, formally evaluated, or advised to stop driving.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — prospective mishap risk data
features.quote: two collisions in the previous 2 years increased their risk by 40%
features.resourceLimitedNote: No accessible crash registry to corroborate self-report in Uganda. Record the source of the information (patient, relative, police record) alongside the count.

features.whyItMatters: ADA advises that at-risk drivers always check glucose before getting behind the wheel and at intervals on journeys of an hour or more, and never begin an extended drive at 3.9–5.0 mmol/L without prophylactic carbohydrate. This field names the exact behaviour to correct and distinguishes a patient who will not check from one who cannot.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — counselling recommendations for drivers at risk of disruptive hypoglycaemia
features.quote: never begin an extended drive with low normal blood glucose (e.g., 70–90 mg/dL, 3.9–5.0 mmol/L) without prophylactic carbohydrate consumption
features.requires: A meter and strips to perform the check
features.resourceLimitedNote: The 'cannot — no meter or strips' option is essential and changes the advice entirely: where pre-driving testing is impossible, the safe plan is a timed carbohydrate rule and avoidance of driving after insulin peaks, not a glucose threshold the patient cannot measure.

features.display: Carries fast-acting carbohydrate and meter in the vehicle
features.whyItMatters: ADA counsels drivers at risk of disruptive hypoglycaemia to always carry a glucose meter and a quick-acting source of sugar in the vehicle, and not to resume driving until glucose and cognition have recovered (usually 30–60 minutes). A negative answer is a concrete, cheap, immediately correctable safety gap.
features.standard: ADA Diabetes and Driving — counselling recommendations
features.quote: always carry a blood glucose meter and appropriate snacks, including a quick-acting source of sugar
features.requires: Access to a meter and to purchasable sugar/glucose
features.resourceLimitedNote: Sugar, sweets or soda are cheap and locally available even where meters are not, so the carbohydrate half of this recommendation is fully actionable in Uganda; consider splitting the field so 'carries sugar' can be recorded as achieved independently of 'carries meter'.

features.display: CGM time below range (% of time <3.9 mmol/L; and <3.0 mmol/L)
features.whyItMatters: Where CGM exists it objectively corroborates or refutes self-reported episode counts against the consensus targets of <4% of time below 3.9 mmol/L and <1% below 3.0 mmol/L, and a value above target is a direct instruction to reduce hypoglycaemia exposure. It must supplement, not replace, the awareness questions: the retrieved evidence shows time below range alone discriminates impaired awareness barely better than chance.
features.standard: International consensus CGM targets for time below range, as reported in the IAH assessment narrative review
features.standardVersion: Reported in Berry et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025
features.quote: <4% of time <3.9 mmol/L; <1% of time <3.0 mmol/L
features.requires: Continuous glucose monitoring with at least 14 days of data and adequate sensor wear
features.resourceLimitedNote: CGM is essentially unavailable in the Ugandan public sector. This field must be optional and must never gate the impaired-awareness assessment. The same review reports time below range alone had an AUC of 0.597 for impaired awareness — so its absence loses little diagnostic ground.

features.display: Deliberately keeps glucose high to avoid hypoglycaemia
features.whyItMatters: Identifies fear of hypoglycaemia as the reason for poor glycaemic control. This inverts the management decision: the correct response is structured education, hypoglycaemia-avoidance training and target renegotiation, not the dose increase that a raised HbA1c would otherwise prompt.
features.standard: Not sourced to a retrieved guideline or instrument; formal measurement uses the Hypoglycemia Fear Survey (HFS-II), which was not retrieved and is copyright-restricted
features.resourceLimitedNote: Equipment-free and cheap to ask. Because the validated instrument (HFS-II) cannot be embedded, a single independently worded screening question is the pragmatic substitute — but it should be labelled as a screening prompt, not a score.

instruments.name: Gold score
instruments.purpose: Single-item self-rated screen for impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia (IAH)
instruments.scoring: One question about whether the person knows when their hypos are commencing, rated on a 7-point scale anchored 1 = 'Always aware' to 7 = 'Never aware'. The score is the raw rating. Note: the care-card I retrieved gives the item as "Do you know when your hypos are commencing?" while the 2025 narrative review renders it as "How often do you feel aware of having a low blood sugar? Please score between 1 and 7 on the scale below." — the two retrieved sources disagree on wording.
instruments.cutoffs: ≥4 = impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia; ≤2 = normal awareness; 3 = borderline. (The narrative review states the cut-off more simply as ≥4 = IAH, <4 = normal.)
instruments.licence: NO OPEN LICENCE VERIFIED — DO NOT EMBED THE ITEM TEXT WITHOUT PERMISSION. The original is Gold AE, Macleod KM, Frier BM, Diabetes Care 1994;17(7):697–703, whose copyright sits with the American Diabetes Association. The diabetesonthenet.com care card reproduces the item and the cut-offs with no licence grant, permission notice or copyright statement of any kind. Absence of a stated restriction is not a grant of permission. Safe path: store and display the score and cut-off interpretation (facts, not expression), and obtain written permission from the ADA/authors before rendering the item wording in the product.

instruments.name: Clarke questionnaire (and the minimally modified version, MMCHS)
instruments.purpose: Eight-item questionnaire assessing awareness of hypoglycaemia, the glucose threshold at which symptoms begin, and exposure to moderate and severe episodes
instruments.scoring: Each response is classified as 'A' (normal awareness) or 'R' (reduced awareness); the score is the count of R responses. Retrieved sources disagree on the range: one states 0–8, another states the R score ranges 0–7 because two of the questions are combined to give one answer. Factor analysis of the MMCHS found items 1, 2, 5/6, 7 and 8 measure awareness status while items 3–4 measure severe-hypoglycaemia experience — so the total score mixes two constructs. The 2012 minimally modified version updated question 4 to the current severe-hypoglycaemia definition and set the glucose thresholds in questions 5–6 to 3.5 mmol/L.
instruments.cutoffs: ≥4 R responses = impaired awareness; ≤2 = normal awareness; 3 = indeterminate. (A separate validation study derived an optimal ROC threshold of ≥5 against an insulin-clamp reference, AUC 0.82, sensitivity 83%, specificity 80% — that is a research-derived optimum, not the conventional clinical cut-off.)
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED — DO NOT EMBED. The original is Clarke WL, Cox DJ, Gonder-Frederick LA, et al., Diabetes Care 1995;18(4):517–522 (© American Diabetes Association). The full-instrument PDF I retrieved carries only an attribution line, 'Based on: Clarke W, Cox DJ, Gonder-Frederick LA, Julian D, Schlundt D, Polonsky W. Reduced awareness of hypoglycaemia in adults...', with no licence, no permission statement and no copyright grant. I did not extract the item text. Written permission from the copyright holder is required before any reproduction; the eight-item length makes a fair-dealing argument much weaker than for a single-item scale.

instruments.name: Pedersen-Bjergaard method (original 2003 and 2022 update)
instruments.purpose: Single-item classification of self-estimated state of awareness of hypoglycaemia into graded categories
instruments.scoring: One question about how often the person feels aware of the start of a hypoglycaemic episode, with four response options: Always / Usually / Occasionally / Never. Original classification: 'Always' = normal awareness; 'Usually' or 'Occasionally' = impaired awareness; 'Never' = unawareness. The 2022 update kept the same response options and renamed the middle class from 'impaired' to 'intermediate' awareness, and showed the normal and intermediate groups carry clinically significantly different severe-hypoglycaemia risk.
instruments.cutoffs: CRITICAL IMPLEMENTATION WARNING — two scoring conventions are in circulation and are NOT interchangeable. Original convention ('Usually'/'Occasionally'/'Never' abnormal) gave 61% IAH prevalence in a 100-patient type 1 diabetes cohort; a revised convention ('Always'+'Usually' = normal, 'Occasionally'+'Never' = impaired) gave 7% in the same cohort. For comparison, Gold gave 19% and Clarke 18% in that cohort. Whichever convention is chosen must be pinned in code and displayed on every stored result.
instruments.licence: NO LICENCE VERIFIED — treat as permission-required. The original is Pedersen-Bjergaard U, Pramming S, Thorsteinsson B, Diabetes Metab Res Rev 2003;19(3):232–240 (Wiley). As with the Gold score, storing and interpreting the four-category result is a different act from reproducing the item wording; obtain permission before rendering the wording.

instruments.name: HypoA-Q (Hypoglycaemia Awareness Questionnaire), Impaired Awareness subscale
instruments.purpose: Modern detailed measure of awareness of hypoglycaemia, designed to separate awareness status from hypoglycaemia experience and to meet FDA patient-reported-outcome standards; included here as the methodologically strongest alternative to Gold and Clarke
instruments.scoring: 18 items plus two free-text responses in the full questionnaire. Principal components analysis yielded three subscales: Impaired Awareness (5 items, Cronbach's alpha 0.79), Symptom Level (3 items, alpha 0.86) and Symptom Frequency (4 items, alpha 0.89). The Impaired Awareness (IA) subscale items are each scored 0 to 4, giving a subscale range of 0–20, with higher scores indicating greater impairment.
instruments.cutoffs: HypoA-Q IA subscale ≥12 = impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia (sensitivity 83%, specificity 80%, AUC 0.86) against an abnormal symptom response to insulin-induced hypoglycaemia as the reference standard.
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED, PERMISSION-CONTROLLED — DO NOT EMBED. The validation paper I retrieved explicitly acknowledges that the questionnaire was 'provided ... under non-commercial agreement', and the developers direct enquiries to a named contact address rather than publishing the instrument openly. A commercial or quasi-commercial deployment would require a negotiated licence from the developers (Speight and colleagues, Australian Centre for Behavioural Research in Diabetes / Deakin University).

THE THREE INSTRUMENTS DO NOT AGREE WITH EACH OTHER and this is a product-design risk, not a detail. In one 100-patient cohort, prevalence was Clarke 18%, Gold 19%, Pedersen 61% (7% on revised scoring); correlations were only moderate (Gold–Clarke Spearman 0.567). A separate 2026 post-hoc analysis title states Gold and Clarke identify different people in almost 60% of cases — I read only the title, not the paper. Choosing a single instrument is therefore a clinical decision with real consequences, not an implementation detail, and results from different instruments must never be stored in a shared 'IAH status' field.
