For an internationally deployed tool the licensing conversation must be jurisdiction-gated, and the branch should express the clinical facts (impairment risk, pre-driving glucose, rescue carbohydrate) separately from any statement about licences or reporting obligations, which will otherwise be wrong in every deployment outside the US.

audit.reason: Verbatim: 'The strongest predictors involved a history of hypoglycemia while driving.' The comparison against awareness scores is also supported in the same document: 'While impaired awareness of hypoglycemia has been found to relate to increased incidence of motor vehicle crashes in some studies, it has not been found to be a relevant variable in other studies.' This is the feature that correctly owns the 'strongest predictor' claim that feature 3 wrongly borrows.
audit.correction: None on sourcing. The trailing clause 'it is also the trigger for licensing referral in many jurisdictions' is an extrapolation beyond the US-specific source — either drop it or make it jurisdiction-conditional, consistent with the driving_status correction.

audit.reason: Both claims are verbatim. The statistic: 'two collisions in the previous 2 years increased their risk by 40%'. The decision: 'a history of mishaps should be used as a basis for identifying insulin-managed drivers with elevated risk of future mishaps. Such individuals are appropriately subjected to additional screening requirements.' The 2-year window on the field matches the source's window.
audit.correction: Present the number carefully. In context the figure is the risk of a hypoglycaemia-related driving mishap in the FOLLOWING 12 MONTHS, in a prospective cohort of 452 drivers with type 1 diabetes, and the source's own phrasing ('increased their risk by 40%') is ambiguous between an absolute risk and a relative increase. Do not render it to clinicians as a clean relative risk. Also note the source counts collisions generally in that clause, not specifically hypoglycaemia-related ones as the field label implies.

audit.reason: One numeric element is wrong. The source says testing 'before driving and at regular intervals in the course of a journey lasting more than 30–60 min' — the proposal renders this as 'at intervals on journeys of an hour or more', which drops the lower bound and roughly doubles the threshold at which a driver is told to re-test. The rest of the feature is verbatim correct: 'never begin an extended drive with low normal blood glucose (e.g., 70–90 mg/dL, 3.9–5.0 mmol/L) without prophylactic carbohydrate consumption to avoid a fall in blood glucose during the drive.'
audit.correction: Change 'journeys of an hour or more' to 'journeys lasting more than 30–60 minutes'. Also note the before-driving testing advice appears in the source as an example measure for drivers with progressive impairment of awareness, and is not one of the four numbered counselling points; the four points are carry meter and snacks, never start an extended drive at 3.9–5.0 mmol/L without carbohydrate, stop the vehicle at first symptoms and measure, and do not resume until glucose and cognition have recovered.

audit.reason: Verbatim counselling point 1: 'always carry a blood glucose meter and appropriate snacks, including a quick-acting source of sugar (such as juice, nondiet soda, hard candy, or dextrose tablets) as well as snacks with complex carbohydrate, fat, and protein (e.g., cheese crackers), in their vehicle'. The 30–60 minute recovery claim is also verbatim: 'the driver should not drive until blood glucose is in a safely acceptable range, usually after 30–60 min because of delayed recovery of cognitive function', and point 4, 'not resume driving until their blood glucose and cognition have recovered'.
audit.correction: A single boolean collapses three distinct things the source separates — meter, quick-acting sugar, and complex-carbohydrate snack — and a patient may carry one without the others. Make it a multi_select mirroring the source, otherwise the 'cheap, immediately correctable safety gap' the rationale promises cannot be identified from the stored answer.

audit.reason: Both figures verified in the cited review (Berry SA, Liarakos AL, Koutroukas V, Choudhary P, Wilmot EG, Iqbal A, Diabetes Obes Metab 2025, PMC11965031): targets '<4% of time is spent <3.9 mmol/L and <1% of time is spent <3.0 mmol/L', and the discrimination caveat verbatim, 'TBR alone had a weak correlation with IAH and SH, only marginally better than random guessing (AUC 0.597 and 0.598 respectively)'. Carrying that caveat into whyItMatters — that TBR must supplement rather than replace the awareness questions — is the most intellectually honest move in the whole proposal.
audit.correction: The consensus targets originate from the international CGM consensus (Battelino et al. 2019), cited here at second hand; for a clinical tool cite the primary. Resource note that should be explicit: CGM is effectively absent from the Ugandan public sector, so this field will be empty in nearly every encounter at the beachhead site — it should be collapsed or hidden by default rather than presented alongside history fields that are always answerable.

audit.reason: The attached URL does not support the feature: I confirmed the Berry 2025 review contains no mention of the Hypoglycemia Fear Survey or HFS-II at all. The proposer was honest that this was unsourced — but they then missed that the field IS squarely guideline-backed. ADA SoC 2026 recommendation 6.12 reads: 'Screen individuals at high risk for hypoglycemia or with severe and/or frequent hypoglycemia for fear of hypoglycemia at least annually' (grade E for screening, A for referral). The decision named in whyItMatters — that a raised HbA1c driven by hypoglycaemia fear calls for education and target renegotiation rather than the dose increase the number would otherwise prompt — is exactly the inversion that recommendation exists to enable.
audit.correction: Recite to ADA SoC 2026 recommendation 6.12 and set fetched status accordingly; drop the Berry URL. Keep the decision not to embed the HFS-II: that instrument is permission-controlled (Cox/Gonder-Frederick) and I could not confirm any free-use grant, so treating it as unusable is the correct call. A single independently worded boolean plus rec 6.12 as the trigger is sufficient and carries no licence exposure.

audit.reason: The proposer's conservative assessment is correct and I independently confirmed it. The diabetesonthenet care card exists and I decoded its full text locally: it prints the title 'Gold score', the item 'Do you know when your hypos are commencing?', the anchors 'Always aware' (1) and 'Never aware' (7), and the cut-off interpretation — and it carries no copyright notice, no licence statement, no permission line, and not even an attribution to Gold et al. anywhere in the document. Copyright in the original (Diabetes Care 1994;17(7):697–703) sits with the American Diabetes Association. The reasoning that absence of a stated restriction is not a grant of permission is exactly right, and the split between storing the score and cut-off (unprotectable facts) versus rendering the item wording (protected expression) is the correct legal line.
audit.correction: One useful addition to the wording-disagreement note: the care-card wording matches the original 1994 Gold item, so it is the Berry 2025 rendering ('How often do you feel aware of having a low blood sugar?') that is the paraphrase, not the other way round. If permission is ever obtained, license the original form. Until then the implementation is: numeric 1–7 capture, cut-off interpretation displayed, item wording supplied by the clinician verbally and never rendered by the product.

audit.reason: The do-not-embed call is correct and should be upheld: the original is Clarke et al., Diabetes Care 1995;18(4):517–522, copyright ADA, and an eight-item instrument has far weaker fair-dealing cover than a single-item scale. The clinical content also verifies: the >=4 R / <=2 A cut-offs are confirmed in Berry 2025; the MMCHS description is confirmed (question 4 updated to the current severe-hypoglycaemia definition, and the question 5–6 threshold reduced to 3.5 mmol/L from 3.9 mmol/L); and the bifactorial finding is confirmed, with factor 1 comprising items 1, 2, 5/6, 7, 8 as 'Awareness of Hypoglycaemia' and factor 2's two items as 'Experience of Hypoglycaemia'. The >=5 ROC threshold with AUC 0.82, sensitivity 83% and specificity 80% is verbatim from Matus et al. 2023.
audit.correction: Material omission that must be fixed before any of this reaches a clinician. That ROC analysis (Matus AM, Flatt AJ, Peleckis AJ, Dalton-Bakes C, Riegel B, Rickels MR, Endocrine Practice 2023, PMC10592063) had a total sample of 21 adults — 10 with impaired awareness, 11 with intact awareness — and the Clarke AUC 95% confidence interval was 0.61–1.00, whose lower bound is close to chance. Presenting a derived threshold from n=21 without stating the sample size or the interval is misleading in a tool used on real patients. State n and the CI, or omit the >=5 threshold entirely and carry only the conventional >=4 cut-off. Incidentally this also explains why the Clarke and HypoA-Q sensitivities and specificities are identical at 83%/80% — same 21 participants, same Youden optimisation — so that coincidence is not evidence of fabrication.

audit.reason: The facts are right but the citation points at a source that does not contain them. The figures 61% (original convention), 7% (revised convention), 19% (Gold) and 18% (Clarke) are all genuine — I verified every one — but they come from Ghandi K, Pieri B, Dornhorst A, Hussain S, Diabetes Therapy 2020;12(1):441–451 (PMC7843675), a 100-person type 1 diabetes cohort, CC BY-NC 4.0. They are not in PMC11965031, the URL given: the Berry 2025 review does not present same-cohort comparisons across the three methods and instead cites Geddes et al. (62.5% Pedersen-Bjergaard versus 24% Gold). The 2022 update is likewise a Danish Medical Journal paper (PubMed 36065886), reported second-hand by Berry.
audit.correction: Repoint the prevalence figures to PMC7843675 and the 2022 update to its Danish Medical Journal primary. Retain the dual-convention implementation warning unchanged — it is the single most valuable safety note in the whole submission, and a 61%-versus-7% swing from a scoring convention alone would be a severe defect if it reached production unpinned. Worth adding for contrast: the 2022 update's own cohort classified 24% (Gold), 17% (Clarke) and 14% (updated Pedersen-Bjergaard) as unaware, which shows the convention gap is not stable across cohorts either. The permission-required licence stance is correct — no licence statement exists in any retrieved document.

audit.reason: The do-not-embed call is correct and I confirmed both supporting facts. The 'non-commercial agreement' quote is verbatim in Matus et al. 2023 (PMC10592063): 'We thank Dr. James Shaw ... and Dr. Jane Speight ... for providing the UK English version of HypoA-Q administered under non-commercial agreement to participants in this study.' The developer-contact claim is also true, though it comes from the ACBRD document rather than Matus: that source prints 'Enquiries Email: jane.speight@ahpresearch.com'. For a commercial or quasi-commercial deployment a negotiated licence would be required, and the subscale structure claimed (Impaired Awareness 5 items alpha 0.79, Symptom Level 3 items alpha 0.86, Symptom Frequency 4 items alpha 0.89) is confirmed exactly.
audit.correction: Three corrections. (1) VERSION MIXING: '18 items plus two free-text responses' is the ACBRD document's description of the instrument; Matus 2023 describes a 33-item instrument, and the >=12 cut-off with sensitivity 83%, specificity 80% and AUC 0.86 belongs to that 33-item version. Carrying the 2013 item count and the 2023 threshold in one entry is an implementation hazard — pin the version. (2) The ACBRD source is a conference POSTER (case-control study of 120 adults, funded by Diabetes UK as part of HypoCOMPaSS), not a peer-reviewed validation paper, and should not be labelled 'the 2013 psychometric validation' without that qualifier. (3) The same n=21 caveat as the Clarke applies to the >=12 threshold — state the sample size. Also flag that the poster itself reproduces verbatim item wording for items 7, 8, 10, 11 and 12 with no licence attached, which is the same trap as the Gold care card: finding the wording freely downloadable is not permission to ship it.

bundle.domain: Psychosocial status and diabetes self-management (ADA Standards of Care, Sections 4 and 5)

features.whyItMatters: Decides whether to make a DSMES referral at this visit. ADA gives DSMES an A grade and defines four critical times at which it must be provided; 'never' or 'over 12 months ago' is itself the indication to refer, independent of glycaemia.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.2 (grade E)
features.quote: Provide DSMES at diagnosis, annually and/or when not meeting treatment goals, when complicating factors develop (e.g., medical, functional, and psychosocial), and when transitions in life and care occur.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Accredited DSMES programmes and certified diabetes care and education specialists are largely absent outside referral hospitals. Allow the field to record structured nurse-, clinical-officer- or peer-educator-delivered education so the record is not falsely 'never'.

options.display: Annual review, or treatment goals not being met
New complicating factor (medical, functional or psychosocial)
Transition in life or in care (e.g. paediatric to adult, new insulin, pregnancy, hospital discharge)

features.whyItMatters: Triggers re-referral to DSMES now rather than at the next annual review. Each option is one of ADA's four critical times, so a tick is a direct referral instruction rather than background data.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.2 (grade E)

options.display: Sick-day rules / when to seek urgent care
Insulin injection technique and site rotation
Foot care and daily foot inspection

features.whyItMatters: Sets the content of the next education contact and flags immediate safety teaching. A gap in sick-day rules or hypoglycaemia recognition is an acute DKA/severe-hypoglycaemia risk that must be closed before the regimen is intensified.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.4 (behavioural strategies to support DSMES) (grade E)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Insulin storage without reliable refrigeration is a locally critical gap that is absent from ADA's framing; it is included here deliberately.

options.display: By a registered dietitian nutritionist within 12 months
By a registered dietitian nutritionist, more than 12 months ago
By another trained clinician (nurse, clinical officer, educator)
No dietitian available at this facility

features.whyItMatters: Absence of individualised MNT is an A-grade gap for every person with type 1, type 2, prediabetes or GDM and is the indication to refer to a dietitian. Recording 'no dietitian available' separately from 'none' tells the service where to deploy a nutrition-trained clinician instead of repeatedly generating unfulfillable referrals.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.10 (grade A)
features.quote: An individualized medical nutrition therapy program, as needed to achieve treatment goals and provided by a registered dietitian nutritionist ... is recommended for all people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, prediabetes, and gestational diabetes mellitus.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Registered dietitian nutritionists are scarce in Ugandan district and regional hospitals. The A-grade recommendation is effectively unmeetable as written; the 'other trained clinician' option preserves an honest record.

options.display: Transitional time in life or care

features.whyItMatters: Converts 'at least annually' into an actionable off-cycle screen. ADA requires repeat distress screening at these points (5.45) and repeat depression screening on complication diagnosis or status change (5.49); ticking one mandates rescreening today rather than at the next annual visit.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Recs 5.45 (grade B) and 5.49 (grade B)

features.whyItMatters: Records that the ADA annual distress screen happened and with what, which is the licence-safe minimum when DDS and PAID item text cannot be embedded. 'Not done' at an annual review is itself a care-gap flag for the quality dashboard.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Recs 5.43 (grade C) and 5.45 (grade B)
features.resourceLimitedNote: All options are paper/verbal and free of equipment. DDS and PAID are copyright-restricted (see instruments); in a facility without a licence, 'clinical enquiry only' is the workable route and must not be treated as a failure to screen.

features.whyItMatters: Decides whether to stop or escalate: a mean below 3 means no further distress action at this visit; 3 or more means administer the full DDS-17 to locate the source of distress and direct the intervention.
features.standard: Diabetes Distress Scale 2-item screener (Fisher et al. 2008); cut point per Diabetes Canada DDS guidance
features.quote: Score is less than 3 No further action this visit / Score is 3 or greater Administer full DDS

features.whyItMatters: Grades distress into the bands that ADA ties to action: 2.0-2.9 moderate and 3.0 or more high distress both warrant clinical attention, and unresolved distress at the appointment triggers referral to a behavioural health professional.
features.standard: Diabetes Distress Scale (Polonsky 2005); cut points Fisher et al., Diabetes Care 2012;35:259-264
features.quote: Current research suggests that a mean item score 2.0 - 2.9 should be considered 'moderate distress,' and a mean item score > 3.0 should be considered 'high distress.'

features.display: DDS-17 subscales at or above moderate distress
features.whyItMatters: Chooses which intervention to deliver, which the total score cannot. Regimen distress points to simplifying the regimen and repeating DSMES; physician distress points to changing the communication approach or the treating clinician; interpersonal distress points to bringing family into the education session.
features.standard: DDS-17 scoring sheet, four-subscale structure

features.whyItMatters: A total of 40 or above marks severe diabetes distress and triggers behavioural health referral; individual items scored 3 or 4 name the specific problem to open the consultation with.
features.standard: Problem Areas In Diabetes (PAID) scale; interpretation per ADA Diabetes and Emotional Health toolkit
features.quote: The scores for each item are summed, then multiplied by 1.25 to generate a total score out of 100. Total scores of 40 and above: severe diabetes distress.

features.whyItMatters: This is the field that actually drives care when the instrument itself cannot be embedded for licence reasons: moderate or high distress triggers a behavioural-health referral under Rec 5.45 and warns against reading poor glycaemia as non-adherence. Capturing the result rather than the items keeps MedSync clear of DDS and PAID copyright.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.45 (grade B)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Deliberately instrument-agnostic so it can be filled from a licensed scale, from a translated local tool, or from structured clinical enquiry.

features.display: Caregiver or family member screened for diabetes distress
features.whyItMatters: ADA requires the annual distress screen to cover caregivers and family members, not only the person with diabetes. A distressed caregiver who administers insulin or prepares meals is a direct cause of regimen failure, and a positive screen means including them in DSMES or referring them.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.45 (grade B)

features.whyItMatters: Changes the screening interval from annual to more frequent under Rec 5.48, and raises the prior probability enough to justify going straight to a PHQ-9 rather than a PHQ-2.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.48 (grade A/B)

features.whyItMatters: A score of 3 or more is the trigger to administer the full PHQ-9 and conduct a clinical interview; below 3 the depression screen is complete for this visit. This two-question gate is what makes annual depression screening feasible in a high-volume outpatient clinic.
features.standard: PHQ-2 (first two PHQ-9 items); PHQ/GAD-7 Instruction Manual (Spitzer, Williams, Kroenke)
features.quote: For the ultra-brief measures (PHQ-2 and GAD-2), a score of 3 or greater should prompt administration of the full PHQ-9 and/or GAD-7, as well as a clinical interview to determine whether a mental disorder is present.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Two questions, verbal delivery, no equipment. The most deployable depression screen in a resource-limited clinic.

features.whyItMatters: The band determines the action directly: 0-4 none, 5-9 watchful waiting and repeat at follow-up, 10-14 treatment plan with counselling and/or pharmacotherapy, 15-19 active treatment, 20-27 immediate pharmacotherapy and expedited mental-health referral.
features.standard: PHQ-9; scoring and proposed treatment actions per PHQ/GAD-7 Instruction Manual (Kroenke & Spitzer 2002)
features.quote: PHQ-9 total score for the nine items ranges from 0 to 27. Scores of 5, 10, 15, and 20 represent cutpoints for mild, moderate, moderately severe and severe depression, respectively.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Free to embed (public domain). Somatic items (sleep, energy, appetite) overlap with uncontrolled hyperglycaemia and with TB/HIV symptoms, so a raised score must be interpreted alongside glycaemic status rather than acted on mechanically.

features.display: PHQ-9 item 9 (thoughts of being better off dead or self-harm)
features.whyItMatters: Any score of 1 or more requires a suicide/self-harm risk assessment at this visit irrespective of the total score. This is the one psychosocial field that must never be deferred to the next appointment, so it is captured and alerted separately from the total.
features.standard: PHQ-9 item 9; escalation rule per ADA Diabetes and Emotional Health toolkit citing Kroenke 2001
features.quote: If the person scores 1 or more on item 9 (referring to suicidal ideation), further assessment for risk of suicide or self-harm is required, irrespective of the total score.
features.resourceLimitedNote: There must be a defined local escalation path before this alert is switched on. Firing a suicide-risk alert into a clinic with no mental-health contact and no safety-planning protocol creates liability without benefit.

features.whyItMatters: A total of 10 or more indicates likely anxiety disorder and requires follow-up with a clinical interview; ADA newly requires at least annual anxiety screening and asks clinicians to address symptoms within their own scope before referring.
features.standard: GAD-7; ADA Standards of Care Section 5 Rec 5.46 (grade B); scoring per PHQ/GAD-7 Instruction Manual
features.quote: GAD-7 total score for the seven items ranges from 0 to 21. Scores of 5, 10, and 15 represent cutpoints for mild, moderate, and severe anxiety, respectively. ... a recommended cutpoint for further evaluation is a score of 10 or greater.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Free to embed (public domain). The 2-item GAD-2 (cut point 3) is the realistic first pass where consultation time is 5 minutes.

features.display: Severe hypoglycaemia episodes in last 12 months
features.whyItMatters: Defines who is 'at high risk of hypoglycaemia' and therefore must be screened for fear of hypoglycaemia under Rec 5.47, and independently mandates relaxing glycaemic targets and de-intensifying insulin or sulfonylurea.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.47 (grade A/E)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Recall-based and prone to under-reporting where episodes are never medically attended. Define 'severe' as requiring another person's help, not as a glucose number, since confirmatory readings are often unavailable.

options.display: Reduces or omits insulin to avoid lows
Eats extra at bedtime to get through the night

features.whyItMatters: Explains otherwise unexplained hyperglycaemia and stops the wrong decision. If a person is running high because they are frightened of lows, the correct action is to treat the fear and rebuild confidence, not to escalate insulin, which will make both the glycaemia and the fear worse.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.47 (grade A/E); behaviour domain per Hypoglycemia Fear Survey-II
features.resourceLimitedNote: Behaviour items adapted rather than the copyrighted 33-item HFS-II, which is University of Virginia copyright. These are clinician-recorded observations, not a scored instrument, and must not be reported as an HFS-II score.

features.whyItMatters: ADA requires screening with validated measures (Rec 5.50); recording which tool was used lets a positive result be interpreted against the right cut-off and lets the service audit whether screening is happening at all.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.50 (grade B)
features.resourceLimitedNote: SCOFF is 5 verbal yes/no questions and is the practical option where forms and literacy are limiting; DEPS-R requires a 16-item written questionnaire.

features.whyItMatters: A score of 20 or more is a positive screen requiring further evaluation for diabetes-specific disordered eating, which changes the whole treatment plan rather than adding a referral.
features.standard: Diabetes Eating Problem Survey-Revised (Markowitz et al. 2010)
features.quote: scores >20 are associated with poorer glycaemic control requiring further evaluation
features.resourceLimitedNote: 16 written items; needs literacy and about 5-10 minutes. Note that retrieved sources disagree on the total score range (see unverifiable) — do not hard-code a maximum until the original Markowitz 2010 paper is checked.

features.whyItMatters: Two or more 'yes' answers indicates a likely eating disorder and warrants specialist evaluation. Being verbal and 5 questions long, it is the only eating-disorder screen realistically deliverable in a busy low-resource clinic.
features.standard: SCOFF questionnaire (Morgan, Reid & Lacey, BMJ 1999)
features.quote: Scores of 2 or greater indicate a likely case of an eating disorder (sensitivity: 100 percent; specificity: 87.5 percent).
features.resourceLimitedNote: The weight item is phrased in stones/pounds and must be converted to kilograms (approximately 6.4 kg in 3 months) before use. Not diabetes-specific: it will miss insulin restriction entirely, so pair it with the insulin-omission item.

features.display: Reduces or omits insulin to influence weight
features.whyItMatters: The single highest-yield question for diabetes-specific disordered eating. Anything above 'never' means recurrent DKA and complications are being caused by deliberate insulin restriction, and the response is joint diabetes and eating-disorder care with a regimen review — not dose escalation, adherence counselling, or discharge for non-attendance.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Recs 5.50 and 5.51 (grade B); construct per DEPS-R insulin-misuse domain
features.resourceLimitedNote: Must be asked privately and without a family member translating. Where insulin is rationed for cost, a positive answer may reflect poverty rather than disordered eating — cross-check against the financial-barriers field before labelling it.

features.display: Treatment plan reviewed for its effect on eating
features.whyItMatters: ADA requires the regimen itself to be re-evaluated when disordered eating is present (5.50, 5.51) — rigid carbohydrate rules, weight gain from insulin or sulfonylureas, and frequent weighing can be the cause. Records whether the clinician changed the plan or only referred.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Recs 5.50 and 5.51 (grade B)

features.whyItMatters: ADA requires routine asking and complete-avoidance advice; current use is the trigger for offering or referring for combination cessation treatment, and independently raises cardiovascular and nephropathy risk enough to change statin and blood-pressure decisions.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.40 (grade A)

features.whyItMatters: Determines which cessation advice and pharmacotherapy apply. ADA explicitly extends the avoidance advice to vaping, and smokeless and waterpipe use are commonly missed by a cigarettes-only question, leaving nicotine dependence untreated.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.40 (grade A) — tobacco and e-cigarette/vaping cessation
features.quote: combination treatment, which includes tobacco and e-cigarette/vaping cessation counseling and pharmacologic therapy
features.resourceLimitedNote: Waterpipe and smokeless options added for international use; they are not enumerated by ADA but are the dominant forms in several of our target settings.

features.whyItMatters: ADA's A-grade action is combination treatment, not advice alone. Recording what was actually offered turns smoking status from a risk label into an auditable intervention, and 'not available' identifies a supply gap rather than a clinician failure.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.40 (grade A)
features.requires: Cessation pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement, bupropion or varenicline) must be on the facility formulary for the 'combination' option to be selectable in practice
features.resourceLimitedNote: Cessation pharmacotherapy is frequently unavailable and out of pocket. The 'not available' option prevents the record from implying a treatment was refused when it was never obtainable.

features.whyItMatters: ADA newly advises people with type 1 diabetes and others at risk of DKA not to use recreational cannabis. Current use changes the differential in a person presenting with vomiting — cannabis hyperemesis mimics and precipitates DKA — and changes the counselling given.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.41 (smoking cessation section, new for 2025)
features.quote: Smoking Cessation: NEW - recommendation to AVOID cannabis due to risk of cannabis hyperemesis
features.resourceLimitedNote: Criminalised in many of our deployment countries; disclosure will be low and the field must not be surfaced in any patient-facing or shared summary.

features.whyItMatters: Gates the rest of the alcohol assessment and, in a person on insulin or a sulfonylurea, mandates delayed-hypoglycaemia education. ADA also advises those who do not drink not to start.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Recs 5.18 and 5.19 (grade B)

features.whyItMatters: A score of 4 or more in men or 3 or more in women identifies alcohol misuse in primary care and changes management: brief intervention, closer hypoglycaemia counselling on insulin or secretagogues, and reconsideration of metformin and hepatotoxic agents.
features.standard: AUDIT-C (first three consumption items of the WHO AUDIT); cut points per Bradley et al. 2007
features.quote: the suggested cut-off score is 4 for men and 3 for women
features.resourceLimitedNote: Standard-drink quantities in the AUDIT-C do not map onto locally brewed spirits and sachet alcohol; a local standard-drink conversion must be supplied or the score will systematically under-count. Licence status is unverified (see unverifiable) — do not embed item text yet.

features.whyItMatters: For anyone drinking while on insulin or an insulin secretagogue, this education is itself the intervention ADA specifies. Recording it as done or not turns a B-grade recommendation into something the service can audit, and its absence is a preventable cause of nocturnal severe hypoglycaemia.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.19 (grade B)
features.quote: Educate people with diabetes about the signs, symptoms, and self-management of delayed hypoglycemia after drinking alcohol, especially when using insulin or insulin secretagogues.

features.whyItMatters: Measured against ADA's 150 minutes per week over at least 3 days with no more than 2 consecutive days off, this decides whether to prescribe an activity increase or to move on. A specific current number also makes a realistic next target negotiable, which a yes/no 'active?' question does not.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.35 (grade B/C); youth Rec 5.34 (60 min/day)
features.quote: engage in 150 min or more of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week, spread over at least 3 days/week, with no more than 2 consecutive days without activity
features.resourceLimitedNote: Occupational and transport activity (farming, walking to market, manual labour) frequently exceeds the target already. Prompt for these explicitly, or the field will record 'inactive' for people who are highly active and generate a pointless exercise prescription.

features.whyItMatters: ADA specifies 2-3 sessions on non-consecutive days, and specifically prioritises muscle-strengthening to preserve lean mass in anyone on weight-management pharmacotherapy or after metabolic surgery — a group in whom sarcopenia changes the drug decision.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Recs 5.36 (grade B/C) and 5.39 (grade E)
features.quote: Counsel adults with type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes to engage in 2-3 sessions/week of resistance exercise on nonconsecutive days.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Gym access is rare; the prescription must be bodyweight or improvised-load based for the field to mean anything.

features.display: Prolonged sitting interrupted at least every 30 minutes
features.whyItMatters: A separate, independently prescribable target: ADA recommends breaking up sitting every 30 minutes for glucose benefit even in people who meet the weekly activity target, so a person can be 'active' and still need this specific advice.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.38 (grade C)
features.quote: Counsel that prolonged sitting should be interrupted at least every 30 min for blood glucose benefits.

options.display: Chest pain or breathlessness on exertion
No safe place to be active

features.whyItMatters: Decides whether to prescribe activity now or address a prerequisite first. Exertional chest pain means assess before prescribing; an active foot ulcer means non-weight-bearing activity only; fear of hypoglycaemia means treat the fear. Prescribing exercise past these is unsafe or futile.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, physical activity recommendations 5.34-5.39; older-adult balance training Rec 5.37 (grade C)

features.whyItMatters: ADA newly treats sleep as a core health behaviour alongside diet and activity. Short or irregular sleep worsens glycaemia and is a modifiable target to address before intensifying drug therapy in someone whose A1C is drifting.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Recs 5.56 (grade B) and 5.57 (grade A)
features.quote: Recommendation 5.56 newly recommends screening for sleep health in people with diabetes and in those at risk for diabetes.

features.whyItMatters: Splits sleep disruption into different actions: snoring with daytime sleepiness means refer for obstructive sleep apnoea assessment; nocturia points to uncontrolled hyperglycaemia to be treated glycaemically; night-time hypoglycaemia worry means adjust the evening insulin rather than counsel on sleep hygiene.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.56 (grade B) — screen for sleep disorders and diabetes-related sleep disruption, refer as indicated
features.resourceLimitedNote: Polysomnography and even home sleep testing are effectively unavailable; a positive OSA flag can usually only lead to clinical management (weight, position, avoiding sedatives) rather than confirmed diagnosis and CPAP. Set referral logic accordingly so the flag is not a dead end.

options.display: Positive — either statement 'often true' or 'sometimes true'

features.whyItMatters: Changes the prescription, not just the referral. Unreliable meals make sulfonylureas and fixed prandial insulin dangerous, and favour agents with low hypoglycaemia risk plus a flexible dosing plan. It also triggers referral to food support and reframes 'poor adherence' as a resource problem.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 1, Rec 1.5 (grade A); Section 4 Rec 4.3 (grade A); tool: Hunger Vital Sign (Hager et al., Pediatrics 2010)
features.quote: Assess food insecurity, housing insecurity/homelessness, financial barriers, and social capital/social community support to inform treatment decisions, with referral to appropriate local community resources.
features.resourceLimitedNote: Two verbal questions, no cost, free of licence. But the wording assumes purchased food and a cash economy; for subsistence-farming households it needs local adaptation and has not been validated in that context. There must also be somewhere to refer, or a positive screen only documents harm.

features.whyItMatters: Determines whether an insulin regimen is deliverable at all — no secure storage or refrigeration, no safe sharps disposal and no fixed address for follow-up all change the drug choice, the supply interval and the follow-up plan.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 1, Rec 1.5 (grade A); Section 5 psychosocial screening updated for 2026 to include housing stability
features.resourceLimitedNote: ADA references a validated brief housing-risk tool developed for US veterans; no such validated instrument is proposed here, so this remains a clinician-recorded category rather than a screen.

options.display: Skipping or stretching medicines/insulin because of cost
Cannot afford glucose strips or monitoring
Cannot afford laboratory tests or consultation fees

features.whyItMatters: Cost-related rationing is a direct and common cause of DKA and persistent hyperglycaemia, and it is invisible unless asked. A positive answer means switch to the lowest-cost effective regimen, lengthen the dispensing interval, and stop escalating doses that will not be taken — the opposite of the usual response to a rising A1C.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 1, Rec 1.5 (grade A); Section 4 Rec 4.3 (grade A)
features.resourceLimitedNote: Transport cost and consultation/laboratory fees are the dominant barriers in out-of-pocket health systems and are absent from ADA's US-framed list; both are included deliberately.

features.display: Health literacy, numeracy and language needs

options.display: Needs pictorial or colour-coded dosing aids
Difficulty with numbers (dose counting, unit conversion)

features.whyItMatters: Determines the format of every instruction given and rules certain regimens out. Numeracy difficulty is a contraindication to carbohydrate-ratio or sliding-scale dosing and mandates fixed-dose regimens with pictorial aids; inability to read written instructions means the discharge sheet will not work and teach-back is required.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 1 — health literacy and numeracy assessment; Section 5 psychosocial screening updated for 2026 to include literacy
features.resourceLimitedNote: ADA names no validated health-literacy instrument in anything retrieved, so this is a clinician judgement and must be labelled as such — it must never be reported as a validated literacy score.

features.whyItMatters: Decides whether a complex or hypoglycaemia-prone regimen is safe and who must be trained. If a caregiver is the primary manager, DSMES and hypoglycaemia teaching must be directed at them, and their distress must be screened too.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 1, Rec 1.5 (grade A) — social capital/social community support; Section 5 2026 update adds social support to psychosocial screening

features.whyItMatters: Triggers enhanced monitoring and additional self-management support under Rec 5.52, and means routine care intervals and standard education are insufficient.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.52 (grade B)

features.whyItMatters: Mandates monitoring of weight, glycaemia and lipids and consideration of changing the antipsychotic agent. This is a concrete, recurring monitoring order rather than a note, and it is routinely missed when psychiatric and diabetes records are separate.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Rec 5.53 (grade C)
features.requires: Weight; fasting or random glucose/A1C; lipid panel for the monitoring the flag orders
features.resourceLimitedNote: Lipid panels are often unavailable or paid out of pocket; weight and glucose monitoring should be the minimum enforced, with lipids optional so the order is not silently dropped.

options.display: Concern reported by patient, family or clinician

features.whyItMatters: Impaired cognition means simplify the regimen, relax glycaemic targets to avoid hypoglycaemia, and shift dosing responsibility to a trained caregiver. ADA requires monitoring across the lifespan and formal assessment when capacity changes, particularly after severe hypoglycaemia.
features.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 5, Recs 5.54 (grade B) and 5.55 (grade E)
features.requires: A brief validated cognitive screen for the 'formal assessment' options
features.resourceLimitedNote: Most brief cognitive screens are literacy- and culture-dependent and poorly validated locally; the 'concern reported' option lets the clinical decision (simplify the regimen) be taken without a formal score that cannot be obtained.

instruments.name: PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9)
instruments.purpose: Depression symptom screening and severity grading; ADA requires depression screening at least annually and more often with a history of depression (Rec 5.48).
instruments.scoring: Each item rated over the last 2 weeks as not at all (0), several days (1), more than half the days (2), nearly every day (3). Sum the 9 items for a total of 0-27. The final functional-difficulty question is not scored and represents the patient's global impression of impairment.
instruments.cutoffs: 5, 10, 15 and 20 are cut points for mild, moderate, moderately severe and severe depression. 10 or more is a 'yellow flag' (possible clinically significant condition) and 15 or more a 'red flag' (active treatment probably warranted). Proposed actions: 0-4 none; 5-9 watchful waiting and repeat at follow-up; 10-14 treatment plan considering counselling and/or pharmacotherapy; 15-19 active treatment; 20-27 immediate pharmacotherapy and expedited mental-health referral. Any score of 1 or more on item 9 (suicidal ideation) requires self-harm risk assessment regardless of the total. The ADA toolkit notes alternative diabetes-specific cut-offs of 12 or more in specialty diabetes clinics and 7 or more in older people in general practice.
instruments.licence: PUBLIC DOMAIN — EMBEDDABLE. The PHQ/GAD-7 instruction manual states verbatim: 'All of the measures included in Table 1 are in the public domain. No permission is required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute.' Developed by Drs Robert L. Spitzer, Janet B.W. Williams, Kurt Kroenke and colleagues with an educational grant from Pfizer Inc; Pfizer announced free public access without copyright restriction on 21 July 2010. Translations are freely downloadable, but the manual warns most translations are linguistically but not psychometrically validated.

instruments.name: PHQ-2
instruments.purpose: Ultra-brief first-pass depression screen; the two core DSM criteria items, used to decide who needs a full PHQ-9.
instruments.scoring: The first two PHQ-9 items (loss of interest; feeling down/depressed/hopeless), same 2-week recall and same 0-3 response options. Sum for a total of 0-6.
instruments.cutoffs: 3 or more should prompt administration of the full PHQ-9 and a clinical interview to determine whether a mental disorder is present.
instruments.licence: PUBLIC DOMAIN — EMBEDDABLE. Covered by the same statement as the PHQ-9 ('All of the measures included in Table 1 are in the public domain').

instruments.name: GAD-7 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7)
instruments.purpose: Anxiety symptom screening and severity; ADA newly requires anxiety screening at least annually (Rec 5.46, 2026).
instruments.scoring: Each item rated over the last 2 weeks as not at all (0), several days (1), more than half the days (2), nearly every day (3). Sum for a total of 0-21. A supplementary difficulty item does not contribute to the total.
instruments.cutoffs: 5, 10 and 15 are cut points for mild, moderate and severe anxiety. When screening for anxiety disorders the recommended cut point for further evaluation is 10 or more, followed up with a clinical interview. The 2-item GAD-2 (items 1 and 2, range 0-6) has a cut point of 3 or more.
instruments.licence: PUBLIC DOMAIN — EMBEDDABLE. Same statement as the PHQ family: 'All of the measures included in Table 1 are in the public domain. No permission is required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute.' Freely available in more than 30 languages; few translations psychometrically validated.

instruments.name: DDS-17 (Diabetes Distress Scale)
instruments.purpose: Measures diabetes-specific emotional distress and locates its source across four domains; used mainly in adults with type 2 diabetes.
instruments.scoring: Each item rated for the past month from 1 (not a problem) to 6 (a very serious problem). Sum the 17 items and divide by 17 for a total mean item score. Four subscales, each summed and divided by its own item count: emotional burden (items 2, 4, 7, 10, 14), physician distress (1, 5, 11, 15), regimen distress (6, 8, 3, 12, 16), interpersonal distress (9, 13, 17).
instruments.cutoffs: Mean item score 1-1.9 low distress; 2.0-2.9 moderate distress; 3.0 or greater high/severe distress. Associations with behavioural management and A1C occur above 2.0. Any single item scored above 3 is worth exploring regardless of the mean. (Fisher et al., Diabetes Care 2012;35:259-264.)
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED — DO NOT EMBED WITHOUT WRITTEN PERMISSION. Marked '© William H. Polonsky & Lawrence Fisher'; the ADA Diabetes and Emotional Health toolkit reproduces it as '© Behavioral Diabetes Institute. All rights reserved' with the note that readers 'are permitted to reproduce the questionnaire for clinical use and non-commercial research purposes' but 'are not permitted to use the questionnaire for commercial research purposes and must seek permission from the copyright holder/developer to do so.' Those terms do not address redistribution inside commercial clinical software. RECORD INSTEAD: the fact that distress screening was done, the tool used, and the resulting level (none/low, moderate, high) — see features diabetes_distress_screen_method and diabetes_distress_level — plus the numeric score if the site holds its own licence.

instruments.name: DDS-2 (2-item Diabetes Distress Screener)
instruments.purpose: Ultra-brief diabetes distress screen used to decide who needs the full DDS-17; the practical instrument for ADA's annual distress screen in a high-volume clinic.
instruments.scoring: Two items drawn from the DDS-17, rated on the same 1-6 scale; the score is the mean of the two items (range 1-6).
instruments.cutoffs: Less than 3: no further action this visit. 3 or greater: administer the full DDS-17 to define the content of the distress and direct the intervention.
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED — same holders and terms as the DDS-17 (Polonsky & Fisher / Behavioral Diabetes Institute). Being only two items does not make it free. RECORD INSTEAD: screening performed plus result level, as for the DDS-17.

instruments.name: T1-DDS (Type 1 Diabetes Distress Scale)
instruments.purpose: Type 1-specific diabetes distress measure, covering domains the DDS-17 does not (hypoglycaemia, powerlessness, eating distress, negative social perceptions).
instruments.scoring: Items rated 1 (not a problem) to 6 (a very serious problem); mean item score for the total and for each of 7 subscales (powerlessness, management, hypoglycaemia, family and friends, physician, negative social perceptions, eating distress).
instruments.cutoffs: Same bands as the DDS: 1-1.9 low, 2-2.9 moderate, 3.0 or greater severe distress; individual items 3.0 or greater to be discussed at the appointment.
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED — '© Behavioral Diabetes Institute. All rights reserved', reproduced in the ADA toolkit by permission for clinical use and non-commercial research only; commercial research requires permission from the copyright holder. Not embeddable without written permission.

instruments.name: PAID (Problem Areas In Diabetes) scale
instruments.purpose: Diabetes distress measure; also used item-by-item to open a conversation about the specific problem areas troubling the person.
instruments.scoring: Each item rated 0 (not a problem) to 4 (a serious problem). Sum the 20 items and multiply by 1.25 to give a total out of 100. Short forms exist: PAID-11, PAID-5, PAID-1.
instruments.cutoffs: Total score 40 or above indicates severe diabetes distress. Individual items scored 3 or 4 indicate moderate to severe distress and should be discussed at the appointment following completion.
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED — DO NOT EMBED WITHOUT WRITTEN PERMISSION. '© Joslin Diabetes Center, 1999 (www.joslin.org). All rights reserved.' The ADA toolkit reproduces it by permission and permits readers to reproduce it 'for clinical use and non-commercial research purposes' but not for commercial research, for which permission must be sought from the copyright holder. Distribution inside a commercial product is not covered by those terms. RECORD INSTEAD: screening performed, tool used and distress level.

instruments.name: AUDIT-C
instruments.purpose: Brief alcohol-misuse screen; the three consumption items of the 10-item WHO AUDIT (drinking frequency, typical quantity, frequency of heavy episodes).
instruments.scoring: Each item scored 0-4 by response category, giving a total of 0-12. (The parent AUDIT has 10 items and a maximum of 40.)
instruments.cutoffs: 4 or more for men and 3 or more for women to identify alcohol misuse in primary care (Bradley et al. 2007).
instruments.licence: NOT ESTABLISHED — the review article retrieved contains no copyright, licensing or permission statement. The AUDIT-C derives from the WHO AUDIT, a WHO publication over which WHO asserts copyright in its manual. Widely reproduced in practice, but do NOT assume public domain. Verify with WHO before embedding item text; until then record only the score and the positive/negative result, or use a locally licensed alcohol screen.

instruments.name: DEPS-R (Diabetes Eating Problem Survey-Revised)
instruments.purpose: Diabetes-specific disordered-eating screen covering dietary habits, insulin misuse for weight control and compensatory behaviours; the only screen here that detects insulin restriction.
instruments.scoring: 16 items each scored on a 6-point Likert scale; higher scores indicate more disordered eating. Takes under 5 minutes and needs no specially trained administrator. NOTE: retrieved sources disagree on the total range (one states 16-96, several secondary descriptions state 0-80) — resolve against Markowitz et al., Diabetes Care 2010;33:495-500 before implementing.
instruments.cutoffs: 20 or more is a positive screen indicating disordered eating and requiring further evaluation; scores above 20 are associated with poorer glycaemic control.
instruments.licence: NOT ESTABLISHED — no copyright, permission or distribution statement was found in any document retrieved, and the original Markowitz 2010 paper was not obtained. Treat as restricted until the rights holder is identified and permission obtained. RECORD INSTEAD: that disordered-eating screening was done, which tool, the result, and the standalone insulin-omission question.

instruments.name: SCOFF questionnaire
instruments.purpose: Generic five-question eating-disorder screen, deliverable verbally; the practical option where written questionnaires and literacy are limiting.
instruments.scoring: Five closed yes/no questions (Sick — self-induced vomiting when uncomfortably full; Control — lost control over eating; One stone — lost more than approximately 14 pounds in 3 months; Fat — believes self fat when others say too thin; Food — thoughts and fears about food and weight dominate life). Each 'yes' scores 1; sum for 0-5. May be delivered verbally.
instruments.cutoffs: 2 or more indicates a likely case of an eating disorder (reported sensitivity 100%, specificity 87.5%) and warrants evaluation by an eating-disorder specialist.
instruments.licence: NOT ESTABLISHED FROM A RETRIEVED DOCUMENT — the source retrieved carries the Morgan, Reid & Lacey (BMJ 1999) citation but no permission or copyright statement. It is widely reproduced on the basis that the five questions were published in the original BMJ paper, but that reasoning came from a search snippet, not a verified licence. Confirm before embedding item text.

instruments.name: Hunger Vital Sign
instruments.purpose: Two-item household food-insecurity screen, derived from the US Household Food Security Survey Module; supports ADA's requirement to assess food insecurity (Rec 1.5, grade A).
instruments.scoring: Two statements, each answered often true / sometimes true / never true: 'Within the past 12 months we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more' and 'Within the past 12 months the food we bought just didn't last and we didn't have money to get more.'
instruments.cutoffs: Positive (at risk for food insecurity) if either or both statements are answered 'often true' or 'sometimes true' (versus 'never true').
instruments.licence: FREE TO USE — EMBEDDABLE WITH CITATION. The developers state verbatim: 'There is no fee or license required to use the Hunger Vital Sign™. We only ask that parties properly cite the tool.' Required citation: Hager ER, Quigg AM, Black MM, et al. Development and Validity of a 2-Item Screen to Identify Families at Risk for Food Insecurity. Pediatrics. 2010;126(1):26-32. doi:10.1542/peds.2009-3146. Note the name is trademarked — cite it, do not rebrand it.

instruments.name: Hypoglycemia Fear Survey-II (HFS-II)
instruments.purpose: Measures behaviours used to avoid hypoglycaemia and worry about hypoglycaemia; relevant to ADA's new annual fear-of-hypoglycaemia screen (Rec 5.47).
instruments.scoring: 33 items in a Behaviour subscale and a Worry subscale, each rated 0 (never) to 4 (almost always) over the last six months (the timeframe can be adapted). Clinically, high-scoring items (3 and 4) are used to open the conversation rather than only the totals.
instruments.cutoffs: No total-score cut-off is given in the ADA toolkit; interpretation is item-level, focusing on items scored 3 or 4.
instruments.licence: COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED — '© University of Virginia', reproduced in the ADA toolkit by permission for clinical use and non-commercial research only; commercial research requires permission from the copyright holder. Not embeddable without written permission. RECORD INSTEAD: the clinician-observed avoidance behaviours captured in the fear_of_hypoglycaemia_behaviours field, clearly labelled as not an HFS-II score.

unverifiable: PRIMARY ADA 2026 TEXT NOT OBTAINED. diabetesjournals.org returned HTTP 403 for both the Section 5 article page and the PDF (dc26s005.pdf), and the PMC copy (PMC12690188) truncated in the Physical Activity subsection, before Psychosocial Care. The verbatim wording and evidence grades for Recs 5.42-5.57 were therefore read only in a third-party guideline summary (Guideline Central, guidelinecentral.com/guideline/14119) plus the ADA Summary of Revisions (PMC12690167). Confirm every 5.4x/5.5x number, wording and grade against the primary article before this ships to a clinical surface.

SECTION 5 RENUMBERED BETWEEN 2025 AND 2026. The 2026 Summary of Revisions describes 5.34 as an obesity/physical-activity recommendation, whereas the 2025 text numbers 5.34 as youth physical activity. The DSMES (5.2), MNT (5.10), physical activity (5.34-5.39) and alcohol (5.18-5.19) quotes used here are from the 2025 text (PMC11635047); their 2026 numbers were not verified and may have shifted.

Exact wording of Recs 5.40 (tobacco/vape) and 5.41 (recreational cannabis) came from a search-result snippet and a third-party paraphrase, not from a fetched ADA document. The tobacco/vaping fragment quoted is from the ADA Summary of Revisions; the cannabis recommendation is corroborated only by a conference-update slide deck (wafp.org).

AUDIT-C LICENCE UNVERIFIED. No copyright, licensing or permission statement for the AUDIT or AUDIT-C was found in anything retrieved; the review article read explicitly contains none. The parent AUDIT is a WHO publication and WHO asserts copyright over its manual. The claim that AUDIT-C is 'public domain' came from a search snippet only and must not be relied on.

DEPS-R: total score range is inconsistent across retrieved sources (one fetched paper states a 16-96 range on a 6-point Likert; multiple secondary descriptions state 0-80 with 0-5 item scoring). The original Markowitz et al. 2010 Diabetes Care paper was not retrieved. DEPS-R licence and rights holder are also unestablished.

SCOFF LICENCE UNVERIFIED. The retrieved PDF carries the Morgan 1999 citation but no permission or copyright statement. The 'freely available because published in the original BMJ paper' rationale came from a search snippet only.

DDS-2 EXACT ITEM WORDING PARTIALLY UNVERIFIED. Only the first item ('Feeling Overwhelmed by the Demands of Living with Diabetes') was seen in a retrieved document; the second item wording attributed to Fisher et al. 2008 (Ann Fam Med) came from a search snippet — the paper itself was not fetched.

COMMERCIAL-EMBEDDING RIGHTS FOR DDS, T1-DDS, PAID AND HFS-II ARE NOT SETTLED. The ADA toolkit terms distinguish 'clinical use and non-commercial research purposes' (permitted) from 'commercial research purposes' (permission required) but say nothing about redistributing item text inside commercial clinical software. Written permission from the Behavioral Diabetes Institute, Joslin Diabetes Center and the University of Virginia respectively is required before embedding; the result-only fields are the safe default until then.

ADA DOES NOT MANDATE ANY SPECIFIC NAMED INSTRUMENT in anything retrieved — Rec 5.43 says age-appropriate validated tools. The choice of DDS/PAID/PHQ/GAD-7/AUDIT-C/DEPS-R/SCOFF here is ours, not ADA's, and should not be presented to clinicians as ADA-mandated.

SECTION 4 (2026) VERBATIM TEXT NOT OBTAINED. Rec 4.3 ('Assess social determinants of health and structural barriers to optimal health and healthcare', grade A) was read in the 2024 Section 4 (PMC10725809). The itemised SDOH list quoted (food insecurity, housing insecurity/homelessness, financial barriers, social capital/social community support) is Rec 1.5 (grade A) in Section 1, not Section 4 — the domain brief's framing of Section 4 as the SDOH source is only partly right.
NO ADA-ENDORSED HEALTH LITERACY OR NUMERACY INSTRUMENT was found in any retrieved document. The health_literacy_and_language_needs field is clinician judgement and must be labelled as such.

NO NAMED HOUSING-INSECURITY INSTRUMENT. ADA Section 1 refers to 'a brief risk assessment tool developed and validated for use among veterans' but the retrieved text does not name it; no validated housing screen is proposed here.

HUNGER VITAL SIGN NOT VALIDATED FOR OUR SETTING. It was validated against the USDA Household Food Security Survey Module in US households; its 12-month, cash-purchase framing has not been validated for subsistence-farming or Ugandan populations in anything retrieved. Local adaptation and revalidation are needed before the positive/negative result is treated as reliable.

PHQ-9 / GAD-7 TRANSLATIONS: the instruction manual states that most translations are linguistically valid but few have been psychometrically validated against an independent structured psychiatric interview. No Luganda, Swahili or other locally relevant validation was sought or found.

ALTERNATIVE PHQ-9 CUT-OFFS for people with diabetes (12 or more in specialty clinics; 7 or more in older people in general practice) come from the ADA 'Diabetes and Emotional Health' toolkit citing secondary references that were not retrieved.

The 2026 claim that youth psychosocial screening should start 'as early as age 7-8 years' came from a search snippet describing the revisions, not from a fetched ADA document. No paediatric age thresholds have been encoded in these fields as a result.

GUIDELINE CENTRAL IS A THIRD-PARTY SUMMARY SERVICE. Its rendering of grades is internally ambiguous in places (5.47 shown as 'A/E', 5.48 as 'A/B') and was not reconciled against ADA primary text. Grades cited from it should be treated as provisional.

NO SOURCED DATA ON LOCAL AVAILABILITY. No cost, supply, workforce or coverage data was gathered on DSMES programmes, registered dietitian nutritionists, cessation pharmacotherapy, sleep testing, behavioural health professionals or food-support programmes in Uganda. Every resourceLimitedNote is reasoned clinical judgement, not a sourced fact.

Recommendations 5.52-5.55 (serious mental illness, antipsychotics, cognitive capacity) sit outside the domain brief as written and were included on clinical grounds; their wording and grades share the same third-party sourcing limitation as the rest of the psychosocial block.

E'. Grade E and the four critical times are exactly as claimed. One defect inside whyItMatters: 'ADA gives DSMES an A grade' is not 5.2. The A grades belong to 5.1 ('All people with diabetes should be advised to participate in developmentally and culturally appropriate diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES)' A) and 5.5 (A).
audit.correction: Change whyItMatters to credit the A grade to Rec 5.1, and keep 5.2/E as the source of the four critical times.

audit.reason: Same fetched text of Rec 5.2. The four ticks map one-to-one onto ADA's four stated critical times (diagnosis; annually / not meeting treatment goals; complicating factors develop; transitions in life and care). Grade E correct. whyItMatters names a real decision (re-refer now versus at annual review) rather than background data.

The cited URL is the 2025 Section 5, where Rec 5.4 reads verbatim: 'Screen for behavioral health concerns at the same critical times as evaluating the need for DSMES and refer to a qualified behavioral health professional if indicated to increase engagement in DSMES. audit.reason: Rec 5.10 fetched verbatim from PMC11635047: 'An individualized medical nutrition therapy program, as needed to achieve treatment goals and provided by a registered dietitian nutritionist... is recommended for all people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, prediabetes, and gestational diabetes mellitus. audit.reason: Attribution holds. Rec 5.43 verbatim: 'Implement screening protocols for psychosocial concerns, preferably using age-appropriate standardized and validated tools. Readers of the guide are permitted to reproduce the questionnaire for clinical use and non-commercial research purposes. Readers of the guide are not permitted to use the questionnaire for commercial research purposes and must seek permission from the copyright holder/developer to do so.'
