Note also the citation token 'DDS 5.8.15' is not a document reference — it is the version stamp printed on the copyright line of the instrument.
audit.correction: Do not ship this field until MedSync holds written permission from Polonsky/Fisher or the Behavioral Diabetes Institute. Until then rely on diabetes_distress_screen_method + diabetes_distress_level, and gate the numeric field behind a per-site 'we hold our own DDS licence' flag.

audit.reason: Cut points verified twice over: the Diabetes Canada scoring sheet states 'a mean item score 2.0 - 2.9 should be considered moderate distress, and a mean item score > 3.0 should be considered high distress... associations between DDS scores and behavioral management and biological variables (e.g., A1C) occur with DDS scores of > 2.0', and the ADA toolkit gives 'scores in the 1-1.9 are considered low distress, scores of 2-2.9 indicate moderate distress, and scores of 3.0 or greater indicate severe diabetes distress.' Fisher 2012 Diabetes Care 35:259-264 is the cited source on the sheet. The blocker is identical to DDS-2: (c) Polonsky & Fisher / Behavioral Diabetes Institute, permission limited to clinical use and non-commercial research.
audit.correction: Same as dds2_mean_score — hold the field behind written permission or a site-held licence; ship diabetes_distress_level instead.

audit.reason: Highest legal exposure of the three, and the submission does not say so. The four subscale groupings are exactly right — the scoring sheet reads 'A. Emotional Burden: Sum of 5 items (2, 4, 7, 10, 14)... B. Physician Distress: Sum of 4 items (1, 5, 11, 15)... C. Regimen Distress: Sum of 5 items (6, 8, 3, 12, 16)... D. Interpersonal Distress: Sum of 3 items (9, 13, 17)' — but that item-to-subscale map IS the copyrighted scoring sheet, not a derived summary the way a single total is. Embedding it reproduces protected structure even without item text. The clinical argument (regimen distress -> simplify regimen; physician distress -> change communication; interpersonal -> bring family in) is the best decision-logic in this whole submission, which makes it worth getting licensed properly rather than dropping.
audit.correction: Do not encode the item-to-subscale mapping. Either obtain written permission, or capture a clinician-selected 'main source of distress' (regimen / emotional burden / clinician relationship / family and friends) as MedSync's own plain-language field, clearly labelled as not a DDS subscale score.

audit.reason: Scoring and cut-off confirmed verbatim in the ADA toolkit I extracted: 'The scores for each item are summed, then multiplied by 1.25 to generate a total score out of 100. > Total scores of 40 and above: severe diabetes distress. > Individual items scored 3 or 4: moderate to severe distress; to be discussed during the appointment following completion.' But the instrument page carries '(c) Joslin Diabetes Center, 1999 (www.joslin.org). All rights reserved.' with the same clinical-use / non-commercial-research-only permission. Same commercial-product gap as the DDS family.
audit.correction: Withhold pending written permission from Joslin Diabetes Center. diabetes_distress_level already carries the decision this field would drive.

audit.reason: This is the correctly engineered field in the distress cluster and the one that should ship. Rec 5.45 (B) verified verbatim, and ADA's 2026 Summary of Revisions states 'Recommendation 5.45 was updated to recommend referral to a qualified behavioral health professional if diabetes distress is not adequately addressed during the medical appointment' — which is precisely the referral trigger whyItMatters claims. Capturing the result band rather than the items keeps MedSync outside the DDS and PAID copyright, and the warning against reading poor glycaemia as non-adherence is a real decision change.

Attribution is exactly right — 5.45 names the population verbatim as 'people with diabetes, caregivers, and family members', which is easy to miss and the submission caught it. Design objection, not a sourcing one: a boolean recording that the caregiver WAS screened captures process, not the finding. Nothing in the care plan changes on 'yes'; it changes on the caregiver's result. As drafted this is the kind of tick-box that teaches clinicians to ignore the form.
audit.correction: Replace the boolean with a three-way result field (not screened / screened - no significant distress / screened - distress present), so a positive value carries the action (include the caregiver in DSMES or refer them).

audit.reason: Rec 5.48 verbatim: 'Screen for depressive symptoms in all people with diabetes at least annually and more frequently among those with a history of depression. B Refer to qualified behavioral health professionals... A'. The 'changes the screening interval from annual to more frequent' claim is precisely ADA's wording, and the A/B split grade is correct. The second clause of whyItMatters — going straight to PHQ-9 rather than PHQ-2 — is the proposer's own clinical reasoning and is not in 5.48; it is defensible but should not read as ADA's.
audit.correction: Mark the 'straight to PHQ-9' step as MedSync clinical logic rather than an ADA recommendation.

audit.reason: Verified verbatim in the fetched PHQ/GAD-7 Instruction Manual: 'For the ultra-brief measures (PHQ-2 and GAD-2), a score of 3 or greater should prompt administration of the full PHQ-9 and/or GAD-7, as well as a clinical interview to determine whether a mental disorder is present.' Range 0-6 confirmed. Licence claim verified verbatim and is correct: 'All of the measures included in Table 1 are in the public domain. No permission is required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute.' Safe to embed. This is also the right instrument for a high-volume low-resource clinic — two questions, no materials, no training.

Every band verified verbatim against the manual's Table 4 (attributed there to Kroenke K, Spitzer RL, Psychiatric Annals 2002;32:509-521): '0-4 None-minimal None / 5-9 Mild Watchful waiting; repeat PHQ-9 at follow-up / 10-14 Moderate Treatment plan, considering counseling, follow-up and/or pharmacotherapy / 15-19 Moderately Severe Active treatment with pharmacotherapy and/or psychotherapy / 20-27 Severe Immediate initiation of pharmacotherapy and, if severe impairment or poor response to therapy, expedited referral to a mental health specialist'. Cut points 5/10/15/20 and the yellow-flag/red-flag framing at 10 and 15 are also verbatim. Public domain confirmed.

The escalation rule is verbatim in the ADA toolkit PDF I extracted: 'If the person scores 1 or more on item 9 (referring to suicidal ideation), further assessment for risk of suicide or self-harm is required, irrespective of the total score.' Independently corroborated in the PHQ manual: 'A particularly important question is how to assess suicide risk in individuals who answer positively to the 9th question of the PHQ-9... a final decision about the actual risk of self-harm requires a clinical interview.' Both the attribution and the 'never defer this one' design are correct, and separating it from the total is the right engineering call.

Both halves of the split attribution hold. Rec 5.46 verbatim: 'Screen for anxiety symptoms at least annually in people with diabetes. Health care professionals can address anxiety symptoms within the scope of their practice. Consider referral to a qualified behavioral health professional... (B)' — so the 'address within their own scope before referring' clause in whyItMatters is genuinely ADA's, corroborated by the 2026 Summary of Revisions. Scoring verbatim from the manual: 'GAD-7 total score for the seven items ranges from 0 to 21. Scores of 5, 10, and 15 represent cutpoints for mild, moderate, and severe anxiety... When screening for anxiety disorders, a recommended cutpoint for further evaluation is a score of 10 or greater.' Public domain confirmed.

Half the whyItMatters is not in the recommendation cited. Rec 5.47 verbatim: 'Screen individuals at high risk for hypoglycemia or with severe and/or frequent hypoglycemia for fear of hypoglycemia at least annually and when clinically appropriate. E Refer to a trained health care professional for evidence-based intervention. A'. It defines who gets screened for fear of hypoglycaemia — that part is right — but it says nothing about relaxing glycaemic targets or de-intensifying insulin or sulfonylureas. I checked ADA's own 2026 Summary of Revisions for 5.47 and it likewise mentions only screening and referral. Those de-intensification actions live in Section 6 (Glycemic Goals) and Section 13 (Older Adults). Also the grade is not 'A/E' as a unit: E attaches to the screening clause, A to the referral clause.
audit.correction: Restrict the 5.47 citation to the fear-of-hypoglycaemia screening trigger with the E/A clauses split. Cite Section 6 (doi 10.2337/dc26-S006) or Section 13 separately for target relaxation and insulin/SU de-intensification.

audit.reason: Clinically this is one of the two most valuable fields proposed — 'running high because they are frightened of lows' is a real and commonly missed reason not to escalate insulin, and it is deliverable anywhere with no equipment. But the option list is sourced to the HFS-II Behaviour subscale, and the ADA toolkit page for that instrument reads '(c) University of Virginia. The copyright holder/developer has given permission for the questionnaire to be reproduced in this guide' with the same clinical-use / non-commercial-research-only limit. Options that paraphrase HFS-II Behaviour items are a derivative-work exposure, and the toolkit gives no total-score cut-off to lean on either — interpretation there is item-level (items scored 3 or 4).
audit.correction: Keep the field, drop the HFS-II lineage. Write the avoidance behaviours in MedSync's own words (runs glucose deliberately high, eats extra at bedtime, skips or reduces insulin before sleep or exercise, avoids being alone, avoids driving), label it explicitly as clinician-observed behaviour and NOT an HFS-II score, and cite Rec 5.47 only for the screening trigger.

audit.reason: Rec 5.50 verbatim: 'Screen for disordered or disrupted eating using validated screening measures. Review the medical treatment plan to identify potential treatment-related effects on hunger/caloric intake. (B)' — grade and 'validated screening measures' are as claimed. Partial objection to whyItMatters, same pattern as the distress-method field: 'lets the service audit whether screening is happening at all' is data collection for its own sake. The other half — recording which tool so a positive result is read against the right cut-off — is a real decision, since DEPS-R (>=20) and SCOFF (>=2) are not interchangeable.
audit.correction: Drop the audit clause from whyItMatters; keep the cut-off-interpretation rationale.

audit.reason: The cut-off is real — the cited article (Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism 2019, 'Assessing the clinical utility of the diabetes eating problem survey-revised (DEPS-R) in adolescents with type 1 diabetes') states 'The DEPS-R is a 16-item questionnaire' and 'Patients with a score >=20 were categorized as positive. A threshold of 20 was selected based on previous studies', and it does cite Markowitz et al. 2010. But the article's open-access CC licence covers the ARTICLE, not the instrument, and it carries no copyright, permission or distribution statement for the DEPS-R itself; the submission's own note concedes this and concedes that retrieved sources disagree on the total range (16-96 versus 0-80). Shipping a number field whose valid range is unresolved is a data-integrity defect on top of the licence gap — a stored '18' is uninterpretable if the range is ambiguous.
audit.correction: Do not implement until (a) Markowitz et al., Diabetes Care 2010;33:495-500 is obtained and the range fixed, and (b) the rights holder is identified and permission granted. In the interim rely on scoff_score plus insulin_omission_for_weight, which cover the same decision.

audit.reason: Content fully verified — the Children's Mercy document (June 2023) states 'A positive score on the SCOFF (>=2) indicates suspicion of an eating disorder', gives all five items verbatim, and reports 'Scores of 2 or greater indicate a likely case of an eating disorder (sensitivity: 100 percent; specificity: 87.5 percent)', citing Morgan, Reid & Lacey, BMJ 1999;319(7223):1467-1468. The resource-limited argument is also sound: five yes/no questions, deliverable verbally, no forms. But I found no copyright, licence or permission statement anywhere in the retrieved document, and BMJ 1999 is not open access — a hospital handout reproducing the items is not evidence of a right to redistribute them in software.
audit.correction: Confirm the position with BMJ Publishing Group (or licence via the authors) before embedding the five item texts. Storing a clinician-entered 0-5 score is materially lower risk than rendering the questions in-app; if you must ship now, ship the score field only and leave administration to the clinician's own materials.

audit.reason: The clinical case is the strongest in the submission and I am not disputing it — deliberate insulin restriction causing recurrent DKA is exactly the finding that must not be met with dose escalation or discharge for non-attendance. But the cited recommendations do not contain it. Rec 5.50 and 5.51 verbatim (5.51: 'Reevaluate the treatment plan of people with diabetes who present with symptoms of disordered eating behaviors, an eating disorder, or disrupted patterns of eating, ideally in consultation with a qualified professional. (B)') mention disordered eating generically; neither mentions insulin omission, insulin restriction, or manipulating insulin to influence weight. The construct is instead attributed to the DEPS-R insulin-misuse domain, and DEPS-R's licence is unestablished — so wording the options close to DEPS-R items inherits that exposure.
audit.correction: Keep the field; fix the provenance. Cite it as MedSync clinical logic supported by 5.50/5.51 rather than stated by them, or source the construct to a citable primary on insulin restriction. Word the options independently of DEPS-R item text.

audit.reason: Well sourced and easy to overlook. Rec 5.50 verbatim carries the second sentence 'Review the medical treatment plan to identify potential treatment-related effects on hunger/caloric intake', and 5.51 (B) requires re-evaluating the plan — so ADA genuinely requires the regimen itself to be interrogated, exactly as claimed. Minor design note: as a boolean it records that an action happened rather than feeding a decision, but unlike the caregiver field the action IS the recommendation, so the tick has a defensible referent.
audit.correction: Consider capturing what changed (carbohydrate rules relaxed / weight-gaining agent reviewed / weighing frequency reduced / referred only) so the field records the decision rather than merely its occurrence.

audit.reason: Rec 5.40 (2026) verbatim: 'Ask people with diabetes routinely about the use of tobacco or vape products. Advise complete avoidance of tobacco and vaping.' The ask-and-advise trigger is correctly attributed. Over-reach in the tail of whyItMatters: 'raises cardiovascular and nephropathy risk enough to change statin and blood-pressure decisions' is not in Rec 5.40 or anywhere in Section 5 — statin and blood-pressure thresholds are Section 10 (Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management). The statement is clinically true but is being credited to the wrong section.
audit.correction: Cite 5.40 for asking and advising only; move the statin/BP consequence to a Section 10 citation or drop it from whyItMatters.

audit.reason: The cited URL does support the core claim — ADA's 2026 Summary of Revisions states 'Recommendation 5.40 was revised to recommend routine assessment and avoidance of tobacco and e-cigarette/vaping use', so the explicit extension to vaping is genuinely ADA's and is correctly flagged as such. Caveat: smokeless and waterpipe products are not named in 5.40 or in the revision text. They are a sensible and locally important extension for a Ugandan deployment, but they are MedSync's addition, not ADA's.
audit.correction: Note in the feature that smokeless and waterpipe options extend beyond ADA's wording, so a later reviewer does not read them as guideline text.

audit.reason: Confirmed, and better supported than the cited URL alone shows. The guidelinecentral rendering of 5.40 omits the treatment clause, but ADA's own 2026 Summary of Revisions supplies it verbatim: 5.40 'also suggests providing or referring individuals for combination treatment, which includes tobacco and e-cigarette/vaping cessation counseling and pharmacologic therapy.' So 'ADA's A-grade action is combination treatment, not advice alone' is accurate. The separate 'not available' option is the right design for a low-resource setting — it distinguishes a supply gap from a clinician omission instead of recording a false negative.
audit.correction: Point sourceUrl at PMC12690167 or the ADA primary, since the guidelinecentral excerpt does not contain the combination-treatment clause the feature relies on.

audit.reason: Substantively verified at the cited URL, which is more than I expected. The WAFP document states verbatim 'Smoking Cessation: NEW - recommendation to AVOID cannabis due to risk of cannabis hyperemesis syndrome and potential DKA' and 'NEW recommendations for persons at risk of DKA: AVOID CANNABIS due to risk of hyperemesis syndrome', and its header confirms it covers '2025 ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes: Updates!' — so 'new for 2025' is correct, and cannabis does not appear in the 2026 revisions list, consistent with it being a 2025 addition. Two weaknesses: the number 5.41 does not appear anywhere in that document (it comes from the 2026 numbering), and the source is a state family-physicians' newsletter summarising ADA rather than ADA itself, which is thin provenance for a field that changes a DKA differential.
audit.correction: Replace sourceUrl with the ADA primary — 2026 Section 5 Rec 5.41 verbatim: 'Advise people with type 1 diabetes and those with other forms of diabetes at risk for diabetic ketoacidosis not to use recreational cannabis in any form' (doi 10.2337/dc26-S005) — and cite the 2025 Section 5 if you want to assert first-appearance.

audit.reason: Rec 5.18 verbatim from PMC11635047: 'Advise adults with diabetes and those at risk for diabetes who consume alcohol to not exceed the recommended daily limits. B Advise abstainers to not start drinking alcohol, even in moderation.' Both the grade and the distinctive 'do not start' clause in whyItMatters are exact. The gating role (this field opening the rest of the alcohol assessment) is a real workflow decision, not data collection.

Two problems. (1) The cut points are not in the cited document. PMC6217805 ('A Review of the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT), AUDIT-C, and USAUDIT for Screening in the United States', Am J Drug Alcohol Abuse 2018) says only 'the authors recommended a cutoff score of 3 points (out of 12)... or a cutoff of 4 points' with no sex differentiation. The >=4 men / >=3 women split is genuinely Bradley 2007 (which reports thresholds maximising sensitivity and specificity of >=4 in men and >=3 in women) but that paper was not retrieved — the citation credits a cut point to a URL that does not state it. (2) Licence: the review carries no copyright or permission statement for the instrument, and AUDIT-C derives from the WHO AUDIT, over which WHO asserts copyright. Widespread reproduction is not a licence.
audit.correction: Cite Bradley KA et al., Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2007;31(7):1208-1217 directly for the sex-specific cut points, and resolve WHO permission before embedding item text. Storing only the score and the positive/negative result is the safe interim, as the submission's own instrument note says.

audit.reason: Rec 5.19 verbatim: 'Educate people with diabetes about the signs, symptoms, and self-management of delayed hypoglycemia after drinking alcohol, especially when using insulin or insulin secretagogues. The importance of monitoring glucose after drinking alcoholic beverages to reduce hypoglycemia risk should be emphasized. B'. Grade and content exact. Unlike the other process booleans in this submission, this one survives the 'does anyone act on it' test: the education IS the intervention ADA specifies, so 'not given' is directly actionable at the same visit rather than a retrospective metric.

Rec 5.35 verbatim: 'Counsel most adults with type 1 diabetes C and type 2 diabetes B to engage in 150 min or more of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week, spread over at least 3 days/week, with no more than 2 consecutive days without activity.' Rec 5.34 confirmed for youth at 60 min/day. Every numeric claim (150, >=3 days, <=2 consecutive days off, 60 min/day youth) is exact, and the B/C split by diabetes type is correctly reported. The argument for a number over a yes/no 'active?' is sound — the target is quantitative, so the field must be.

Rec 5.36 verbatim: 'Counsel adults with type 1 diabetes C and type 2 diabetes B to engage in 2-3 sessions/week of resistance exercise on nonconsecutive days.' Rec 5.39 verbatim: 'Counsel adults and youth treated with weight management pharmacotherapy or metabolic surgery that meeting physical activity recommendations, and in particular muscle-strengthening exercises, may be beneficial for maintaining lean body mass. E'. Both grades correct, and the lean-mass/sarcopenia rationale for the pharmacotherapy and post-surgical group is exactly what 5.39 says.

Rec 5.38 verbatim ends: 'Counsel that prolonged sitting should be interrupted at least every 30 min for blood glucose benefits. C'. Grade C correct and the 30-minute interval is exact. The design argument is also correct and non-obvious: this sits in the same recommendation as the baseline-activity advice but is a separately prescribable target, so a patient meeting 150 min/week can still need it — which a single activity field would hide.

The framing citation is fine and Rec 5.37 is exact ('Recommend flexibility training and balance training 2-3 times/week for older adults with diabetes. C'). But the option list is not in 5.34-5.39. I read all six recommendations in the cited article and none mentions exertional chest pain, active foot ulcer, or fear of hypoglycaemia as barriers or prerequisites to prescribing activity — those safety gates come from the physical-activity narrative and from the complications sections (Section 12 for neuropathy and foot care), not from the recommendations cited. The whyItMatters is a genuine safety decision and the field should stay; the sourcing overstates what 5.34-5.39 say.
audit.correction: Cite 5.37 for balance/flexibility only, and attribute the barrier options to the Section 5 physical-activity narrative plus Section 12 (foot care / neuropathy) rather than to recommendations 5.34-5.39.

audit.reason: Recommendation 5.57 is not in the cited document. PMC12690167 is the Summary of Revisions 2026, and its Section 5 entry mentions only 'Recommendation 5.56 was amended to recommend screening for sleep health in people with diabetes and in those at risk for diabetes' — 5.57 appears nowhere in it, so the claimed 'Rec 5.57 (grade A)' cannot be supported from that URL, and I could not confirm grade A for it anywhere. Separately, 5.56 requires screening for sleep HEALTH; it does not specify duration in hours, so a numeric hours field is MedSync's operationalisation rather than an ADA-specified capture. The underlying rationale (short/irregular sleep as a modifiable target before intensifying drug therapy) is reasonable but is not stated by the recommendation cited.
audit.correction: Point sourceUrl at the 2026 Section 5 primary (doi 10.2337/dc26-S005), verify 5.57's grade there before asserting A, and describe the hours field as an operationalisation of 5.56's sleep-health screen.

audit.reason: Rec 5.56 verbatim: 'Screen for sleep health in people with prediabetes or diabetes and in those at risk for diabetes, including screening for sleep disorders and diabetes-related sleep disruptions. Refer to sleep medicine specialists and/or qualified behavioral health professionals or diabetes care team as indicated. (B)'. Grade B correct, and the recommendation genuinely distinguishes sleep disorders from diabetes-related sleep disruption — which is exactly the split the option list encodes. The differentiated actions in whyItMatters (snoring plus daytime sleepiness -> OSA assessment; nocturia -> treat the hyperglycaemia; nocturnal hypoglycaemia worry -> adjust evening insulin, not sleep hygiene) are three genuinely different decisions from one field.

The instrument half is impeccable and the guideline half is stale. Verified at childrenshealthwatch.org verbatim: 'There is no fee or license required to use the Hunger Vital Sign(TM). We only ask that parties properly cite the tool', with both statements, the either/or positive rule, the Hager 2010 Pediatrics citation and the trademark — so FREE TO USE / EMBEDDABLE is correct, and this is the only scored instrument here that is unambiguously safe to embed. Three attribution defects: (1) the cited article is Section 1 of the 2024 Standards, where Rec 1.5 is 'Assess food insecurity, housing insecurity/homelessness, financial barriers, and social capital/social community support to inform treatment decisions... A' — but in the 2026 Standards that content has moved to Rec 1.7, and 1.5 now reads 'Health systems should adopt a culture of continuous quality improvement...'. Citing '1.5' against the current Standards points at the wrong recommendation. (2) 'Section 4 Rec 4.3' is not in the cited URL at all — that article contains recommendations 1.1-1.7 only. (3) The article does not name the Hunger Vital Sign; it refers to 'a validated two-item screening tool'.
audit.correction: Re-cite as ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 1 Rec 1.7 (doi 10.2337/dc26-S001), drop or separately verify the Section 4 Rec 4.3 claim, and source the tool itself to childrenshealthwatch.org / Hager 2010 rather than to the ADA section.

audit.reason: Both citations are wrong, though the field itself is one of the most important in the set for a Ugandan deployment. (1) The 2024 Rec 1.5 does cover 'housing insecurity/homelessness' at grade A, but in the 2026 Standards that recommendation is renumbered 1.7; 1.5 is now continuous quality improvement by health systems. (2) The claim that 'Section 5 psychosocial screening updated for 2026 to include housing stability' is false. I checked ADA's own 2026 Summary of Revisions: the addition of 'routine screening for food insecurity, housing stability, literacy, and social support' is in Section 14 (Children and Adolescents), not Section 5, and I separately confirmed that no Section 5 recommendation mentions housing stability. The whyItMatters is excellent and genuinely decision-changing — no refrigeration or secure storage changes insulin choice, supply interval and follow-up plan — so fix the citation, do not drop the field.
audit.correction: Cite ADA 2026 Section 1 Rec 1.7 for the SDOH assessment, and either delete the Section 5 claim or re-cite it as Section 14 and scope it to paediatric care.

audit.reason: Same renumbering defect plus a phantom recommendation. The 2024 Rec 1.5 does name 'financial barriers' at grade A, and the 2026 successor Rec 1.7 retains them ('food insecurity, housing insecurity, financial barriers, health insurance and health care access, environmental and neighborhood factors, and social capital/social community support'), so the substance is sound — but '1.5' is the wrong number against the current Standards, and 'Section 4 Rec 4.3 (grade A)' does not exist at the cited URL, which contains only recommendations 1.1-1.7. The clinical argument is the sharpest in the SDOH group: cost-related rationing as a cause of DKA, and the instruction to stop escalating doses that will not be taken, is a genuine reversal of the default response to a rising A1C.
audit.correction: Re-cite to ADA 2026 Section 1 Rec 1.7. Either verify Section 4 Rec 4.3 against the 2026 Section 4 (doi 10.2337/dc26-S004) and quote it, or remove it.

audit.reason: The weakest sourcing in the submission. Neither cited claim survives. (1) There is no numbered Section 1 recommendation on health literacy or numeracy in either year: the 2024 Rec 1.5 covers food insecurity, housing, financial barriers and social capital, and the 2026 Rec 1.7 adds health insurance/access and neighbourhood factors — literacy and numeracy appear in narrative text only. (2) 'Section 5 psychosocial screening updated for 2026 to include literacy' is false; per ADA's own 2026 Summary of Revisions that update is Section 14 (Children and Adolescents). The clinical decisions named are real and unusually concrete — numeracy difficulty ruling out carbohydrate-ratio and sliding-scale dosing in favour of fixed doses with pictorial aids is exactly the kind of decision a Ugandan IM ward needs recorded — so the field earns its place on merit, not on the citations given.
audit.correction: Drop the recommendation-level citations. Cite the Section 1 health-literacy/numeracy narrative (2026, doi 10.2337/dc26-S001) as narrative, or cite Section 14 explicitly for the paediatric literacy screen, and present the numeracy-to-regimen logic as MedSync clinical policy.

audit.reason: Same two defects. The 2024 Rec 1.5 does say 'social capital/social community support' at grade A and the 2026 Rec 1.7 preserves it, so the substance holds — but the number is stale (1.5 is now continuous quality improvement), and the '2026 update adds social support to psychosocial screening' claim belongs to Section 14 (Children and Adolescents), not Section 5. The whyItMatters is sound and links correctly to caregiver_distress_screened: if a caregiver is the primary manager, the DSMES and hypoglycaemia teaching must be aimed at them.
audit.correction: Re-cite to ADA 2026 Section 1 Rec 1.7; remove or re-scope the Section 5 2026 claim to Section 14.

audit.reason: Rec 5.52 verbatim: 'Provide an increased level of support for people with diabetes and serious mental illness through enhanced monitoring of and assistance with diabetes self-management behaviors. (B)'. Grade B correct, and 'enhanced monitoring and additional self-management support' in whyItMatters tracks the recommendation's own wording almost exactly rather than embellishing it. The conclusion that routine intervals and standard education are insufficient follows directly from 'increased level of support'.

The monitoring half is right and the action half is invented. Rec 5.53 verbatim: 'Monitor changes in body weight, glycemia, and lipids in adolescents and adults with diabetes who are prescribed second-generation antipsychotic medications; adjust the treatment plan accordingly, if needed. (C)'. Weight/glycaemia/lipid monitoring and grade C are correct. But 'consideration of changing the antipsychotic agent' is not there — 'adjust the treatment plan accordingly' refers to the diabetes treatment plan, and reading it as authority to switch a psychiatric medication is a meaningful and potentially unsafe misreading for a decision-support tool. Note also 5.53 is specific to SECOND-GENERATION antipsychotics, which the feature's generic boolean loses.
audit.correction: Restate whyItMatters as the monitoring order plus adjustment of the diabetes treatment plan, and drop the antipsychotic-switching claim. Narrow the field to second-generation antipsychotics, or add an agent-class option, to match 5.53's scope.

audit.reason: The recommendations cited say only monitor and refer. Rec 5.54 verbatim: 'Monitor cognitive capacity throughout the life span for all individuals with diabetes, particularly in those who have documented cognitive disabilities, those who experience severe hypoglycemia, very young children, and older adults. (B)'. Rec 5.55 verbatim: 'Consider referral for a formal assessment if cognitive capacity changes or appears to be suboptimal for decision-making and/or behavioral self-management. (E)'. Grades B and E are correct, and the post-severe-hypoglycaemia trigger is genuinely in 5.54. But 'simplify the regimen, relax glycaemic targets to avoid hypoglycaemia, and shift dosing responsibility to a trained caregiver' appears in neither — those actions belong to Section 13 (Older Adults). Every one of them is clinically right; all three are credited to the wrong recommendations.
audit.correction: Cite 5.54/5.55 for the monitoring and formal-assessment trigger only, and cite Section 13 (Older Adults, doi 10.2337/dc26-S013) separately for regimen simplification, target relaxation and caregiver-administered dosing.
